15. Spring Core: IoC Container & Dependency Injection

Every Spring interview eventually becomes a container interview. "What happens when the application starts?", "Why did this bean get a proxy?", "Why does this circular dependency fail?". A candidate who can walk through refresh(), explain where a BeanPostProcessor fits, and reason about the three-level cache can answer almost any "why did Spring do that?" question from first principles. This chapter builds that model; Chapter 16 continues with proxies and Chapter 17 with Boot's auto-configuration.

15.1 IoC vs DI

Inversion of Control is the general principle: a framework calls your code and controls the flow, instead of your code calling a library. Dependency Injection is one form of IoC: an object receives its dependencies instead of creating or finding them. DIP (Chapter 1) is the design principle that makes the injected type an abstraction. They are three different ideas.

Without DI you cannot swap the repository in a test without changing the class. With DI, new ReconService(fakeRepo) is a plain constructor call, and the container also gets a single place to apply cross-cutting behaviour: it can hand out a proxy instead of the bean, and the service never knows.

15.2 BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext

Feature BeanFactory ApplicationContext
Bean creation and DI Yes Yes, by delegating to a DefaultListableBeanFactory
Singleton instantiation Lazy, on first getBean Eager at startup, so errors surface early
BeanPostProcessor registration Manual Automatic
BeanFactoryPostProcessor run Manual Automatic
Events No publishEvent
Environment, profiles, properties No Yes
i18n (MessageSource) and resources No Yes

In a servlet Boot application the concrete class is AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext; in a WebFlux one, such as our api-gateway, it is the reactive equivalent. You only touch BeanFactory directly in framework-level code.

15.3 Container startup: what refresh() really does

SpringApplication.run prepares the Environment, creates the context, then calls AbstractApplicationContext.refresh(). This is the most valuable sequence in Spring to memorise.

refresh()
 1. prepareRefresh                  init property sources, validate required properties
 2. obtainFreshBeanFactory          get the DefaultListableBeanFactory
 3. prepareBeanFactory              class loader, resolvable deps (BeanFactory, ApplicationContext...)
 4. postProcessBeanFactory          subclass hook (web scopes)
 5. invokeBeanFactoryPostProcessors ConfigurationClassPostProcessor runs here: all definitions appear
 6. registerBeanPostProcessors      instantiate BPPs early, sorted by Ordered
 7. initMessageSource
 8. initApplicationEventMulticaster
 9. onRefresh                       Boot creates embedded Tomcat here
10. registerListeners
11. finishBeanFactoryInitialization preInstantiateSingletons: your beans are built here
12. finishRefresh                   lifecycle start, ContextRefreshedEvent, web server start

The key separation: first Spring produces BeanDefinitions, which are metadata (class, scope, constructor args, init method, lazy flag). No application object exists yet. Then it creates objects from them. That is why a BeanFactoryPostProcessor can change a definition before any bean is built, and why auto-configuration can decide "no bean of this type is registered yet".

RefinePoint: PlatformDefaults in ryfn-platform is an EnvironmentPostProcessor, which runs even earlier, before the context exists. It adds shared Kafka settings as the lowest-priority property source (producer acks=all, idempotence, serializers, SASL from KAFKA_* variables), so every service gets them and any service's application.yml or the environment still wins. Understanding that ordering is what makes this trick possible.

15.4 The bean lifecycle

Details that interviewers probe:

  • @PostConstruct runs inside "BPP before init", handled by CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor, so it precedes afterPropertiesSet, which precedes the @Bean(initMethod=...) method.
  • Field injection is itself done by a BPP: AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor.postProcessProperties, during populate.
  • Only some Aware interfaces are direct. BeanNameAware, BeanClassLoaderAware and BeanFactoryAware are invoked by the factory. EnvironmentAware, ApplicationEventPublisherAware and ApplicationContextAware come from ApplicationContextAwareProcessor, a BPP.
  • The proxy appears at step 6. During @PostConstruct, this is the raw target, so a @Transactional method called from @PostConstruct runs without a transaction.
  • Destroy order is the reverse of dependency order: dependents go first, so a bean can still use its dependencies in @PreDestroy.
  • Spring does not call destroy methods for prototypes. It hands them over and forgets them.
  • @Bean infers a destroy method: a public close() or shutdown() is called automatically. Disable it with @Bean(destroyMethod = "").
  • SmartInitializingSingleton.afterSingletonsInstantiated runs after all singletons exist, which is a safe place for "all beans are ready" work.
  • kill -9 runs nothing; SIGTERM triggers the shutdown hook, which closes the context.
@Component
public class DemoBean implements BeanNameAware, InitializingBean, DisposableBean {
    public DemoBean(Dep dep)             { log("1 constructor"); }
    @Autowired void setOther(Other o)    { log("2 populate"); }
    public void setBeanName(String n)    { log("3 aware"); }
    @PostConstruct void pc()             { log("4 @PostConstruct"); }
    public void afterPropertiesSet()     { log("5 afterPropertiesSet"); }
    @PreDestroy void pd()                { log("9a @PreDestroy"); }
    public void destroy()                { log("9b destroy"); }
}

RefinePoint: RunWorker.stop() is a real @PreDestroy with business meaning. On SIGTERM it sets stopping, runs UPDATE recon_runs SET status='QUEUED', instance=NULL ... WHERE instance=? AND status='RUNNING' so another instance picks those runs up immediately, removes itself from run_workers, then shuts its pools down. A hard kill skips all of it, and that is why a heartbeat reaper exists too: it fails runs whose instance has been silent for two minutes. Always design for both paths.

15.5 Constructor, setter and field injection

Constructor Setter Field
Immutability (final) Yes No No
Required dependencies are explicit Yes No No
Object valid after new Yes Not until set No
Testable without Spring new X(mock) Yes Needs reflection
Too many dependencies are visible Painfully, which is good Somewhat Hidden
Detects cycles early Yes, fails at startup No No
Good for Everything by default Optional, re-configurable Tests only 
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor                     // Lombok generates the single constructor
public class PaddleWebhookProcessor {
    private final OrgSubscriptionRepository subscriptionRepo;
    private final PaddleApi paddle;
    private final AuditTrail audit;
}

Since Spring 4.3, a class with a single constructor needs no @Autowired. With several constructors you must mark one, or provide a no-arg one for Spring to use.

// ryfn-expression: three constructors, one for the container
public ExpressionEngine() { this((Supplier<LookupSource>) () -> null); }   // tests and tools
@Autowired public ExpressionEngine(ObjectProvider<LookupSource> lookups) { this((Supplier<LookupSource>) lookups::getIfAvailable); }
public ExpressionEngine(Supplier<LookupSource> lookups) { this.lookups = lookups; }

Trap: Lombok's @RequiredArgsConstructor does not copy @Qualifier or @Value from fields to constructor parameters unless lombok.config has lombok.copyableAnnotations += org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Qualifier. Without it the qualifier is silently ignored. Our EmailSender uses @Value on a non-final field for this reason.

15.6 How @Autowired resolves a dependency

Order: by type, narrowed by @Qualifier, then @Primary, then @Priority, and finally the field or parameter name as the fallback. Spring 6.2, which Boot 3.4 uses, adds @Fallback, the mirror of @Primary: a bean used only if no other candidate exists.

@Bean public ApiKeyAuthenticationFilter apiKeyFilter(ApiKeyVerifier v)         { return new ApiKeyAuthenticationFilter(v, true); }
@Bean public ApiKeyAuthenticationFilter internalApiKeyFilter(ApiKeyVerifier v) { return new ApiKeyAuthenticationFilter(v, false); }

@Bean
FilterRegistrationBean<ApiKeyAuthenticationFilter> reg(@Qualifier("apiKeyFilter") ApiKeyAuthenticationFilter f) { /* ... */ }

That is real code from PlatformSecurityAutoConfiguration: two beans of one type, and an explicit qualifier for each. Its bean also has setEnabled(false), since a Filter bean is auto-registered with the servlet container unless told otherwise.

Optional and multiple dependencies:

public X(Optional<Foo> foo) { }             // absent = Optional.empty()
public X(@Nullable Foo foo) { }             // absent = null
@Autowired(required = false) Foo foo;       // absent = left alone
public X(ObjectProvider<Foo> foo) { }       // deferred: getIfAvailable, getIfUnique, stream
public X(List<Foo> all) { }                 // all beans, in @Order / Ordered order
public X(Map<String, Foo> byName) { }       // bean name -> bean

An injected empty List is not given to you when there are no beans: resolution fails unless the injection is optional or an ObjectProvider is used. @Order affects the order in collections only, not which bean is chosen for a single injection point. Generics are honoured: Repo<Run> will not receive a Repo<Break>.

Trap: the name fallback relies on the parameter name being in the bytecode. Spring 6.1 removed the debug-info (LocalVariableTable) based lookup, so you need -parameters, which spring-boot-starter-parent sets by default. A custom compiler setup can break working injection after an upgrade.

RefinePoint: EmailSender takes ObjectProvider<JavaMailSender> because mail is optional: Boot creates that bean only if spring.mail.host is set. configured() is simply mailSender.getIfAvailable() != null, which is how the "send test" button can report "Email: not configured on this server". Optional would work too, but the provider re-reads on every call and never fails.

15.7 Bean scopes

Scope Instances Destroy callback Notes
singleton (default) One per container per definition Yes Created at startup
prototype New per lookup or injection No Container forgets it
request One per HTTP request Yes Bound to the request thread
session One per HTTP session Yes Serializable if sessions replicate
application One per ServletContext Yes Can span contexts, visible as an attribute
websocket One per WebSocket session Yes STOMP message scope

Injecting a prototype into a singleton

The classic bug: the singleton is built once, so its dependency is resolved once. You get the same "prototype" forever.

// 1. ObjectProvider: the recommended approach
@Service @RequiredArgsConstructor
class Exporter {
    private final ObjectProvider<CsvBuffer> buffers;
    void export() { CsvBuffer b = buffers.getObject(); /* a new one each call */ }
}

// 2. @Lookup: the container generates a CGLIB subclass that overrides this method
@Service abstract class Exporter2 {
    @Lookup abstract CsvBuffer newBuffer();
}

// 3. Scoped proxy: the injected object is a proxy that resolves per call
@Component @Scope(value = "prototype", proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)
class CsvBuffer { }
Option Good for Watch out
ObjectProvider Default choice, explicit Spring API in your class; jakarta.inject.Provider is the neutral form
@Lookup Keeping the class free of Spring API calls Needs a subclassable class, and it doesn't apply on @Bean-created beans
Scoped proxy Request and session beans With a prototype each method call gets a new instance, which surprises people

A request-scoped bean in a singleton needs a proxy, which is why @RequestScope sets proxyMode = TARGET_CLASS for you. The proxy looks up the current request through RequestContextHolder, a ThreadLocal. On an @Async thread it fails with "No thread-bound request found".

RefinePoint: we use no custom scopes at all, and that is a defensible design. Everything is a singleton. Request data is passed as method parameters, or read from RequestContextHolder at one controlled point: AuditTrail.currentRequest() checks instanceof ServletRequestAttributes and returns null otherwise, so the same audit call works in a controller, in a scheduled job and in a Kafka listener.

15.8 Circular dependencies and the three-level cache

DefaultSingletonBeanRegistry holds three maps:

Level Map Holds
1 singletonObjects Fully initialised beans
2 earlySingletonObjects Early references already handed to someone: not yet fully initialised
3 singletonFactories ObjectFactory lambdas that produce an early reference on demand

Why three levels, not two? The early reference might have to be a proxy. If B injected the raw A while A later got wrapped at step 6, B would hold the wrong object. The factory at level 3 calls getEarlyBeanReference, letting AbstractAutoProxyCreator make the proxy early, but only if a cycle actually occurs; otherwise the normal after-init path runs. Level 2 stores the result so every other bean in the cycle gets the same object.

Why constructor cycles fail: an early reference needs an instance to exist. In new A(new B(new A(...))) no instance exists at the time, so Spring throws BeanCurrentlyInCreationException. Setter and field injection work because the object exists after its no-arg constructor has run. Prototype cycles always fail, since they aren't cached.

Boot 2.6+ prohibits all cycles by default (spring.main.allow-circular-references=false), so even field-injected cycles fail on startup with a report drawing the loop. You can turn it back on, but that treats a design smell as a config problem.

How to fix one, in order of preference:

  1. Redesign. Extract the shared logic into a third bean; cycles usually mean mixed responsibilities.
  2. Use an event when one side only needs to notify the other.
  3. ObjectProvider resolves the dependency on use, so construction has no cycle.
  4. @Lazy on the constructor parameter injects a lazy-resolving proxy.

RefinePoint: we have a real example. In lookup-service RuleFunctionService depends on LocalFunctionSource to forget cached definitions when one changes, and LocalFunctionSource must call back to RuleFunctionService to read definitions. That is a cycle, and LocalFunctionSource breaks it with ObjectProvider<RuleFunctionService>, calling functions.getObject().definitions(org) on use. No setting was changed, both classes keep constructor injection, and the dependency is visible right in the signature.

Trap: with allow-circular-references=true and @Async on a bean in a cycle, startup fails with "has been injected into other beans in its raw version". AsyncAnnotationBeanPostProcessor wraps at step 6 without supporting early references, so the raw early reference and the final proxy differ. @Transactional does not have this problem because its auto-proxy creator supports getEarlyBeanReference.

15.9 @Component, @Bean, @Configuration

@Component family @Bean
Declared on Class Method in a config class
Discovery Component scanning Reading the configuration class
Control over creation Container calls the constructor You write the code
Third-party classes No, cannot annotate Yes
Conditional wiring On class On method, more fine-grained
Multiple beans of one class Not directly Yes

Stereotypes: @Component is the base. @Service adds only meaning. @Repository adds exception translation (PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor converts to DataAccessException). @Controller and @RestController make a class a handler for RequestMappingHandlerMapping. @Configuration is a meta-annotated @Component with bean-method handling.

Scanning: ClassPathBeanDefinitionScanner reads class files with ASM, without loading the classes, and creates definitions. Boot scans from the package of the @SpringBootApplication class downward. Default bean name is the decapitalised simple class name. Two beans with one name fail in Boot, since spring.main.allow-bean-definition-overriding defaults to false.

@Configuration full mode vs lite mode

@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    @Bean DataSource dataSource() { return new HikariDataSource(); }
    @Bean JdbcTemplate jdbc() { return new JdbcTemplate(dataSource()); }   // returns the singleton: CGLIB intercepts
}

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
public class LiteConfig {
    @Bean DataSource dataSource() { return new HikariDataSource(); }
    @Bean JdbcTemplate jdbc(DataSource ds) { return new JdbcTemplate(ds); } // inject as a parameter, always correct
}

Full mode needs the class to be non-final and its @Bean methods non-private, non-final. Lite mode is faster to start and is what Boot's own auto-configurations use (@AutoConfiguration is proxyBeanMethods = false). If you always declare dependencies as method parameters, it is also safe. Our PlatformEventsAutoConfiguration is written like this: each @Bean method takes its dependencies as parameters.

Trap: @Bean methods returning a BeanFactoryPostProcessor must be static. Otherwise creating that bean forces the configuration class to be instantiated very early, before BPPs are registered, so @Autowired and @Value inside that config break, with a warning in the log.

15.10 @Conditional, profiles, Environment

@Conditional takes a Condition that is evaluated while definitions are registered. Boot's versions are built on it:

Annotation Registers the bean when
@ConditionalOnProperty A property has the value
@ConditionalOnClass A class is on the class path
@ConditionalOnMissingBean No bean of that type is defined yet
@ConditionalOnBean A bean of that type is defined
@ConditionalOnWebApplication Running as a web app
@Profile A profile is active (it is itself @Conditional(ProfileCondition.class)) 
// ryfn-platform's PlatformEventsAutoConfiguration
@Bean @ConditionalOnMissingBean
public AuditTrail auditTrail(EventPublisher events) { return new AuditTrail(events); }

@Bean @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "rp.kafka.enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)
public OutboxRelay outboxRelay(EventStore store, KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka, TopicNames topics, TransactionTemplate tx) { ... }

@ConditionalOnMissingBean lets a service override any platform default by defining its own bean. It depends on ordering, so it is only reliable in auto-configurations, which are processed after user configuration (DeferredImportSelector).

RefinePoint: we use no @Profile in Java code. Behaviour differs per environment through properties, not by naming environments: rp.kafka.enabled=false in tests lets events wait in the outbox, and ai.digest.enabled turns the DigestScheduler on. A property answers "what does this environment do?", which stays true when someone adds a fourth environment. Profile-coded logic tends to rot.

Environment and property sources

Environment is a chain of PropertySources searched in order, with first match winning.

Highest priority (Boot)
  1. Test properties (@SpringBootTest, @TestPropertySource)
  2. Command-line arguments             --server.port=9000
  3. SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON
  4. Servlet parameters
  5. JNDI
  6. Java system properties             -Dserver.port=9000
  7. OS environment variables           SERVER_PORT=9000
  8. random.* values
  9. Profile-specific files, outside the jar then inside
 10. application.yml, outside the jar then inside
 11. @PropertySource on @Configuration
 12. SpringApplication.setDefaultProperties, and sources added last
Lowest priority

Our PlatformDefaults adds its source at the end of the chain, which is why a service's application.yml overrides it.

@Value vs @ConfigurationProperties

@Value @ConfigurationProperties
Binding One value A typed tree
Relaxed binding (max-size, MAX_SIZE) Limited Full
Validation No @Validated with JSR-380
SpEL #{...} No
IDE metadata No Yes, with the processor
Immutable With constructor Records, constructor binding
Lists and maps Awkward Natural
Best for One or two values Anything grouped 
// Real: ryfn-platform, every service shares this under rp.*
@Getter @Setter
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "rp")
public class PlatformProperties {
    private String internalToken = "";
    private Map<String, String> services = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    private Duration cacheTtl = Duration.ofSeconds(30);      // "30s" in YAML binds to Duration
}

// The modern immutable form
@ConfigurationProperties("export") @Validated
public record ExportProps(@Min(1) int workers, @NotNull Duration timeout) {}

Register them with @EnableConfigurationProperties or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan. AiConfig does the first for AiProperties.

15.11 Application events

Kind When it runs Thread Exception effect
@EventListener During publishEvent Publisher's Propagates, can roll back
@EventListener + @Async Queued Executor Goes to the AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler
@TransactionalEventListener Transaction phase, default AFTER_COMMIT Publisher's Cannot undo the commit
Both @Async and @TransactionalEventListener After commit, queued Executor Isolated

The phases are BEFORE_COMMIT, AFTER_COMMIT, AFTER_ROLLBACK, AFTER_COMPLETION.

Key mechanics:

  • EventListenerMethodProcessor finds @EventListener methods and wraps each in an ApplicationListenerMethodAdapter.
  • The default SimpleApplicationEventMulticaster is synchronous. Use a custom executor on it only with care, since every listener becomes asynchronous.
  • If no transaction is active, a @TransactionalEventListener is dropped, unless fallbackExecution = true.
  • Writing inside AFTER_COMMIT: the old transaction has committed, and its resources are still bound, so a plain save will not be committed. Use REQUIRES_NEW or @Async. Since Spring 6.1 a @Transactional on such a listener must be REQUIRES_NEW or NOT_SUPPORTED; otherwise startup fails.
  • @EventListener can have a condition (condition = "#e.orgId != null") and can return a new event to publish.

RefinePoint: NotificationService.onAlertRaised combines @Async with @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT, fallbackExecution = true). It runs only after the alert is really committed, on another thread, so a slow SMTP server never holds a transaction, and a failing webhook never affects the save. fallbackExecution = true is there because an alert may also be raised outside any transaction. RunWorker.onQueued uses the same listener to wake the poller, so the poll sees the committed row and picks up a new run at once, rather than waiting for the next scheduled tick.

15.12 FactoryBean, BeanPostProcessor, lazy init, thread safety

FactoryBean

A bean that produces another bean. getBean("x") returns the product, getBean("&x") the factory itself. It is how complex setups plug into the container: LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean, JpaRepositoryFactoryBean (creates your Spring Data repository proxy), ProxyFactoryBean.

FactoryBean vs BeanFactory: BeanFactory is the container. A FactoryBean is one bean in it, which makes a product.

BeanFactoryPostProcessor vs BeanPostProcessor

BeanFactoryPostProcessor BeanPostProcessor
Works on Definitions, before beans exist Instances, one by one
Runs Once, at refresh step 5 For every bean, around init
Examples ConfigurationClassPostProcessor, PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor, CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor, AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator, AsyncAnnotationBeanPostProcessor, ScheduledAnnotationBeanPostProcessor, ConfigurationPropertiesBindingPostProcessor 
@Component
public class SlowInitDetector implements BeanPostProcessor, PriorityOrdered {
    private final Map<String, Long> started = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    @Override public Object postProcessBeforeInitialization(Object bean, String name) {
        started.put(name, System.nanoTime());
        return bean;
    }
    @Override public Object postProcessAfterInitialization(Object bean, String name) {
        Long t = started.remove(name);
        if (t != null && System.nanoTime() - t > 1_000_000_000L) log.warn("Slow init: {}", name);
        return bean;                                 // returning a different object replaces the bean
    }
    @Override public int getOrder() { return Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE; }
}

Trap: a BeanPostProcessor is created early. Anything it injects is built before other BPPs are ready, so those dependencies miss AOP and more. Look for the log line "is not eligible for getting processed by all BeanPostProcessors". Keep BPPs dependency-free, and take an ObjectProvider if you need one.

Lazy initialisation

@Lazy on a bean defers creation to first use; on an injection point it injects a proxy. spring.main.lazy-initialization=true applies it globally. Faster startup, but config errors surface at the first request, and the first request is slow. So use it in development or for rarely used heavy beans, and not broadly in production. Our services use it nowhere.

Are Spring singletons thread-safe?

Not automatically. Spring guarantees one instance and safe publication, but one instance serves all threads. Thread safety depends on the state you put in it. Stateless services with final dependencies are safe. Any mutable field needs a thread-safe type.

// Bug: one SimpleDateFormat, not thread-safe, shared across request threads
@Service class Bad { private final SimpleDateFormat f = new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd"); }

// Bug: per-request data in a singleton field
@Service class AlsoBad { private UUID currentOrg; }

RefinePoint: RunWorker is a singleton with real mutable state, and each field shows the right tool: private volatile boolean stopping, AtomicBoolean polling (CAS guard so only one poll runs at a time), Set<UUID> working = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(), and final executor pools. RateLimitFilter holds its buckets in a ConcurrentHashMap. That is a good answer to "have you ever had state in a singleton?".

15.13 Interview questions and answers

Q1. What is IoC, and how does it differ from DI?

IoC means a framework controls the flow and calls your code. DI is one form of it, where dependencies are given to an object rather than created or located by it. Event callbacks and template methods are IoC without DI.

Q2. What is a Spring bean?

An object that is instantiated, wired and managed by the container from a BeanDefinition. An object you new yourself is not a bean, so it receives no injection, proxying or lifecycle callbacks.

Q3. BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext?

BeanFactory is the core: definitions, lazy getBean, DI. ApplicationContext extends it with eager singleton creation, automatic post-processor registration, events, Environment and i18n. A context delegates bean work to an internal DefaultListableBeanFactory.

Q4. Walk me through what happens when a Spring Boot app starts.

SpringApplication.run prepares the Environment, running EnvironmentPostProcessors, and creates the context. refresh() then runs ConfigurationClassPostProcessor, which scans and reads @Bean, @Import and auto-configurations to produce definitions. It registers BeanPostProcessors, creates the embedded server in onRefresh, instantiates all non-lazy singletons, starts lifecycle beans, publishes ContextRefreshedEvent and opens the port. CommandLineRunners run, and ApplicationReadyEvent fires.

Q5. What is a BeanDefinition?

Metadata describing how to build a bean: class or factory method, scope, constructor and property values, lazy flag, primary flag, init and destroy methods, dependencies. It is what makes conditional registration and post-processing possible, since definitions exist before objects.

Q6. Give the full bean lifecycle.

Instantiate → populate (@Autowired) → BeanNameAware, BeanClassLoaderAware, BeanFactoryAware → BPP before-init (ApplicationContextAware, @PostConstruct) → afterPropertiesSet → custom init → BPP after-init (AOP proxy) → in use → @PreDestroy → DisposableBean.destroy → custom destroy.

Q7. Order of @PostConstruct, afterPropertiesSet and initMethod?

@PostConstruct first, as it is run by a BPP before init; then afterPropertiesSet; then the initMethod. If all three name the same method, it runs once.

Q8. Can I use injected dependencies in a constructor? In @PostConstruct?

With constructor injection, yes: those dependencies are parameters. Field-injected values are still null in the constructor. In @PostConstruct all of them are set. But proxies aren't applied yet, so @Transactional on a self-call doesn't apply.

Q9. How do you run code after the app has fully started?

ApplicationRunner or CommandLineRunner, or listen to ApplicationReadyEvent. Use SmartInitializingSingleton for "all singletons exist" work, and SmartLifecycle for start and stop with ordered phases. For a transactional startup task, avoid @PostConstruct.

Q10. ContextRefreshedEvent vs ApplicationReadyEvent?

ContextRefreshedEvent is a Spring event on each refresh, and it can fire more than once with child contexts. ApplicationReadyEvent is Boot's, fired once after runners complete, when the app is ready for traffic. Prefer the latter.

Q11. Why is constructor injection recommended?

Dependencies can be final, the object is valid once constructed, tests can call new, required dependencies are visible, an overlong parameter list exposes a design smell, and cycles fail fast. Field injection hides all of these and needs reflection in tests.

Q12. When would you use setter injection?

For a genuinely optional dependency with a sensible default, or one re-assignable after creation. It's also how a few older frameworks must be configured. It's rare in modern code.

Q13. Is @Autowired required on a constructor?

Not if the class has one constructor (Spring 4.3+). With several, annotate one, or Spring looks for a no-arg constructor and fails if there is none. Our ExpressionEngine has three constructors, with @Autowired on the ObjectProvider one.

Q14. How does Spring resolve when two beans match a type?

Filter by @Qualifier, then pick @Primary, then highest @Priority, then a bean whose name matches the field or parameter name. Otherwise NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. In 6.2 @Fallback beans are considered only if no regular bean qualifies.

Q15. @Primary vs @Qualifier?

@Primary sets a default at the definition. @Qualifier is an explicit choice at the injection point, and it wins over @Primary. Use @Primary when one bean is usually right, such as in tests, and @Qualifier when callers genuinely differ.

Q16. How do you create a custom qualifier?

Define an annotation meta-annotated with @Qualifier, such as @ReadOnly, and put it on both bean and injection point. It's type-safe and avoids string names.

Q17. How do you inject all implementations of an interface?

List<T> in @Order order or Map<String, T> by bean name. Useful for strategy dispatch. For zero-or-more semantics use ObjectProvider<T>.stream(), as a plain List fails when there are none.

Q18. Does @Order affect which bean is injected?

No, it affects only collection order, and things like filter and aspect order. To choose a single bean use @Primary or @Qualifier.

Q19. ObjectProvider vs Optional vs @Autowired(required=false)?

Optional and required=false resolve once at injection. ObjectProvider resolves on each call, supports getIfAvailable, getIfUnique, stream, and defers creation, so it also handles cycles and prototypes. It's the most flexible.

Q20. What are the bean scopes?

Singleton, prototype, request, session, application, websocket, plus custom ones via Scope and registerScope. Web scopes need a web-aware context.

Q21. How does Spring handle a prototype bean's destruction?

It doesn't. After creating and initialising it, the container keeps no reference, so @PreDestroy never runs. The caller must clean up, or use a custom BPP to track them.

Q22. Inject a prototype into a singleton. What happens? How do you fix it?

It's resolved once when the singleton is built, so it stays one instance. Fix with ObjectProvider.getObject(), @Lookup, or a scoped proxy. Injecting the ApplicationContext also works but it's service locator style.

Q23. How does @Lookup work?

The container generates a CGLIB subclass overriding the method to call getBean. So the class must be non-final, and it doesn't work for beans from @Bean factory methods, because the container doesn't control their instantiation.

Q24. Singleton scope vs application scope?

Singleton is per ApplicationContext; application is per ServletContext, can be shared across contexts in one web app, and is exposed as a servlet attribute. With a single Boot context they behave nearly the same.

Q25. What is a scoped proxy?

A proxy bean of the same type injected in place of the short-lived bean. Each method call resolves the actual target from the current scope. Needed because a singleton gets wired once while the request bean doesn't exist at startup. @RequestScope and @SessionScope set it up by default.

Q26. Why does a request-scoped bean fail in an @Async method?

Request attributes live in a ThreadLocal on the request thread. The async thread has none, hence "No thread-bound request found". Pass values explicitly as parameters, or use a TaskDecorator that copies the attributes, while remembering the request may finish first.

Q27. How does Spring resolve circular dependencies?

For singleton field or setter injection, A is instantiated and a factory for its early reference is placed in singletonFactories. When B needs A it gets that early reference and finishes; then A finishes. The three caches keep this consistent. Boot 2.6+ disallows this by default.

Q28. Why three caches? Wouldn't two do?

Two would suffice with no proxies. Level 3 allows lazy creation of an early proxy via getEarlyBeanReference only when a cycle actually occurs, so non-cyclic beans still get proxied at the normal stage. Level 2 ensures all beans in the cycle get the same early object.

Q29. Why do constructor cycles fail?

Early exposure requires an instance. Each constructor needs the other's finished instance, so no object can exist first, hence BeanCurrentlyInCreationException. @Lazy on one parameter breaks it by injecting a proxy.

Q30. How did you deal with a circular dependency in your project?

"RuleFunctionService calls LocalFunctionSource to forget cached definitions, while LocalFunctionSource reads definitions from RuleFunctionService. I kept constructor injection on both and gave the source an ObjectProvider<RuleFunctionService>, resolved at use. Startup has no cycle, and no global setting changed."

Q31. @Component vs @Bean?

@Component goes on your class and is found through scanning. @Bean goes on a factory method and is used for third-party classes, conditional or multiple instances, or construction logic. AiConfig uses @Bean because it chooses which LlmClient to return.

Q32. @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller: any real difference?

All are components. @Repository adds exception translation; @Controller makes it a web handler. @Service carries only intent, though aspects can target it.

Q33. What does @Configuration do that @Component with @Bean doesn't?

It's enhanced by CGLIB, so an inter-bean call returns the container's singleton. In a @Component a @Bean method call is a plain Java call that creates another object, so a second, unmanaged instance appears.

Q34. What is proxyBeanMethods = false, and when use it?

It turns off CGLIB enhancement, giving lite mode: faster startup, less memory, compatible with native images. Use it whenever bean methods take dependencies as parameters and don't call each other. It's what auto-configurations do.

Q35. Why must a BeanFactoryPostProcessor @Bean method be static?

So the container can call it without creating the config instance. A non-static one forces the config class to be created during step 5, before BPPs exist, breaking its @Autowired and @Value.

Q36. BeanPostProcessor vs BeanFactoryPostProcessor?

BFPP edits definitions before instantiation; BPP handles instances around initialisation and may replace them. @Value placeholders in definitions are resolved through PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer, a BFPP, and @Autowired is executed by a BPP.

Q37. Why might a bean not get proxied though it has @Transactional?

It may be created too early, as a dependency of a BPP or BFPP ("not eligible for getting processed by all BeanPostProcessors"). Other causes: it isn't a Spring bean, or the call is a self-invocation. Check with AopUtils.isAopProxy(bean).

Q38. What is FactoryBean? How do you get the factory itself?

A bean that creates another object, exposed under the factory's name. Prefix with &: ctx.getBean("&myFactory"). Spring Data repositories are built by JpaRepositoryFactoryBean.

Q39. How does component scanning work, and what if my class is outside the base package?

ASM reads class metadata in the base packages without loading classes, filters by annotation, and registers definitions. Classes outside aren't found. Widen with scanBasePackages, use @Import, or better for libraries, register an auto-configuration in META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports, as ryfn-platform does.

Q40. How do profiles work?

spring.profiles.active activates them. @Profile filters definitions, and application-{profile}.yml adds property sources. Use profile groups for bundles. Keep logic out of them and use feature properties to describe behaviour; we use no @Profile in our Java code.

Q41. What is the order of property sources? Give examples.

Command line > SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON > system properties > OS environment > external profile file > packaged profile file > external application.yml > packaged one > @PropertySource > defaults. So SERVER_PORT=9000 in the environment overrides the packaged YAML, and --server.port beats both.

Q42. Why can a @Value be null or the literal ${x}?

Null: the object was created with new, or read in a constructor under field injection. A literal ${x}: no PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer is active (Boot adds it), or a non-static BFPP disturbed it. A missing key without a default fails startup: ${x:default} fixes that.

Q43. @Value vs @ConfigurationProperties?

@Value is for one or two values and supports SpEL. @ConfigurationProperties gives typed, validated, relaxed-bound groups with IDE metadata. Use records for immutability. Ours are PlatformProperties for rp.* and AiProperties for ai.*.

Q44. How does relaxed binding work, and where does it fail?

app.max-size, app.maxSize, APP_MAXSIZE and app.max_size all bind to maxSize. @ConfigurationProperties is fully relaxed. @Value needs the canonical kebab-case form in the placeholder to benefit from any relaxed matching at all.

Q45. Default event listener behaviour: sync or async?

Synchronous, on the publisher's thread and inside its transaction. An exception propagates to the publisher. Add @Async per listener, or configure a task executor on the multicaster for all of them.

Q46. @EventListener vs @TransactionalEventListener?

The first runs immediately and joins the transaction. The second is held as a TransactionSynchronization and runs at a phase, by default after commit. So it sees committed data and won't act on rolled-back work. Without a transaction it's dropped unless fallbackExecution = true.

Q47. Why might a @TransactionalEventListener not fire, or its writes not be saved?

Not fired: no active transaction, the transaction rolled back (for AFTER_COMMIT), or publishEvent was on another thread. Not saved: after commit the old transaction is finished, so writes need REQUIRES_NEW. Since 6.1 a plain @Transactional on it fails at startup.

Q48. How is an in-process event different from the outbox?

An in-process event dies with the JVM: AFTER_COMMIT listeners aren't called if the instance crashes right after commit. The outbox stores the event in the same transaction, so it survives. We use @TransactionalEventListener for local, losable side effects such as waking the poller (the scheduled poll catches anything missed), and the outbox for events that must arrive.

Q49. Are singleton beans thread-safe?

Not inherently. Creation is safe, but one instance serves all threads, so mutable fields need a thread-safe approach. Keep services stateless; where state is required use volatile, atomics, or concurrent collections, like RunWorker.

Q50. Does @Lazy speed up startup? What are the downsides?

Yes, but errors appear at first use, and the first request is slow. Probes may report healthy although a broken bean exists. Use it on selected heavy beans, or in local development.

Q51. How can I detect or debug bean wiring problems?

Read Boot's FailureAnalyzer report. Use /actuator/beans for the graph, /actuator/conditions for why auto-configs did or didn't apply, and --debug. logging.level.org.springframework.beans=DEBUG shows creation, and ApplicationStartup with BufferingApplicationStartup shows slow beans.

Q52. How do you speed up slow context startup?

Measure first using /actuator/startup. Exclude unused auto-configurations, narrow scanning, avoid I/O in @PostConstruct, and defer heavy work. Spring 6.2 offers @Bean(bootstrap = BACKGROUND) for parallel initialisation, CDS archives help, and AOT and native images are the extreme.

Q53. Can two contexts share beans? What is a parent context?

A child context sees its parent's beans, not the reverse. Old web apps had a root context plus a servlet context; Boot usually has one. Spring Cloud's bootstrap context and management-port child contexts still use the idea. BPPs and AOP don't cross contexts.

Q54. Why is ctx.getBean() in business code bad?

It's service locator: hidden dependencies, runtime failures, harder tests. Acceptable in framework-level code, bootstrap, or factories when the bean type is decided at runtime, and ObjectProvider or a Map injection usually does better.

Q55. How do you override a bean from a shared library?

Define a bean of that type in your service. If the library's auto-configuration has @ConditionalOnMissingBean, it backs off, as with AuditTrail, EventStore and EventPublisher in ryfn-platform. Without that condition you get a name clash or NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException, so library authors should always use it.

Q56. Design question: how would you build a plug-in point with Spring?

Define an interface, inject List<Plugin> or ObjectProvider<Plugin>, and have each plug-in be a bean. Library plug-ins register through auto-configuration, with @ConditionalOnMissingBean defaults. For dropping jars in at runtime Spring isn't enough: we use ServiceLoader in Plugins.load and pass the results into beans.

Q57. A bean's @PreDestroy doesn't run in Kubernetes. Why?

The pod got SIGKILL: terminationGracePeriodSeconds expired, the OOM killer struck, or the process wasn't PID 1 and SIGTERM never reached it (a shell-form ENTRYPOINT). Set server.shutdown=graceful, an adequate grace period, and exec-form entrypoints. And always design for the crash path too, like our heartbeat reaper.

Q58. Tricky: two @Bean methods have the same name in two config classes. What happens?

Boot fails with BeanDefinitionOverrideException, since overriding is off by default. In plain Spring, or with spring.main.allow-bean-definition-overriding=true, the later silently replaces the earlier, which is a nasty, order-dependent bug.

16. Spring AOP, Proxies & How @Transactional Really Works

More production bugs come from misunderstood proxies than from any other part of Spring. Typical ones: a @Transactional method that never opened a transaction, an @Async method that ran on the caller's thread, a @Cacheable that never cached, a checked exception that committed half a payment. Each is explained by one sentence: the annotation is implemented by a proxy, and only calls that go through the proxy get the behaviour. This chapter makes that sentence concrete: how the proxy is created, what runs inside it, and every way to accidentally bypass it.

16.1 AOP terminology

Aspect-Oriented Programming modularises cross-cutting concerns: logic needed in many places that is not the business purpose of any of them, such as transactions, security, auditing, metrics, retries and caching.

Term Meaning Example
Aspect A module holding a cross-cutting concern TimingAspect class
Join point A point in execution where advice can run. In Spring AOP: only method execution on a bean ExportService.export(..) being called
Pointcut A predicate selecting join points execution(* com.ryfnflow..service.*.*(..))
Advice The code to run at the join point, and when @Around, @Before, ...
Advisor Spring's pairing of one pointcut with one advice BeanFactoryTransactionAttributeSourceAdvisor
Target The original object being advised Your JournalService instance
Proxy The object created to apply advice; callers hold this JournalService$$SpringCGLIB$$0
Weaving Linking aspects with targets Spring: at runtime, by proxy creation
Introduction Adding an interface to an advised object @DeclareParents (rare)

Advice types

Advice Can stop the call? Can change arguments or result? Use
@Before Only by throwing No Validation, access checks
@AfterReturning No Can read the result; changing a mutable result works but is bad form Audit on success
@AfterThrowing No, cannot swallow Can rethrow a different exception Exception translation, alerting
@After No No Cleanup, like finally
@Around Yes (don't call proceed) Yes Transactions, timing, retry, caching

Use the weakest advice that does the job: an @Around that forgets to call proceed() or forgets to return its result silently breaks the method.

16.2 Spring AOP vs AspectJ

Spring AOP AspectJ
Mechanism Runtime proxies (JDK or CGLIB) Bytecode weaving
When At bean creation Compile time (ajc), post-compile, or load time (LTW, a Java agent)
Join points Public (and with CGLIB, protected/package) method execution on Spring beans Method call and execution, constructors, field get/set, static initialisers, any object
Self-invocation advised No Yes, the code itself is modified
Objects created with new No Yes
Final or private methods No Yes
Performance One proxy hop plus an interceptor chain per call Near zero, inlined into the code
Setup None: spring-boot-starter-aop Compiler plugin or -javaagent
Syntax Uses AspectJ's annotations and pointcut language Full AspectJ language

Spring AOP borrows AspectJ's annotations and pointcut parser (aspectjweaver), but weaving is pure Spring proxies. That's why @Aspect works without the AspectJ compiler. You can switch transactions to AspectJ mode with @EnableTransactionManagement(mode = AdviceMode.ASPECTJ), which solves self-invocation, at the cost of build or agent setup. Few teams need it.

16.3 JDK dynamic proxy vs CGLIB

JDK dynamic proxy CGLIB proxy
How java.lang.reflect.Proxy creates a class implementing the bean's interfaces Generates a subclass of the bean's class
Requires At least one interface Non-final class; a constructor Spring can call (Objenesis usually bypasses it)
Inject by concrete class Fails: proxy is only the interface type Works
Advises Interface methods only Any non-final, non-private, non-static method
getClass() jdk.proxy2.$Proxy87 JournalService$$SpringCGLIB$$0
Default in Spring Framework When interfaces exist When no interfaces exist
Default in Spring Boot Only if spring.aop.proxy-target-class=false Always (proxy-target-class=true since Boot 2.0)

Why Boot made CGLIB the default: with JDK proxies, injecting JournalService (the class) instead of JournalOps (the interface) failed with BeanNotOfRequiredTypeException, a constant source of confusion. Since Spring 4, CGLIB is repackaged inside spring-core (org.springframework.cglib), and Objenesis creates the proxy instance without calling your constructor, so the old "constructor runs twice" problem is gone.

// What a JDK proxy does, by hand
JournalOps proxy = (JournalOps) Proxy.newProxyInstance(
    JournalOps.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{ JournalOps.class },
    (p, method, args) -> {
        long t = System.nanoTime();
        try { return method.invoke(target, args); }                 // delegate to the real object
        catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); } // unwrap
        finally { log.info("{} took {} µs", method.getName(), (System.nanoTime() - t) / 1000); }
    });

Important structural fact: a Spring CGLIB proxy is a subclass, but it does not use super.post(). It holds a reference to a separate, fully initialised target instance and delegates to it. The proxy's own fields (inherited from your class) are never initialised and stay null/zero. Consequences come up below: field access through the proxy, final methods, and this inside the target.

16.4 How the proxy gets created

Key points:

  • AbstractAutoProxyCreator is a BeanPostProcessor. Boot registers AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator (via AopAutoConfiguration) which collects all Advisor beans: your @Aspects (each advice method becomes an advisor) plus infrastructure advisors for transactions, caching, method security.
  • One proxy per bean, however many concerns. A bean that is @Transactional and has @PreAuthorize gets one proxy whose interceptor chain contains both interceptors.
  • Not all proxies come from the auto-proxy creator. @Async uses AsyncAnnotationBeanPostProcessor, and @Validated uses MethodValidationPostProcessor. If the bean is already a proxy, these add their advisor to the existing proxy rather than wrapping it again.
  • The decision is per bean, the matching is per method. At call time, the proxy looks up (and caches) the interceptor chain for that Method. Methods with no matching advisor go straight to the target.

16.5 What happens inside the proxy on each call

The chain is a ReflectiveMethodInvocation. Each interceptor receives the invocation and calls invocation.proceed(), which moves an index to the next interceptor, and finally reflectively calls the target. This is the Chain of Responsibility pattern: any interceptor can stop the call (security throws AccessDeniedException), and each sees the result on the way out.

Advice ordering

  • Between aspects: @Order or Ordered on the aspect class. Lower value = higher precedence = outermost (runs first on the way in, last on the way out).
  • Infrastructure order: @EnableTransactionManagement(order = ...), @EnableCaching(order = ...). Both default to Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE, so their relative order is undefined unless you set it.
  • Inside one aspect, advice types run in a fixed order since Spring 5.2.7: @Around, @Before, then after the method @AfterReturning/@AfterThrowing, @After, then @Around completes. Two advices of the same type in one aspect have no guaranteed order — split them into two aspects with @Order.
  • Method security (@EnableMethodSecurity) uses fixed ordered interceptors, with @PreAuthorize before the transaction interceptor, so a denied call never opens a transaction.

Why ordering matters: a retry aspect must be outside the transaction aspect. If it's inside, every retry runs in the same (already rollback-only, or with a stale persistence context) transaction. If it's outside, each attempt gets a fresh transaction.

@Aspect @Component @Order(1)          // outermost
class RetryAspect { /* ... */ }
// @EnableTransactionManagement(order = 100)  → transaction inside the retry

16.6 Pointcut expressions

Designator Matches Example
execution Method signature execution(public * com.ryfnflow..*Service.*(..))
within All methods of types in a package or type within(com.ryfnflow.crm.journal..*)
@annotation Methods carrying an annotation @annotation(com.ryfnflow.Timed)
@within Methods of types carrying an annotation @within(org.springframework.stereotype.Service)
args Runtime argument types args(java.util.UUID, ..)
@args Runtime argument's type has an annotation @args(com.x.Sensitive)
this Proxy is an instance of type this(com.x.Auditable)
target Target is an instance of type target(com.x.JournalService)
bean Spring bean name (Spring-only) bean(*Service)

execution syntax: execution(modifiers? return-type declaring-type? name(params) throws?)

execution(* *(..))                               any method
execution(* com.ryfnflow..service.*.*(..))       any method of any class in any 'service' package below com.ryfnflow
execution(* *..JournalService.post(java.util.UUID, ..))   first parameter UUID, then anything
execution(java.util.List *.find*(*))             returns List, name starts with find, exactly one parameter
..  in a package = any sub-package;   ..  in parameters = zero or more arguments;   *  = exactly one

Combine with &&, ||, !, and name reusable pointcuts:

@Aspect @Component
class Pointcuts {
    @Pointcut("within(com.ryfnflow.crm..*)") void ours() {}
    @Pointcut("@within(org.springframework.stereotype.Service)") void services() {}
    @Pointcut("ours() && services() && execution(public * *(..))") void publicServiceMethods() {}
}

Performance tip: within and execution with a narrow package are evaluated statically at proxy-creation time. args, this, target, @args may need a runtime check on each call. Always narrow with within(...) first, and never write a pointcut like execution(* *(..)) without a package scope — it tries to advise every bean, including Spring's own.

16.7 Writing custom aspects

Timing with Micrometer

@Target(ElementType.METHOD) @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface Timed { String value(); }

@Aspect @Component @RequiredArgsConstructor
class TimingAspect {
    private final MeterRegistry meters;

    @Around("@annotation(timed)")                         // binds the annotation instance
    public Object time(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp, Timed timed) throws Throwable {
        Timer.Sample sample = Timer.start(meters);
        String outcome = "ok";
        try {
            return pjp.proceed();                         // must return the result!
        } catch (Throwable t) {
            outcome = t.getClass().getSimpleName();
            throw t;                                      // never swallow
        } finally {
            sample.stop(meters.timer(timed.value(), "outcome", outcome));
        }
    }
}

(Micrometer already ships @Timed/@Observed with ObservedAspect; write your own only when you need different tags.)

Audit trail

@Target(ElementType.METHOD) @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface Audited { String action(); String entityType(); }

@Aspect @Component @RequiredArgsConstructor
class AuditAspect {
    private final AuditTrail audit;

    @AfterReturning(pointcut = "@annotation(a) && args(orgId, id, ..)", argNames = "a,orgId,id")
    public void record(Audited a, UUID orgId, UUID id) {
        audit.record(orgId, a.action(), a.entityType(), id, Map.of());
    }
}

RefinePoint: we deliberately do not audit with an aspect. Services call audit.record(orgId, "JOURNAL_POSTED", "JOURNAL", id, Map.of("number", j.number(), "target", t, "externalId", externalId)) explicitly. The reasons are worth saying in an interview: the details map needs values computed in the middle of the method (the external id returned by the accounting system), some actions are audited only on certain branches, and an explicit call is visible in code review — nobody can remove auditing by renaming a method so the pointcut stops matching. AuditTrail writes through the outbox, so the entry commits or rolls back with the business change. Aspects shine for uniform concerns (timing, tracing); audit in a finance product is business data.

Retry

@Aspect @Component @Order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)   // outside the transaction
class OptimisticRetryAspect {
    @Around("@annotation(RetryOnConflict)")
    public Object retry(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable {
        for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
            try { return pjp.proceed(); }
            catch (ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException e) {
                if (attempt == 3) throw e;
                Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(20, 50L * attempt));  // jittered backoff
            }
        }
    }
}

Retry only idempotent work, cap attempts, back off with jitter, and retry only exceptions that are transient. Spring Retry's @Retryable and Resilience4j's @Retry are this aspect, packaged.

Rate limit and tenant check

@Aspect @Component @RequiredArgsConstructor
class TenantGuardAspect {
    private final WorkspaceAccess access;

    @Before("within(com.ryfnflow.crm..controller..*) && args(orgCode, ..)")
    public void check(String orgCode) {
        access.resolve(orgCode, OrgRole.VIEWER);   // throws AccessDeniedException
    }
}

RefinePoint: our tenant check is not an aspect but a HandlerInterceptor — OrgAccessInterceptor.preHandle matches /api/v1/organizations/{code}/..., requires VIEWER for GET/HEAD and MEMBER for writes, and checks workspace locks. An interceptor sees the URL and HTTP method, which is exactly what the rule depends on, and it applies to every endpoint by path without each method opting in. Finer rules sit on controller methods as @PreAuthorize("@orgAuth.can('journals.post')") — which is AOP, via method security. Rate limiting lives in the gateway's RateLimitFilter, before any service is reached. Choosing filter vs interceptor vs aspect by what information the rule needs is the senior answer.

16.8 Spring features implemented as proxies

Annotation Enabled by Created by Interceptor
@Transactional @EnableTransactionManagement (Boot auto) Auto-proxy creator + BeanFactoryTransactionAttributeSourceAdvisor TransactionInterceptor
@Cacheable, @CachePut, @CacheEvict @EnableCaching Auto-proxy creator + BeanFactoryCacheOperationSourceAdvisor CacheInterceptor
@Async @EnableAsync AsyncAnnotationBeanPostProcessor AnnotationAsyncExecutionInterceptor
@Retryable @EnableRetry Spring Retry advisor RetryOperationsInterceptor
@PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize @EnableMethodSecurity Auto-proxy creator + method security advisors AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor
@Validated + JSR-380 on params MethodValidationPostProcessor (Boot auto) That BPP MethodValidationInterceptor
@Lookup, scoped proxy, @Configuration Container CGLIB directly Method interceptors in the generated class
Spring Data repository interface @EnableJpaRepositories JpaRepositoryFactoryBean Query method interceptors around SimpleJpaRepository

@Async in short: the interceptor wraps the call in a Callable, submits it to the TaskExecutor (Boot's applicationTaskExecutor, virtual threads with spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true), and returns immediately: nothing for void, or a CompletableFuture that completes when the task does. Any other return type is unsupported (older versions handed the caller null; current ones reject it), so declare void or CompletableFuture<T>. Exceptions from void methods go to the AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler (logged by default) — the caller never sees them.

@Cacheable in short: build the key (SimpleKeyGenerator: the single argument, or SimpleKey of all args), look in the Cache; hit → return without calling the target; miss → call, store, return. sync = true makes concurrent misses on one key compute once. Caches need a CacheManager; with none configured Boot uses a ConcurrentMapCacheManager with no eviction or TTL.

RefinePoint: we have no @Cacheable — cross-service answers (access decisions, plan limits, API-key checks) are cached by TtlCache in ryfn-platform for rp.cache-ttl (30 s by default), called explicitly from the remote clients. A plain TTL cache is easy to reason about and is never bypassed by self-invocation. @Async is used where it pays: NotificationService.onAlertRaised and ChatDispatcher deliver email, webhooks and chat posts off the request thread, and several services have @EnableAsync on their application class. @PreAuthorize("@orgAuth.can('...')") is on most controller methods — OrgAuth is a bean named orgAuth that evaluates the caller's permission in the workspace of the request, because Keycloak realm roles cannot express per-workspace owners and admins.

16.9 How @Transactional really works

Step by step, TransactionAspectSupport.invokeWithinTransaction:

  1. Find the attribute. AnnotationTransactionAttributeSource reads @Transactional from the method, then the class (method wins), caching the result per method. No attribute → call target directly.
  2. Pick the manager. transactionManager qualifier on the annotation, else the single PlatformTransactionManager bean (JpaTransactionManager with JPA on the class path).
  3. getTransaction(attr) applies propagation: join the existing transaction (REQUIRED), suspend it and start a new one (REQUIRES_NEW), create a savepoint (NESTED), and so on. A new transaction obtains a connection, sets autoCommit=false, applies isolation, timeout and read-only, and binds resources to the thread in TransactionSynchronizationManager (a set of ThreadLocals). That's why JdbcTemplate and the EntityManager in other beans join the same transaction transparently.
  4. Proceed through the rest of the chain to your method.
  5. On exception: completeTransactionAfterThrowing asks rollbackOn(ex). Default: RuntimeException or Error → rollback; checked exception → commit. Rollback rules from rollbackFor/noRollbackFor are checked first (the closest matching exception type in the hierarchy wins).
  6. On success: commitTransactionAfterReturning → beforeCommit synchronizations (Hibernate flush), commit, afterCommit synchronizations (@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)), then unbind and release.
  7. If an inner participant marked the transaction rollback-only, commit by the outer one throws UnexpectedRollbackException.

Because state lives in ThreadLocals, a transaction does not cross threads: work submitted to an executor, @Async methods, parallelStream() and CompletableFuture.supplyAsync run outside the caller's transaction.

Rollback rules

@Transactional                                  // rolls back on RuntimeException and Error only
@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)   // also on checked exceptions
@Transactional(noRollbackFor = BusinessWarning.class)

Why checked exceptions commit by default: the rule copies EJB's convention that checked exceptions are "expected business outcomes" the caller handles. In practice this surprises people: throws IOException from a file upload step commits everything written before it.

RefinePoint: we use the rule on purpose in JournalService.post, annotated @Transactional(noRollbackFor = IllegalArgumentException.class). When posting a journal to the external accounting system fails, the method records the failure — UPDATE journals SET post_error = ?, target = ?, connection_id = ? — and then throws IllegalArgumentException("Posting failed: ...") so the user sees a 400. Without noRollbackFor, the throw would roll back the very row that explains the failure. With it, the error message is committed and the caller still gets an exception. A nice example of rollback rules being a design tool, not just a gotcha.

The swallowed exception

@Transactional
public void importAll(List<Row> rows) {
    for (Row r : rows) {
        try { rowImporter.importRow(r); }          // a @Transactional(REQUIRED) bean → joins the outer tx
        catch (RuntimeException e) { log.warn("skip {}", r, e); }   // swallowed
    }
}   // commit → UnexpectedRollbackException: Transaction silently rolled back because it has been marked as rollback-only

The inner proxy's TransactionInterceptor saw a RuntimeException and, being a participant, could not roll back — so it marked the shared transaction rollback-only. Catching the exception in the outer method doesn't clear the flag. Fixes: REQUIRES_NEW for each row (its own transaction, committed or rolled back independently), NESTED (savepoint per row, JDBC only), or validate before writing so nothing throws. The opposite bug — catching an exception inside the transactional method without rethrowing — commits partial work because the interceptor never sees an exception.

16.10 Every way to bypass the proxy

Self-invocation

Inside the target, this is the target, not the proxy. this.exportOne() is a plain Java call, so @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW), @Async, @Cacheable and @PreAuthorize on exportOne are all ignored.

Fixes, best first:

// 1. Move the method to another bean (cleanest; usually reveals a real responsibility)
@Service @RequiredArgsConstructor
class ExportService {
    private final ExportStep step;                               // separate bean → called through its proxy
    @Transactional public void exportAll(List<UUID> ids) { ids.forEach(step::exportOne); }
}

// 2. Programmatic transaction — no proxy needed at all
private final TransactionTemplate tx;
public void exportAll(List<UUID> ids) {
    ids.forEach(id -> tx.executeWithoutResult(s -> exportOne(id)));
}

// 3. Self-injection (works, but a smell)
@Autowired @Lazy private ExportService self;   // the proxy
self.exportOne(id);

// 4. AopContext.currentProxy() with @EnableAspectJAutoProxy(exposeProxy = true) — couples code to AOP
// 5. AspectJ weaving mode — the call itself is woven

RefinePoint: OutboxRelay.relay() loops tx.execute(status -> sendBatch()) until a batch comes back short. A @Transactional sendBatch() called from relay() would be self-invocation and silently run with no transaction — the FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED locks would be released immediately and two instances could send the same events. TransactionTemplate makes each batch its own transaction explicitly. RunWorker.claim() and WorkspaceDataService.purge() use TransactionTemplate for the same reason: the transaction boundary is a part of the method, not the whole of it.

Other bypasses

Situation What happens Why
private method with @Transactional Ignored, no error Proxies can't override private methods; AnnotationTransactionAttributeSource only considers public by default
protected / package-private Applied since Spring 6.0 for class-based (CGLIB) proxies publicMethodsOnly default changed; JDK proxies still interface-only
final method on a CGLIB proxy Not advised; the call runs on the proxy instance itself, whose fields are null → often a NullPointerException Subclass can't override final; the proxy's own fields were never initialised
final class Proxy creation fails at startup (CGLIB) Can't subclass
static method Never advised Not dispatched through an instance
Object created with new No proxy at all Not a Spring bean
Called in @PostConstruct No transaction Proxy is created after init (BPP after-init)
@Transactional on interface method, CGLIB proxy Works in Spring 6 Attribute source checks interfaces too; older versions were inconsistent
Checked exception thrown Commits Default rollback rule
Exception caught inside the method Commits Interceptor never sees it
Work on another thread Outside the transaction ThreadLocal-bound resources
Wrong transaction manager (two DataSources) Transaction on the other database Specify @Transactional("billingTx")

Trap: Kotlin classes are final by default — the kotlin-spring (all-open) plugin opens Spring-annotated classes. In Java, Lombok or records can bite: records are final, so a record can never be a CGLIB-proxied bean.

16.11 Proxies, equals, getClass and debugging

  • getClass() on a CGLIB proxy returns the generated subclass (JournalService$$SpringCGLIB$$0). Use AopUtils.getTargetClass(bean) or ClassUtils.getUserClass(bean) for the real class. Code doing bean.getClass().getAnnotation(...) misses annotations unless they are @Inherited; use AnnotationUtils.findAnnotation / MergedAnnotations.
  • equals/hashCode: proxies delegate equals to the target only if the target implements equals; JDK proxies treat two proxies as equal when their interfaces, advisors and targets are equal. Don't put beans in hash-based sets keyed by identity expectations.
  • Field access through a proxy: proxy.someField (package-private access from the same package) reads the proxy's uninitialised field — always null. Always go through methods.
  • instanceof: a JDK proxy is instanceof its interfaces only, not the class.
  • Hibernate proxies are a different family (lazy loading of entities, HibernateProxy), with the same getClass() trap in equals — use Hibernate.getClass(entity) or instanceof.

Debugging a proxy problem

AopUtils.isAopProxy(bean);          // any Spring AOP proxy?
AopUtils.isCglibProxy(bean);
AopUtils.isJdkDynamicProxy(bean);
((Advised) bean).getAdvisors();      // which advisors, in what order
AopTestUtils.getTargetObject(bean);  // unwrap in tests
TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive();   // inside the method: is there really a tx?
TransactionSynchronizationManager.getCurrentTransactionName();
# see transactions begin, join, commit and roll back
logging.level.org.springframework.transaction.interceptor=TRACE
logging.level.org.springframework.orm.jpa.JpaTransactionManager=DEBUG
# see which beans get proxied and why
logging.level.org.springframework.aop=DEBUG

In a debugger, a stack trace through a proxy shows CglibAopProxy$DynamicAdvisedInterceptor.intercept → ReflectiveMethodInvocation.proceed → TransactionInterceptor.invoke → your method. If TransactionInterceptor is missing from the trace, the call didn't go through the proxy.

16.12 Performance and design guidance

  • A proxy hop plus a short interceptor chain costs nanoseconds to low microseconds — irrelevant next to a database round trip. Thousands of aspects with runtime-checked pointcuts (args, target) on hot paths is where it shows.
  • Keep transactions short: no HTTP calls, no file uploads, no waiting on Kafka inside them. A transaction pins a pooled connection for its whole duration; ten slow external calls inside @Transactional can exhaust a Hikari pool of ten.
  • Put @Transactional on service methods, not repositories (they already have their own) and not controllers (mixes web and transaction lifecycles).
  • @Transactional(readOnly = true) on query services: Hibernate skips dirty checking and flush (FlushMode.MANUAL), and with read replicas a routing data source can send it to a replica. Several of our query services are annotated @Transactional(readOnly = true) at class level.
  • Prefer explicit code (TransactionTemplate, explicit audit.record) when the boundary is part of an algorithm; prefer annotations when the boundary is the method.

16.13 Propagation as the interceptor sees it

Propagation is decided inside getTransaction(attr) — the interceptor asks "is there a transaction bound to this thread?" and acts per the attribute. (Chapter 21 covers isolation levels and database behaviour; here is what the proxy does.)

Propagation Existing transaction on thread No transaction Typical use
REQUIRED (default) Join it (participant) Start new Almost everything
REQUIRES_NEW Suspend it, start a new physical one, resume after Start new Audit log that must survive rollback, per-item work in a batch
NESTED Savepoint inside it (JDBC DataSourceTransactionManager; JPA only with JDBC savepoint support) Start new Partial rollback of one step
SUPPORTS Join Run without Read methods usable both ways
NOT_SUPPORTED Suspend, run without Run without Long non-transactional work called from a transaction
MANDATORY Join Throw IllegalTransactionStateException Methods that must never be the boundary
NEVER Throw Run without Assert no transaction (rare)

Three consequences seniors mention:

  1. REQUIRES_NEW needs a second pooled connection while the first is suspended. Under load, if every request holds one connection and waits for a second, a pool of N connections deadlocks at N concurrent requests — the pool waits forever for itself. Size pools with this in mind, or avoid REQUIRES_NEW on hot paths.
  2. The inner commit is final. If the outer transaction later rolls back, the inner work stays — which is exactly what you want for "record the failure" and exactly what you don't want for business data.
  3. Propagation only applies through the proxy. A self-invoked REQUIRES_NEW method silently joins the outer transaction (Q56).

Participants and rollback-only: only the interceptor that started a physical transaction commits or rolls it back. A participant that sees an exception marks the shared transaction rollback-only (globalRollbackOnParticipationFailure, default true). That's the mechanism behind UnexpectedRollbackException.

16.14 Declarative vs programmatic transactions

// Programmatic: the boundary is explicit and cannot be bypassed by self-invocation
@Component @RequiredArgsConstructor
class Claimer {
    private final TransactionTemplate tx;
    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;

    UUID claimNext() {
        return tx.execute(status -> {
            List<UUID> ids = jdbc.queryForList(
                "SELECT id FROM recon_runs WHERE status = 'QUEUED' ORDER BY queued_at LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED", UUID.class);
            if (ids.isEmpty()) return null;
            jdbc.update("UPDATE recon_runs SET status = 'RUNNING', started_at = now() WHERE id = ?", ids.get(0));
            return ids.get(0);
        });   // committed here: the lock is released, the run is ours
    }
}
// The long engine work then runs outside any transaction, with its own short transactions for results.
@Transactional TransactionTemplate PlatformTransactionManager directly
Boundary Whole method A lambda Explicit begin/commit/rollback
Bypassed by self-invocation Yes No No
Mixed with non-transactional work in one method No Yes Yes
Boilerplate None Low High, error-prone
Rollback Rules on exception types Exception in lambda, or status.setRollbackOnly() Manual
Reactive @Transactional on Mono/Flux with ReactiveTransactionManager TransactionalOperator —

RefinePoint: RunWorker.claim() is the real version of the code above: tx.execute(...) takes a PostgreSQL advisory transaction lock (pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('run-queue'))) so one claim at a time holds the per-workspace cap exactly, selects the next run with FOR UPDATE OF r SKIP LOCKED, marks it RUNNING with this instance's name and commits — all in milliseconds. The engine then runs the reconciliation on a pool thread outside that transaction. If the whole poll() were @Transactional, the advisory lock and the row lock would be held for the entire reconciliation and every other instance would stall. This is the clearest example in our code of "the transaction boundary is part of the method, not the method".

16.15 Reactive and virtual-thread considerations

  • Reactive (WebFlux): @Transactional works on methods returning Mono/Flux with a ReactiveTransactionManager (R2DBC). Transaction state lives in the Reactor Context, not a ThreadLocal, because a reactive pipeline hops threads. Blocking JPA inside a reactive pipeline gets no reactive transaction. Our api-gateway is reactive (Spring Cloud Gateway) and has no database transactions at all, which keeps it simple.
  • Virtual threads (spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true): each request still runs on one (virtual) thread from start to finish, so ThreadLocal-based transactions, security context and request attributes work unchanged. What changes: @Async and @Scheduled executors use virtual threads too, and synchronized blocks around I/O can pin carrier threads on Java 21 — prefer ReentrantLock in aspects or interceptors that lock.
  • Context propagation: for @Async, register a TaskDecorator (or Micrometer's context-propagation library) to copy MDC, security context and tracing into the task. It never copies the transaction — by design.

16.16 Interview questions and answers

Q1. What is AOP and why use it?

A way to modularise cross-cutting concerns — transactions, security, metrics, caching, retries — so they are written once and applied declaratively instead of being copy-pasted into every method. Business methods stay focused on business logic; the concern can be changed in one place.

Q2. Define aspect, join point, pointcut, advice, weaving.

Aspect: the module containing the concern. Join point: a point in execution — in Spring AOP only a bean method execution. Pointcut: a predicate selecting join points. Advice: the code run at a selected join point (before, after, around). Weaving: linking aspects to targets — Spring does it at runtime by creating proxies.

Q3. What advice types exist, and which is most powerful?

@Before, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing, @After (finally) and @Around. @Around is the most powerful: it decides whether to call proceed(), can change arguments and the result, and can catch exceptions. Use the weakest type that works, because @Around bugs (forgotten proceed or return) silently break methods.

Q4. Can @AfterThrowing swallow an exception?

No. It runs when the method throws and can throw a different exception, but the original propagates otherwise. To suppress or convert an exception into a return value you need @Around with a try/catch.

Q5. Spring AOP vs AspectJ?

Spring AOP uses runtime proxies, advises only public (or with CGLIB, non-private) method executions on Spring beans, and needs no build changes. AspectJ weaves bytecode at compile or load time and can advise constructors, field access, private and static methods, objects created with new, and self-invocation. Spring uses AspectJ's annotation syntax and pointcut parser but not its weaver.

Q6. When would you actually choose AspectJ weaving?

When you need advice on self-invocation, domain objects created with new (@Configurable), private methods or field access, or when per-call proxy overhead on an extremely hot path matters. Otherwise the build and agent complexity isn't worth it.

Q7. JDK dynamic proxy vs CGLIB?

JDK proxies implement the target's interfaces using java.lang.reflect.Proxy and an InvocationHandler; they need interfaces and the bean is only usable as the interface type. CGLIB generates a subclass at runtime, so it works without interfaces, can be injected as the concrete class, but cannot advise final methods or proxy final classes.

Q8. Which one does Spring Boot use by default?

CGLIB, for all beans: spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true has been Boot's default since 2.0. Plain Spring Framework uses JDK proxies when interfaces are present. Set the property to false to get JDK proxies for interface-based beans.

Q9. Why did Boot switch the default to CGLIB?

Injecting a bean by its class type failed with JDK proxies (BeanNotOfRequiredTypeException) whenever the class happened to implement any interface, which confused developers constantly. CGLIB proxies are type-compatible with the class, and modern CGLIB with Objenesis doesn't call the constructor twice.

Q10. Does a CGLIB proxy call super.method()?

No. Spring's CGLIB proxy is a subclass instance that holds a reference to a separate, fully initialised target and delegates to it. The proxy's inherited fields are never initialised — which is why final methods (executed on the proxy) see null fields.

Q11. When is the proxy created in the bean lifecycle?

In postProcessAfterInitialization of AbstractAutoProxyCreator (a BeanPostProcessor), after @PostConstruct and init methods. Earlier only if the bean is part of a circular reference, via getEarlyBeanReference. So code in @PostConstruct runs on the raw target.

Q12. A bean has @Transactional, @PreAuthorize and a custom aspect. How many proxies?

One. The auto-proxy creator collects all matching advisors into one proxy with an ordered interceptor chain. Post-processors like AsyncAnnotationBeanPostProcessor add their advisor to an existing proxy instead of wrapping again.

Q13. What is the self-invocation problem?

A call from one method of a bean to another method of the same bean via this goes directly to the target, bypassing the proxy, so annotations on the called method (@Transactional, @Async, @Cacheable, @PreAuthorize) have no effect. No error is reported.

Q14. How do you fix self-invocation?
