Best: move the method to a separate bean. Or use programmatic control (TransactionTemplate). Or inject the bean's own proxy (@Lazy self-injection) or use AopContext.currentProxy() with exposeProxy = true — both work but couple the class to AOP. Or switch to AspectJ weaving.

Q15. Give a real case where you avoided self-invocation by design.

"Our OutboxRelay loops batches with tx.execute(status -> sendBatch()). Had I written @Transactional sendBatch() and called it from relay(), it would run with no transaction, the FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED row locks would release immediately, and two instances could send the same events. TransactionTemplate makes each batch its own transaction explicitly."

Q16. Does @Transactional work on private methods?

No — proxies cannot intercept private methods, and nothing warns you. Since Spring 6.0, protected and package-private methods are supported for class-based (CGLIB) proxies; earlier versions supported only public methods.

Q17. What happens with @Transactional on a final method?

The CGLIB subclass can't override it, so the call executes on the proxy instance directly — no transaction, and since the proxy's own fields are uninitialised, injected dependencies are null, typically causing a NullPointerException. Spring logs a warning at startup for final methods in proxied classes.

Q18. Can a record or final class be a proxied bean?

Not with CGLIB — creation fails because it can't be subclassed. A final class implementing an interface can be proxied with a JDK proxy if proxy-target-class=false, and then must be injected by the interface.

Q19. How is advice ordered across aspects?

By @Order/Ordered on the aspect class: lowest value = highest precedence = outermost, running first before and last after. Without an order the sequence is undefined. Infrastructure advisors have their own order (@EnableTransactionManagement(order=...)).

Q20. And within one aspect?

Since Spring 5.2.7: @Around, @Before, the method, @AfterReturning or @AfterThrowing, @After, end of @Around. Two advices of the same type in the same aspect have no defined order — split them into separate ordered aspects.

Q21. Why must a retry aspect be outside the transaction?

If the retry is inside, every attempt reuses the same transaction — which may be rollback-only already and has a persistence context holding the stale entity, so retries can never succeed. Outside, each attempt starts a fresh transaction with fresh data. Give the retry aspect higher precedence (lower order value).

Q22. Explain the execution pointcut syntax.

execution(modifiers? return-type declaring-type? method-name(params) throws?). * matches one element, .. in a package means any sub-package, .. in parameters means any number of arguments. Example: execution(public * com.ryfnflow..service.*Service.find*(java.util.UUID, ..)).

Q23. within vs execution vs @annotation vs @within?

within selects by type or package location. execution by method signature. @annotation by an annotation on the method. @within by an annotation on the declaring class. @annotation(x) can also bind the annotation instance to an advice parameter.

Q24. this vs target pointcuts?

this(T) matches when the proxy is an instance of T; target(T) when the target is. They differ with JDK proxies: the proxy implements only interfaces, so this(ConcreteClass) doesn't match while target(ConcreteClass) does.

Q25. How do you access method arguments and the annotation in advice?

Use JoinPoint.getArgs() and getSignature(), or bind them: @Around("@annotation(timed) && args(orgId, ..)") Object x(ProceedingJoinPoint p, Timed timed, UUID orgId). Binding is type-safe and also filters by type. Compile with -parameters or specify argNames.

Q26. Write an @Around timing aspect — what are the common mistakes?

Call pjp.proceed() exactly once (unless retrying deliberately), return its result, rethrow exceptions (throws Throwable), and record in finally. Mistakes: returning null or void, swallowing exceptions, forgetting @Component so the aspect is never registered, pointcuts that are too broad.

Q27. Why might my aspect not apply?

The aspect isn't a bean (missing @Component), spring-boot-starter-aop isn't on the class path, the pointcut doesn't match (package typo, wrong annotation import), the target isn't a Spring bean, the call is a self-invocation, the method is private/final/static, or the bean was created too early to be proxied.

Q28. Can an aspect advise another aspect?

No. Classes annotated with @Aspect are excluded from auto-proxying by other aspects in Spring AOP. AspectJ weaving can, but it's rarely a good idea.

Q29. Where would you use an aspect vs a filter vs an interceptor?

Filter: raw HTTP concerns before Spring MVC — authentication, CORS, rate limits, request logging. Interceptor: MVC-level concerns needing the handler or path — our OrgAccessInterceptor checks the workspace role from the URL. Aspect: method-level concerns on any bean, web or not — transactions, metrics, method security.

Q30. Why don't you implement the audit trail as an aspect?

"Audit details need values computed mid-method (the external id returned by the accounting system), some actions are audited only on some branches, and an explicit audit.record(...) is visible in code review — nobody can silently disable it by renaming a method so the pointcut stops matching. It writes through the outbox in the same transaction, so audit and change commit together."

Q31. How does @Transactional work internally?

The bean is proxied; TransactionInterceptor reads the method's TransactionAttribute, asks the PlatformTransactionManager for a transaction according to propagation, binds the connection and EntityManager to the thread via TransactionSynchronizationManager, calls the method, then commits or rolls back according to rollback rules, running synchronization callbacks around commit.

Q32. How does a repository called inside a service join the same transaction?

Through the thread-bound resources. JpaTransactionManager binds an EntityManagerHolder and a ConnectionHolder to the current thread. Spring's shared EntityManager proxy and DataSourceUtils.getConnection (used by JdbcTemplate) look there first, so they use the same connection.

Q33. Which exceptions roll back by default?

Unchecked ones: RuntimeException and Error. Checked exceptions commit. Change with rollbackFor/noRollbackFor; the most specific matching rule wins.

Q34. Why don't checked exceptions roll back?

Spring inherited the EJB convention: checked exceptions represent expected, recoverable business outcomes, unchecked ones represent failures. Many teams set rollbackFor = Exception.class as a convention, or avoid checked exceptions in service code.

Q35. Give an example where noRollbackFor was the correct design.

"In JournalService.post, if pushing a journal to the accounting system fails, we save the failure (post_error, target, connection) and throw IllegalArgumentException("Posting failed: ...") so the user gets a clear 400. The method is @Transactional(noRollbackFor = IllegalArgumentException.class) — otherwise the throw would roll back the very row that records why it failed."

Q36. What is UnexpectedRollbackException?

Thrown when an outer transaction tries to commit but an inner participant (same physical transaction, REQUIRED) has marked it rollback-only after an exception the outer code caught. Spring rolls back and tells the caller its "commit" didn't happen. Fix with REQUIRES_NEW/NESTED for the inner unit or don't swallow the failure.

Q37. What happens if you catch an exception inside a @Transactional method?

The interceptor never sees it, so it commits whatever was done before — including partial writes. Catch only if you can genuinely recover, or call TransactionAspectSupport.currentTransactionStatus().setRollbackOnly(), or rethrow.

Q38. Does a transaction propagate to @Async methods or other threads?

No. Transaction resources are ThreadLocal-bound, so the new thread has no transaction (and no persistence context). @Async methods that need one must declare their own @Transactional, and should receive ids rather than managed entities.

Q39. @Async + @Transactional on the same method — what happens?

The async interceptor runs first (the call is handed to an executor), then on the executor thread the transaction interceptor starts a new transaction. It works, but the transaction is independent of the caller's — the caller may not have committed yet, so the async method may not see the caller's data. Combine with @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) to start async work only after commit, as our NotificationService.onAlertRaised does.

Q40. How does @Async work, and what are its pitfalls?

AsyncAnnotationBeanPostProcessor proxies the bean; the interceptor submits the call to a TaskExecutor and returns immediately. Pitfalls: self-invocation runs synchronously, exceptions from void methods are only logged by AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler, ThreadLocals (security context, MDC, request attributes) are not propagated without a TaskDecorator, an unbounded queue can hide overload, and it requires @EnableAsync.

Q41. How does @Cacheable work, and why might it not cache?

CacheInterceptor computes a key from the arguments, returns a cached value on a hit without invoking the method, otherwise calls it and stores the result. It doesn't cache on self-invocation, without @EnableCaching, when unless/condition exclude it, or when keys differ unexpectedly (mutable arguments, missing equals). The default ConcurrentMapCacheManager never evicts.

Q42. How is @PreAuthorize implemented?

@EnableMethodSecurity registers advisors with AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor, which evaluates the SpEL expression against the current Authentication before invoking the method and throws AccessDeniedException if it fails. It runs before the transaction interceptor, so denied calls never open a transaction.

Q43. How do you do tenant-aware method security?

Expose a bean and call it from SpEL. "Ours is @PreAuthorize("@orgAuth.can('journals.post')"): OrgAuth is a bean named orgAuth that resolves the workspace of the current request (org code in the URL or X-Org-Code) and checks the caller's permission in that workspace, because Keycloak realm roles can't express per-workspace owners and admins."

Q44. What does readOnly = true actually do?

It's a hint: JpaTransactionManager sets Hibernate's flush mode to MANUAL (no dirty checking or flush), the JDBC connection gets setReadOnly(true) (drivers may optimise; PostgreSQL issues SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY, rejecting writes), and routing data sources can send it to a replica. It does not by itself prevent writes in every database.

Q45. Where should @Transactional go — controller, service, or repository?

On service methods representing a use case. Repositories already have their own (Spring Data's SimpleJpaRepository is @Transactional(readOnly = true) with write methods overridden). Controllers would tie the transaction to the HTTP lifecycle, including serialization, and encourage long transactions.

Q46. Why are long transactions dangerous?

Each holds a pooled connection, row locks and a growing persistence context for its whole duration. External HTTP calls or file processing inside a transaction can exhaust the connection pool and block other writers. In PostgreSQL long transactions also hold back vacuum. Keep I/O outside, and use TransactionTemplate around just the database part.

Q47. How do you check at runtime whether a transaction is active?

TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive() and getCurrentTransactionName(); or TRACE logging for org.springframework.transaction.interceptor shows every "Getting transaction for [...]" and "Completing transaction". In a stack trace, look for TransactionInterceptor.invoke.

Q48. How do you tell whether a bean is a proxy, and get the real class?

AopUtils.isAopProxy, isCglibProxy, isJdkDynamicProxy; AopUtils.getTargetClass(bean) or ClassUtils.getUserClass(bean) for the class; cast to Advised to list advisors; AopTestUtils.getTargetObject in tests.

Q49. Why does bean.getClass().getAnnotation(X.class) return null for a proxied bean?

getClass() returns the generated CGLIB subclass, and annotations aren't inherited unless meta-annotated @Inherited. Use AnnotationUtils.findAnnotation(AopUtils.getTargetClass(bean), X.class) or MergedAnnotations.

Q50. How do proxies affect equals and hashCode?

A JDK proxy's equals considers two proxies equal when they have equal configuration (interfaces, advisors, target); otherwise it delegates to the target if the target implements equals. A CGLIB proxy delegates to the target's equals. Comparing a proxy with its raw target can be asymmetric, so avoid mixing raw and proxied references.

Q51. Is @Transactional on an interface honoured?

In Spring 6 yes, for both JDK and CGLIB proxies — the attribute source also searches interface methods. Spring's documentation still recommends annotating concrete classes, because interface annotations are invisible to AspectJ weaving and not inherited by Java rules.

Q52. What is the performance cost of proxies?

A proxy hop plus a cached interceptor chain: nanoseconds to a microsecond or so per call — negligible compared with I/O. It matters only for extremely hot, tiny methods or for broad pointcuts with runtime checks (args, this, target) on every bean. Scope pointcuts with within.

Q53. How does Spring choose the transaction manager when there are two databases?

By the transactionManager (or value) attribute: @Transactional("billingTx"). Without it Spring uses the single PlatformTransactionManager bean, or the @Primary one; with two and no primary it fails. Writing to two databases in one method gives two independent transactions — not atomic without XA.

Q54. What are TransactionSynchronization callbacks used for?

To run code at transaction phases: beforeCommit (Hibernate flushes), beforeCompletion, afterCommit, afterCompletion (resource cleanup). @TransactionalEventListener is built on them. Register manually with TransactionSynchronizationManager.registerSynchronization for "do this only if the transaction commits".

Q55. Design question: add per-tenant timing metrics to all service methods without touching them.

An @Around aspect on within(com.ryfnflow.crm..service..*) && execution(public * *(..)), using Micrometer Timer tagged by class, method and outcome — but take the tenant from a bounded source, not raw org ids, to avoid tag-cardinality explosion (or record tenant only in traces). Order it outermost so it measures transaction time too, and exclude health and scheduler beans. Or use @Observed with ObservedAspect and let tracing carry the tenant.

Q56. Tricky output: what does this print?

@Service class S {
    @Transactional public void a() { b(); }
    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW) public void b() {
        System.out.println(TransactionSynchronizationManager.getCurrentTransactionName());
    }
}
s.a();

S.a (the fully qualified method name of a) — b() is self-invoked, so no new transaction starts and b runs inside a's transaction. Called from another bean, it would print S.b.

Q57. Tricky: @Transactional method throws IOException after saving an entity. Is it saved?

Yes — IOException is checked, so the default rule commits. Add rollbackFor = IOException.class (or Exception.class) if the save must be undone.

Q58. Tricky: why is the transaction not rolled back when @Transactional is on a method of a class that implements a JDK-proxied interface, but the method isn't in the interface?

With a JDK proxy only interface methods go through the proxy; a method not declared on the interface can't even be called through the bean reference without casting to the class (which fails). If it's called internally from an interface method, it's self-invocation. Either declare it on the interface or use CGLIB (Boot's default).

Q59. What does REQUIRES_NEW do, and what is its hidden cost?

It suspends the current transaction (unbinding its resources from the thread) and starts an independent physical transaction that commits or rolls back on its own. The cost is a second pooled connection held while the first is suspended — under load a pool can deadlock waiting for itself. And it only works through the proxy.

Q60. REQUIRES_NEW vs NESTED?

REQUIRES_NEW is a separate transaction: its commit survives an outer rollback, and it can't see the outer transaction's uncommitted changes. NESTED is a savepoint in the same transaction: rolling it back undoes only the nested part, but an outer rollback undoes everything. NESTED needs savepoint support (JDBC transaction manager); JpaTransactionManager supports it only for JDBC-level savepoints.

Q61. What does MANDATORY buy you?

A guarantee that the method is never the transaction boundary: called without an active transaction it throws IllegalTransactionStateException. Useful for repository-like helpers that must always be part of a caller's unit of work.

Q62. When do you choose TransactionTemplate over @Transactional?

When the transaction is only part of the method — claiming a row and then doing long work outside, looping batches that each commit, or retry loops — or where self-invocation would otherwise bite. "Our RunWorker.claim() and OutboxRelay.relay() both use it: the claim commits in milliseconds and the reconciliation runs outside any transaction."

Q63. How does @Transactional work in WebFlux?

With a ReactiveTransactionManager (R2DBC) the interceptor wraps the returned Mono/Flux, and transaction state is stored in the Reactor Context instead of a ThreadLocal, because the pipeline may switch threads. Blocking JPA calls inside a reactive chain don't participate. TransactionalOperator is the programmatic form.

Q64. Do virtual threads change how proxies and transactions behave?

No for request handling: one virtual thread per request keeps ThreadLocal-bound transactions and security working. Watch synchronized around blocking I/O (pins the carrier on Java 21), and remember @Async tasks still start without the caller's transaction or context unless a TaskDecorator copies the context.

Q65. How would you explain proxies to a junior who says "my @Transactional doesn't work"?

"The annotation does nothing by itself. Spring replaces your bean with a stand-in that opens the transaction and then calls your real object. Only calls that come through the stand-in get a transaction. So check three things: is the object a Spring bean, is the call coming from another bean (not this), and is the method public and not final. Then turn on TRACE logging for org.springframework.transaction.interceptor and look for 'Getting transaction for'."

17. Spring Boot Internals

A senior interview rarely asks "what is Spring Boot?" and stops. The follow-ups are "what exactly happens between main() and the first request?", "how does Boot decide to create a DataSource?", "your property is ignored in production, how do you find out why?", and "how did you share configuration across your services?". This chapter walks the startup path, the auto-configuration engine, configuration binding, Actuator, packaging and the Boot 2 → 3 migration at the level where you can answer those follow-ups from memory, and uses RefinePoint's shared ryfn-platform starter as the worked example.

17.1 What Boot adds over plain Spring

Spring Framework gives you the IoC container, AOP, transactions, MVC and data access. It does not decide which beans you need. Before Boot, every project wrote the same DataSource, EntityManagerFactory, DispatcherServlet and ObjectMapper configuration, deployed a WAR to an external Tomcat, and pinned compatible library versions by hand.

Boot adds five things on top of the framework:

Boot feature Problem it removes Mechanism
Auto-configuration Boilerplate bean definitions @Conditional configuration classes listed in AutoConfiguration.imports
Starters Picking compatible dependency sets Dependency-only POMs + spring-boot-dependencies BOM
Embedded server External container, WAR deployment ServletWebServerFactory creates Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow inside the JVM
Externalized configuration Hard-coded settings per environment Ordered PropertySources, profiles, @ConfigurationProperties binding
Production features Ad-hoc health checks and metrics Actuator endpoints, Micrometer, health groups, graceful shutdown

The key insight interviewers want: Boot is not a different framework. It is a set of @Configuration classes and a launcher. Everything it creates is an ordinary bean you could have declared yourself, and anything you declare wins over what Boot would have created (the "back-off" principle).

17.2 @SpringBootApplication decomposed

@Target(ElementType.TYPE) @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) @Documented @Inherited
@SpringBootConfiguration                       // = @Configuration, marks THE boot config (tests find it)
@EnableAutoConfiguration                       // = @AutoConfigurationPackage + @Import(AutoConfigurationImportSelector)
@ComponentScan(excludeFilters = {
    @Filter(type = FilterType.CUSTOM, classes = TypeExcludeFilter.class),
    @Filter(type = FilterType.CUSTOM, classes = AutoConfigurationExcludeFilter.class) })
public @interface SpringBootApplication { ... }
  • @SpringBootConfiguration is @Configuration with one extra meaning: @SpringBootTest and slice tests search up the package tree for it to find the application's configuration. There must be exactly one.
  • @EnableAutoConfiguration imports AutoConfigurationImportSelector, a DeferredImportSelector. "Deferred" is the important word: it runs after all your @Configuration classes are parsed, which is why @ConditionalOnMissingBean in an auto-configuration can see your beans and back off.
  • @AutoConfigurationPackage registers the main class's package in a bean called AutoConfigurationPackages. JPA entity scanning and Spring Data repository scanning use it, which is why entities outside the main package are not found unless you add @EntityScan.
  • @ComponentScan with no basePackages scans the package of the annotated class and below. AutoConfigurationExcludeFilter stops auto-configuration classes from being picked up twice if they happen to sit in a scanned package.

Trap: putting the main class in the default package (no package statement) makes component scanning walk the entire classpath, including every jar. Startup becomes very slow or fails. Always put the main class in a root package such as com.ryfnflow.crm.recon.

17.3 SpringApplication.run() step by step

SpringApplication.run(App.class, args) does two things: constructs a SpringApplication, then calls run(args).

Construction (new SpringApplication(primarySources)):

  1. Deduce the WebApplicationType from the classpath: SERVLET if jakarta.servlet.Servlet and ConfigurableWebApplicationContext are present, REACTIVE if only WebFlux's DispatcherHandler is present, otherwise NONE.
  2. Load BootstrapRegistryInitializers, ApplicationContextInitializers and ApplicationListeners from META-INF/spring.factories across the classpath.
  3. Deduce the main application class from the stack trace (used for logging and as the default source).

run(args):

Step by step, with what matters in each:

  1. Bootstrap context. A small DefaultBootstrapContext lives only until the ApplicationContext is ready. Config data loaders (for example a config-server client) register expensive objects here so they can be reused while loading configuration. Run listeners are loaded; the main one is EventPublishingRunListener, which turns each phase into an event.
  2. Starting. ApplicationStartingEvent is published. Logging is initialised very early by LoggingApplicationListener reacting to this event.
  3. Environment. An ApplicationServletEnvironment is created, command-line arguments are added as a property source, and ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent triggers EnvironmentPostProcessorApplicationListener, which runs every EnvironmentPostProcessor. The most important one is ConfigDataEnvironmentPostProcessor, which loads application.yml, profile files and spring.config.import locations. spring.main.* properties are then bound onto the SpringApplication itself.
  4. Banner. Printed to console/log unless spring.main.banner-mode=off.
  5. Context creation. The type follows the web application type: AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext for MVC, AnnotationConfigReactiveWebServerApplicationContext for WebFlux, AnnotationConfigApplicationContext otherwise.
  6. Prepare. ApplicationContextInitializers run, ApplicationContextInitializedEvent fires, the bootstrap context closes, the startup info line is logged ("Starting ReconApplication using Java 21..."), the ApplicationArguments singleton is registered, bean-definition overriding is set to disallowed (default since Boot 2.1), and the main class is registered as a bean definition. ApplicationPreparedEvent fires — bean definitions from sources exist, but nothing has been refreshed.
  7. Refresh — the heart of the framework (AbstractApplicationContext.refresh()):
    • invokeBeanFactoryPostProcessors: ConfigurationClassPostProcessor parses your configuration, runs component scanning, processes @Import, and last the deferred AutoConfigurationImportSelector, evaluating conditions and registering auto-configured bean definitions.
    • registerBeanPostProcessors: autowiring, @PostConstruct, AOP proxy creators, @ConfigurationProperties binding post-processor.
    • onRefresh: the web context creates the embedded server (ServletWebServerFactory.getWebServer), initialising the servlet context but not yet accepting connections.
    • finishBeanFactoryInitialization: all non-lazy singletons are instantiated, injected, initialised and proxied.
    • finishRefresh: the lifecycle processor starts SmartLifecycle beans — including WebServerStartStopLifecycle, which starts the connector (port opens, ServletWebServerInitializedEvent) — then ContextRefreshedEvent is published. A JVM shutdown hook is registered.
  8. Started. "Started ReconApplication in 4.2 seconds" is logged, ApplicationStartedEvent and AvailabilityChangeEvent(LivenessState.CORRECT) fire.
  9. Runners. All ApplicationRunner and CommandLineRunner beans run, sorted by @Order, on the main thread. An exception here fails startup.
  10. Ready. ApplicationReadyEvent and AvailabilityChangeEvent(ReadinessState.ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC) fire. The readiness probe turns green only now.

If anything throws, ApplicationFailedEvent is published, FailureAnalyzers turn known exceptions into readable reports ("Port 8104 was already in use", "Parameter 0 of constructor required a bean of type ... that could not be found"), and the context is closed.

Event order summary (memorise it; it is a classic question):

# Event Context exists? Typical use
1 ApplicationStartingEvent No Very early setup
2 ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent No Inspect/modify environment
3 ApplicationContextInitializedEvent Yes, no bean definitions loaded Context tweaks
4 ApplicationPreparedEvent Yes, definitions loaded, not refreshed Rare
5 WebServerInitializedEvent Refreshing Learn the actual port (server.port=0)
6 ContextRefreshedEvent Refreshed Framework internals
7 ApplicationStartedEvent + Liveness CORRECT Ready, runners not run —
8 ApplicationReadyEvent + Readiness ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC Fully ready Warm caches, start consumers
— ApplicationFailedEvent Maybe Alerting

Trap: a @Component with @EventListener(ApplicationStartingEvent.class) never fires. Events 1–4 are published before the context can contain your beans. Listeners for those events must be registered in META-INF/spring.factories under org.springframework.context.ApplicationListener or via SpringApplication.addListeners(...).

17.4 The auto-configuration mechanism

Where the candidates come from

Since Boot 2.7, auto-configuration classes are listed one per line in:

META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports

Boot 3.0 removed support for the old org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.EnableAutoConfiguration= key in META-INF/spring.factories. spring.factories itself still exists for other extension points: EnvironmentPostProcessor, ApplicationListener, FailureAnalyzer, ApplicationContextInitializer, TemplateAvailabilityProvider. A library that only uses spring.factories for auto-configuration silently does nothing on Boot 3 — a very common migration bug.

spring-boot-autoconfigure alone lists about 150 classes. Evaluating every condition on every class by loading it would be slow, so Boot does it in two phases:

The metadata file META-INF/spring-autoconfigure-metadata.properties is generated at build time by spring-boot-autoconfigure-processor. It holds entries like ...DataSourceAutoConfiguration.ConditionalOnClass=javax.sql.DataSource,...EmbeddedDatabaseType, so the filter can drop a class whose required classes are absent without even loading it.

The @Conditional family

Annotation Matches when Example
@ConditionalOnClass / OnMissingClass Class is / is not on the classpath Jackson config only if ObjectMapper exists
@ConditionalOnBean / OnMissingBean A bean of that type/name exists / does not Default ObjectMapper only if you did not define one
@ConditionalOnSingleCandidate Exactly one bean, or one @Primary JdbcTemplate needs a single DataSource
@ConditionalOnProperty Property has a value (havingValue, matchIfMissing) rp.kafka.enabled=true
@ConditionalOnResource A resource exists classpath:logback.xml
@ConditionalOnWebApplication(type=SERVLET) / OnNotWebApplication Web type MVC-only config
@ConditionalOnExpression SpEL is true Complex property combinations
@ConditionalOnJava JVM version range Version-specific features
@ConditionalOnThreading(VIRTUAL) Virtual threads enabled (Boot 3.2) Virtual-thread executors
@ConditionalOnCloudPlatform Kubernetes, Cloud Foundry, ... Probes on k8s

Under the hood every one is a Condition (most extend SpringBootCondition, which adds logging to the report). You can write your own and combine them with AnyNestedCondition, AllNestedConditions or NoneNestedConditions.

Class conditions on a @Bean method are dangerous. If a @Bean method's return type refers to a missing class, the configuration class itself fails to load when Spring introspects its methods. Put @ConditionalOnClass at class level, or on a nested static @Configuration class.

@ConditionalOnMissingBean only sees bean definitions registered so far. It is reliable in auto-configuration (which runs after user configuration) and unreliable in your own @Configuration classes, where order of parsing is not guaranteed.

Ordering

@AutoConfiguration(after = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class) (or @AutoConfigureAfter/@AutoConfigureBefore, and @AutoConfigureOrder for a numeric order) control the order in which auto-configurations are parsed. They have no effect on user @Configuration classes and do not control bean instantiation order — that comes from dependencies. Ordering matters for conditions: a @ConditionalOnBean(DataSource.class) only sees the DataSource if DataSourceAutoConfiguration was processed first.

Debugging and excluding

java -jar recon.jar --debug          # or debug=true in application.yml

prints the CONDITIONS EVALUATION REPORT:

Positive matches:
   DataSourceAutoConfiguration matched:
      - @ConditionalOnClass found required classes 'javax.sql.DataSource', ... (OnClassCondition)
Negative matches:
   MongoAutoConfiguration:
      Did not match:
         - @ConditionalOnClass did not find required class 'com.mongodb.client.MongoClient' (OnClassCondition)
Exclusions:
   org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.security.servlet.UserDetailsServiceAutoConfiguration
Unconditional classes:
   org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.context.ConfigurationPropertiesAutoConfiguration

At runtime the same report is at /actuator/conditions; /actuator/beans lists every bean with its dependencies and /actuator/configprops shows bound property values (sanitised).

Excluding:

@SpringBootApplication(exclude = { DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class, KafkaAutoConfiguration.class })
spring:
  autoconfigure:
    exclude:
      - org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.security.servlet.UserDetailsServiceAutoConfiguration

The property form is better when only some environments need the exclusion (put it in a profile document).

17.5 Writing a custom starter — RefinePoint's ryfn-platform

The official layout for a starter named acme is two modules: acme-spring-boot-autoconfigure (the configuration classes) and acme-spring-boot-starter (an empty jar whose POM pulls in the autoconfigure module plus the libraries it needs). Third-party starters must not start with spring-boot- — that prefix is reserved for Spring's own. Small teams often ship one jar that is both, and that is what we did.

RefinePoint: all 13 services depend on one shared library, ryfn-platform. Its AutoConfiguration.imports lists six classes: PlatformSecurityAutoConfiguration, PlatformRemoteAutoConfiguration, PlatformEventsAutoConfiguration, PlatformWebAutoConfiguration, PlatformOpenApiAutoConfiguration and PlatformObservabilityAutoConfiguration. Adding the dependency gives a service Keycloak JWT + API-key security, the InternalClient for service-to-service calls, the transactional outbox and Kafka relay, the OrgAccessInterceptor for org-scoped routes, Swagger and tracing — without one line of configuration in the service.

The real code shows the patterns interviewers probe:

@AutoConfiguration(after = { DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class, HibernateJpaAutoConfiguration.class,
                             KafkaAutoConfiguration.class, FlywayAutoConfiguration.class })
public class PlatformEventsAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean @ConditionalOnMissingBean          // a service may replace it
    public EventPublisher eventPublisher(EventStore store, ObjectMapper mapper /* ... */) { ... }

    @Bean @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    public ConsumedEvents consumedEvents(EventStore store, ObjectMapper mapper) { ... }

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "rp.kafka.enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)
    public OutboxRelay outboxRelay(EventStore store, KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka, TopicNames topics /* ... */) { ... }
}
  1. after = ... guarantees the DataSource, JdbcTemplate and KafkaTemplate definitions exist before our conditions and beans that need them are evaluated.
  2. @ConditionalOnMissingBean on every default bean: a service can override any piece by declaring its own bean.
  3. @ConditionalOnProperty(matchIfMissing = true): with KAFKA_ENABLED=false (tests, or one service running alone on a laptop) the relay is not created and events simply wait in outbox_events.

Shared defaults come from an EnvironmentPostProcessor, registered in META-INF/spring.factories (the one place Boot 3 still uses that file for us):

org.springframework.boot.env.EnvironmentPostProcessor=com.ryfnflow.crm.common.autoconfig.PlatformDefaults
public class PlatformDefaults implements EnvironmentPostProcessor {
    @Override
    public void postProcessEnvironment(ConfigurableEnvironment env, SpringApplication app) {
        Map<String, Object> d = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        d.put("spring.datasource.url",
            "jdbc:postgresql://${DB_HOST:localhost}:${DB_PORT:5432}/${DB_NAME:non_prd_db}?currentSchema=${rp.schema}");
        d.put("spring.jpa.open-in-view", "false");
        d.put("spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto", "validate");
        d.put("management.endpoints.web.exposure.include", "health,info,metrics,prometheus");
        d.put("management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled", "true");
        d.put("spring.kafka.producer.acks", "all");
        // ... about 70 defaults
        env.getPropertySources().addLast(new MapPropertySource("ryfnPlatformDefaults", d));
    }
}

addLast makes these the lowest-priority source, so a service's own application.yml, an environment variable or a command-line argument always wins. Each service then needs only spring.application.name, rp.schema and its port.

RefinePoint: PlatformSecurityAutoConfiguration declares the ApiKeyAuthenticationFilter as a bean so it can be injected into the security chains — but Boot automatically registers every Filter bean with the servlet container too, so it would run twice (once in the main filter chain, once inside Spring Security). We add a FilterRegistrationBean with setEnabled(false) for each such filter. That is a real bug custom starters hit.

Trap: the platform jar is copied inside each service's fat jar at build time. After changing ryfn-platform, every service must be rebuilt with mvn clean package; a service that was not rebuilt keeps running the old platform code, even though the source looks right.

Testing an auto-configuration without starting an app uses ApplicationContextRunner:

new ApplicationContextRunner()
    .withConfiguration(AutoConfigurations.of(PlatformEventsAutoConfiguration.class))
    .withPropertyValues("rp.kafka.enabled=false")
    .run(ctx -> assertThat(ctx).doesNotHaveBean(OutboxRelay.class));

17.6 Starters and dependency management

A starter is a POM with dependencies and no code: spring-boot-starter-web pulls spring-boot-starter (core, logging, YAML), spring-boot-starter-json (Jackson), spring-boot-starter-tomcat, and spring-webmvc. Versions come from the spring-boot-dependencies BOM, inherited through spring-boot-starter-parent or imported with <scope>import</scope> in dependencyManagement. The parent also configures resource filtering, compiler -parameters (needed for constructor binding and @PathVariable without names), and the spring-boot-maven-plugin.

To override a managed version, set the property the BOM uses: <jackson-bom.version>2.18.2</jackson-bom.version>. Overriding one artifact's version directly breaks alignment with its siblings.

17.7 The embedded server

Boot does not use web.xml or the Servlet container's ServletContainerInitializer scanning. It registers servlets and filters through ServletContextInitializer beans: DispatcherServletRegistrationBean, every FilterRegistrationBean, and any raw Filter/Servlet bean wrapped automatically. server.* properties are applied by WebServerFactoryCustomizer beans; you can add your own.

Switching server: exclude spring-boot-starter-tomcat from spring-boot-starter-web and add spring-boot-starter-jetty (or -undertow). The factory auto-configuration's @ConditionalOnClass picks whichever is present. (Boot 4 drops Undertow, so Jetty is the safer alternative.)

Tomcat threading model (NIO connector):

 clients ──► Acceptor thread ──► Poller thread(s) (NIO selector)
                                        │ socket readable
                                        ▼
                       Executor: http-nio-8104-exec-1 .. exec-200
                       (one worker per in-flight request, blocking servlet API)
 Pending connections beyond max-connections wait in the OS backlog (accept-count)
Property Default Meaning
server.tomcat.threads.max 200 Max worker threads = max concurrent requests being processed
server.tomcat.threads.min-spare 10 Threads kept alive when idle
server.tomcat.max-connections 8192 Open connections NIO will keep (most idle, keep-alive)
server.tomcat.accept-count 100 OS backlog queue when max-connections is reached
server.tomcat.connection-timeout 60s (Tomcat's built-in default; the 20s you may remember is from a standalone server.xml) Time to wait for the request line after connect
spring.threads.virtual.enabled false Boot 3.2+: Tomcat uses a virtual thread per request

Tuning rules: the thread count should match what downstream resources can absorb. With a Hikari pool of 10 connections, 200 threads all doing DB work mostly wait on the pool (connection-timeout 30 s) — raising threads does not help. With virtual threads, the thread cap disappears, so the connection pool and downstream limits become the only backpressure; size them deliberately and add bulkheads/semaphores for slow dependencies.

RefinePoint: PlatformDefaults sets DB_POOL_SIZE to 5 per instance by default, which keeps total connections modest across 13 services on one PostgreSQL. Run capacity scales by adding run-service instances, not by adding Tomcat threads.

17.8 Externalized configuration

Precedence order

Later sources override earlier ones (Boot 3 documentation order, lowest first):

Within config data, the order (lowest first) is: application.yml inside the jar → application-{profile}.yml inside the jar → application.yml outside the jar → application-{profile}.yml outside the jar. Default search locations are classpath:/, classpath:/config/, file:./, file:./config/, file:./config/*/, later ones winning. If both .properties and .yml exist in the same location, .properties wins.

Trap: @PropertySource files are added during refresh — too late for logging.*, spring.main.* and spring.config.*, which are read before refresh. Use spring.config.import instead.

Relaxed binding maps spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size, spring.datasource.hikari.maximumPoolSize and SPRING_DATASOURCE_HIKARI_MAXIMUMPOOLSIZE to the same property. For environment variables: replace . with _, remove -, uppercase; list index rp.security.public-paths[0] becomes RP_SECURITY_PUBLICPATHS_0. @Value supports relaxed binding only when you write the canonical kebab-case form.

Placeholders with defaults (${DB_HOST:localhost}) resolve against the whole environment at the time the property is read, which is how PlatformDefaults can reference environment variables that each deployment sets.

Profiles and profile groups

spring:
  application.name: run-service
  profiles:
    group:
      prod: "prodDb,prodKafka,json-logs"     # activating prod activates all three
---
spring.config.activate.on-profile: local
rp.kafka.enabled: false
logging.level.com.ryfnflow: DEBUG
---
spring.config.activate.on-profile: prod
server.tomcat.threads.max: 100
  • Activate with --spring.profiles.active=prod or SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod; spring.profiles.default applies when none is active (default default).
  • Since Boot 2.4, spring.profiles.active and spring.profiles.include cannot appear in a profile-specific document (one activated with on-profile); use groups instead. This prevents profile activation cycles.
  • @Profile("!prod") on a bean or configuration class; Environment.acceptsProfiles(Profiles.of("prod | staging")) in code.

Keep profiles for environment shape (which beans exist), not for every value; values belong in environment variables or a secret store. Twelve-factor style: one artifact, configuration from the environment.

spring.config.import

spring:
  config:
    import:
      - optional:file:./.env[.properties]     # local secrets, if present
      - optional:configtree:/run/secrets/     # Docker/Kubernetes secret files: file name = property name
      - optional:configserver:http://config:8888

Imports are processed by ConfigDataEnvironmentPostProcessor before the rest of the configuration is resolved, so they can affect profiles and logging. optional: prevents startup failure when the location is missing.

@ConfigurationProperties

@Validated
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.storage")
public record StorageProperties(
        @NotBlank String provider,                 // s3 | azure | local
        @NotNull Duration timeout,                 // "60s" converts automatically
        @DefaultValue("4") @Min(1) int maxConcurrent,
        DataSize maxUpload) { }                    // "20MB"

@SpringBootApplication
@ConfigurationPropertiesScan                       // or @EnableConfigurationProperties(StorageProperties.class)
public class App { }

How it works: ConfigurationPropertiesBindingPostProcessor uses the Binder to walk ConfigurationPropertySources (a relaxed-name view of the environment), converting via the ConversionService (Duration, DataSize, Period, enums case-insensitive, comma lists). Records and classes with a single constructor use constructor binding automatically in Boot 3 (@ConstructorBinding is needed only to pick one of several constructors). JavaBean binding uses setters.

With @Validated and a Jakarta Validation provider on the classpath, invalid configuration fails startup with a clear report — far better than discovering a blank API key at the first call. Add spring-boot-configuration-processor (annotation processor) to generate META-INF/spring-configuration-metadata.json, which gives IDE auto-completion and documentation for your properties.

@Value @ConfigurationProperties
Relaxed binding Limited Full
Type-safe groups, nested objects, lists, maps No Yes
Validation No @Validated
SpEL Yes (#{...}) No
IDE metadata No Yes
Best for One-off value Any group of settings

17.9 Actuator

Actuator adds operational endpoints under /actuator. Since Boot 2.5 only health is exposed over HTTP by default. JMX is a separate switch (spring.jmx.enabled) and is off by default.

Endpoint Purpose
health Aggregated status of HealthIndicators; liveness/readiness groups
info Build info, git info, custom info.*
metrics, prometheus Micrometer meters; Prometheus scrape format
env, configprops Property sources and bound values (sanitised; values hidden by default in Boot 3)
beans, conditions, mappings Beans, auto-config report, request mappings
loggers Read and change log levels at runtime
threaddump, heapdump Diagnostics (protect heapdump: it contains secrets)
startup Startup steps (with BufferingApplicationStartup)
scheduledtasks, caches, flyway, httpexchanges, sbom Specific subsystems
shutdown Graceful shutdown over HTTP; disabled by default

Health and health groups

HealthEndpoint collects every HealthIndicator bean (db via a validation query, diskSpace, kafka-related, redis, ping) and aggregates with a StatusAggregator (DOWN > OUT_OF_SERVICE > UP > UNKNOWN). Overall DOWN maps to HTTP 503.

management:
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes.enabled: true          # /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness (auto on Kubernetes)
      show-details: when-authorized
      group:
        readiness:
          include: readinessState, db

Liveness must not include external dependencies. If the database blips and liveness checks the database, Kubernetes restarts every pod at once — turning a database hiccup into a full outage. Liveness = "is this JVM broken?"; readiness = "should I receive traffic?" (DB and critical downstreams can go here).

Custom indicator:

@Component("tempSpace")
class TempSpaceHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {
    private final Path tempDir;
    TempSpaceHealthIndicator(@Value("${app.temp-dir}") Path tempDir) { this.tempDir = tempDir; }

    @Override public Health health() {
        long freeMb = tempDir.toFile().getUsableSpace() / 1_048_576;
        return freeMb > 2048
            ? Health.up().withDetail("tempFreeMb", freeMb).build()
            : Health.down().withDetail("tempFreeMb", freeMb).withDetail("reason", "spill space low").build();
    }
}

Metrics with Micrometer

Micrometer is a facade (like SLF4J for metrics). Boot auto-configures a composite MeterRegistry plus one registry per backend on the classpath (micrometer-registry-prometheus, OTLP, Datadog). Instrumentation out of the box: http.server.requests, http.client.requests (for RestClient/WebClient built from Boot's builders), JVM memory/GC/threads, Hikari pool, Tomcat sessions, Kafka clients, executor and cache metrics.

@Service
class MatchMetrics {
    private final Counter breaks;
    private final Timer runTimer;
    MatchMetrics(MeterRegistry registry) {
        breaks = Counter.builder("recon.breaks").tag("type", "amount").register(registry);
        runTimer = Timer.builder("recon.run.duration").publishPercentileHistogram().register(registry);
    }
    <T> T timeRun(Supplier<T> run) { return runTimer.record(run); }
}

Boot 3 introduced the Observation API: one Observation produces both a timer metric and a trace span, and Micrometer Tracing replaced Spring Cloud Sleuth. Trace and span ids are put in the logging MDC automatically.

Trap: high-cardinality tags (user id, org code, raw URL with ids) create one time series per value and can take down Prometheus. Use templated URIs (Boot does: uri=/api/v1/organizations/{code}/runs/{id}) and bounded tag values.

RefinePoint: PlatformDefaults tags every metric with application and environment, enables percentile histograms for server and client requests, samples 10% of traces, and exports spans over OTLP only when OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT is set. PlatformObservabilityAutoConfiguration adds a dedicated security chain that lets Prometheus scrape /actuator/prometheus with a metrics token, and a filter that returns the trace id in an X-Trace-Id response header so a support ticket can quote it.

Securing Actuator

Options, usually combined: expose only what you need (management.endpoints.web.exposure.include), put management on a separate port not routed by the gateway (management.server.port=9001), and secure the endpoints with a dedicated SecurityFilterChain using EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint(). Never expose env, heapdump or configprops publicly — heapdump contains every secret in memory.

17.10 Logging

Boot uses Commons Logging internally and Logback via SLF4J by default (spring-boot-starter-logging); swap to Log4j2 by excluding it and adding spring-boot-starter-log4j2.

  • Levels: logging.level.root=INFO, logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG; groups: logging.group.recon=com.ryfnflow.crm.recon,com.ryfnflow.engine.
  • File: logging.file.name, rolling with logging.logback.rollingpolicy.max-file-size.
  • logback-spring.xml (not logback.xml) lets Boot initialise it and enables <springProfile name="prod"> and <springProperty>.
  • Structured logging (Boot 3.4): logging.structured.format.console=ecs (or logstash, gelf) writes one JSON object per line. RefinePoint switches this on with LOG_FORMAT=json.
  • Change level at runtime without restart:
curl -X POST localhost:8104/actuator/loggers/com.ryfnflow.crm.recon \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}'

This changes only the instance you call; in a multi-instance deployment you call each instance (or use a config-refresh mechanism).

17.11 Graceful shutdown

Boot 3.4 enables graceful shutdown by default for all embedded servers (server.shutdown=graceful; in earlier versions you had to set it). The sequence on SIGTERM:

spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase (default 30 s) bounds each lifecycle phase. On Kubernetes, the pod is removed from endpoints asynchronously, so add a preStop sleep of a few seconds to avoid new requests arriving after the server stopped accepting. Background work must also be graceful: a DB-queue worker should stop claiming new rows and let the current one finish or release it.

RefinePoint: run-service workers claim a run with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and commit the claim (status = 'RUNNING', instance, heartbeat_at), so no lock is held while the run executes. On a normal stop, RunWorker's @PreDestroy puts that instance's runs back to QUEUED for another instance. If the JVM is killed, @PreDestroy never runs: the 15-second heartbeat goes stale and a reaper on another instance fails any run silent for two minutes, so no run stays RUNNING forever. Design for the kill, not only for the polite stop.

17.12 Fat jar layout and layered jars

recon-service.jar
├── META-INF/MANIFEST.MF
│     Main-Class: org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher   (Boot 3.2+ package)
│     Start-Class: com.ryfnflow.crm.recon.ReconApplication
│     Spring-Boot-Classes: BOOT-INF/classes/
│     Spring-Boot-Lib: BOOT-INF/lib/
├── org/springframework/boot/loader/...     ← the launcher, stored uncompressed at the root
├── BOOT-INF/classes/                       ← your classes and application.yml
├── BOOT-INF/lib/                           ← every dependency jar, nested, NOT unpacked
│     ryfn-platform-1.0.jar, spring-webmvc-6.2.x.jar, ...
├── BOOT-INF/classpath.idx                  ← jar order on the classpath
└── BOOT-INF/layers.idx                     ← which file goes in which Docker layer

The JVM cannot load classes from a jar inside a jar. JarLauncher creates a class loader with a custom jar:nested: URL handler that reads nested entries directly (they are stored uncompressed), then calls Start-Class.main() reflectively on a new thread context class loader.

Layered jars split the content into layers ordered by change frequency: dependencies, spring-boot-loader, snapshot-dependencies, application. In a Dockerfile:

java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract --layers --launcher --destination extracted   # Boot 3.3+

then COPY each layer separately. Code changes rebuild only the small application layer; the 80 MB of dependencies stay cached in the registry and on nodes. Cloud Native Buildpacks (mvn spring-boot:build-image) do this automatically.

17.13 Boot 2 → 3 migration

Area Boot 2.x Boot 3.x
Java baseline 8 / 11 17 (21 recommended)
Jakarta EE javax.* jakarta.* (Servlet 6, JPA 3.1, Validation 3)
Spring Framework 5.3 6.x
Hibernate 5.x 6.x (new SQM query engine, sequence naming changes)
Auto-config registration spring.factories AutoConfiguration.imports only
Security WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter (deprecated 5.7) SecurityFilterChain beans, lambda DSL, requestMatchers
Tracing Spring Cloud Sleuth Micrometer Tracing + Observation API
URL matching /runs/ matched /runs Trailing slash match disabled
Errors Custom bodies ProblemDetail (RFC 7807/9457) support
HTTP clients RestTemplate, WebClient + RestClient (3.2), HTTP interfaces
Native Experimental (Spring Native) AOT + GraalVM native built in

Migration path that works: upgrade to the latest 2.7 first and remove deprecation warnings, add spring-boot-properties-migrator temporarily (it logs renamed properties at startup), move to Java 17, then switch to 3.x and run the OpenRewrite UpgradeSpringBoot_3_x recipe for javax → jakarta. Check every third-party library for a Jakarta-compatible version — that is usually the long pole.

17.14 AOT, native images and CRaC

Spring AOT runs at build time: it starts the application context in analysis mode with the build classpath, evaluates conditions, and generates Java source for bean definitions (plain new and method calls instead of reflection), plus RuntimeHints (reflection, resources, proxies, serialization) for GraalVM.

GraalVM native image compiles the application into a platform binary under a closed-world assumption: everything reachable must be known at build time.

JVM Native image
Startup Seconds Tens of milliseconds
Memory Higher Much lower
Peak throughput Best (JIT) Lower without PGO
Build time Fast Minutes, memory-hungry
Reflection/dynamic proxies Free Must be declared (hints)
@Profile / @ConditionalOnProperty Evaluated at runtime Fixed at build time

Native fits serverless, CLIs and scale-to-zero. Long-running services under steady load (like reconciliation workers) are better on the JVM. Middle-ground options: CDS/AppCDS (Boot 3.3 supports extracting and training a class-data archive, roughly 30–40% faster startup), AOT on the JVM (-Dspring.aot.enabled=true) and CRaC (Boot 3.2: checkpoint a warmed JVM and restore it).

17.15 DevTools and startup optimisation

DevTools (scope developmentOnly/optional, excluded from the fat jar) uses two class loaders: a base loader for jars that do not change and a restart loader for your classes. On a class change, only the restart loader is thrown away, so a restart takes about a second. It also disables template caching, enables LiveReload and applies developer-friendly defaults. It is disabled automatically when running from a fat jar.

Startup time checklist:

  1. Measure first: BufferingApplicationStartup + /actuator/startup, or the --debug report.
  2. Exclude auto-configurations you do not need; narrow component scanning.
  3. spring.main.lazy-initialization=true for dev/test (in production it hides wiring errors until the first request and shifts latency to that request).
  4. Avoid heavy work in @PostConstruct — move warm-up to ApplicationReadyEvent or async.
  5. Hibernate: ddl-auto=validate (not update), avoid scanning huge packages; Flyway validation is fast but migrations on startup are not.
  6. CDS archive, AOT, or native image for the remaining gap.
  7. JVM flags: -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 only for local dev.

17.16 Interview questions and answers

Q1. What is Spring Boot and how is it different from Spring Framework?

Spring Boot is an opinionated layer on Spring Framework that auto-configures beans from the classpath, provides starters, an embedded server and production features. The framework provides the container, AOP, MVC and data access; Boot decides which framework beans to create and with what defaults. Everything Boot creates is a normal bean you can replace — that is the key difference from a "black box" framework.

Q2. What does @SpringBootApplication do?

It combines @SpringBootConfiguration (a @Configuration that tests can find), @EnableAutoConfiguration (imports the deferred AutoConfigurationImportSelector and registers the auto-configuration package) and @ComponentScan of the main class's package with filters that skip auto-configuration classes. You can use the three annotations separately when you need different scanning.

Q3. Walk me through what happens when SpringApplication.run() is called.

Construction deduces the web type and loads initializers and listeners from spring.factories. run() then creates the bootstrap context, publishes ApplicationStartingEvent, prepares the environment (command-line args, config data, EnvironmentPostProcessors), prints the banner, creates the right ApplicationContext, runs initializers, registers the main class, refreshes the context (bean factory post-processors including auto-configuration, bean post-processors, web server creation, singleton instantiation, web server start), publishes ApplicationStartedEvent, calls runners and finally publishes ApplicationReadyEvent. Mention readiness turning green only at the end — it shows you understand why probes matter.

Q4. In what order are Spring Boot application events published?

ApplicationStartingEvent → ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent → ApplicationContextInitializedEvent → ApplicationPreparedEvent → (during refresh) WebServerInitializedEvent and ContextRefreshedEvent → ApplicationStartedEvent + LivenessState.CORRECT → runners → ApplicationReadyEvent + ReadinessState.ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC. ApplicationFailedEvent on failure. The first four happen before your beans exist.

Q5. Why does my @EventListener(ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent.class) bean never fire?

Because the event is published before the context is refreshed, so the listener bean does not exist yet. Register the listener in META-INF/spring.factories (org.springframework.context.ApplicationListener=...) or with springApplication.addListeners(...) before run(). For changing the environment, an EnvironmentPostProcessor is the cleaner tool.

Q6. How does auto-configuration work internally?

@EnableAutoConfiguration imports AutoConfigurationImportSelector, a DeferredImportSelector. After user configuration is parsed, it reads all META-INF/spring/...AutoConfiguration.imports files, removes exclusions, pre-filters with build-time metadata (OnClass, OnBean, OnWebApplication) without loading classes, sorts by @AutoConfigureOrder/before/after, and hands the survivors to ConfigurationClassPostProcessor. Each class and @Bean method is then guarded by @Conditional annotations, so beans appear only when the classpath, properties and existing beans call for them. The outcome is recorded in the ConditionEvaluationReport.

Q7. What changed between spring.factories and AutoConfiguration.imports?

Boot 2.7 introduced the AutoConfiguration.imports file and the @AutoConfiguration annotation; Boot 3.0 removed the EnableAutoConfiguration key from spring.factories. The new file is one class per line, simpler to read and merge. spring.factories still registers other extension points such as EnvironmentPostProcessor and FailureAnalyzer — RefinePoint uses both files in ryfn-platform.

Q8. What is @AutoConfiguration and how is it different from @Configuration?

It is a meta-annotation of @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false) with before/after/beforeName/afterName attributes for ordering. proxyBeanMethods = false means no CGLIB subclass: calling one @Bean method from another creates a new object instead of returning the singleton, so auto-configurations inject dependencies through method parameters. It also signals that the class must be loaded via the imports file, not component scanning.

Q9. How does @ConditionalOnMissingBean let me override Boot's beans?

User configuration is processed first because the auto-configuration selector is deferred. When Boot reaches, say, JacksonAutoConfiguration, your ObjectMapper definition already exists, so the condition fails and Boot's bean is skipped. It matches on type by default (and optionally name or annotation). It is only reliable in auto-configuration classes; in your own @Configuration classes the parsing order is not guaranteed.

Q10. Name the most important @Conditional annotations.

@ConditionalOnClass/OnMissingClass, @ConditionalOnBean/OnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnSingleCandidate, @ConditionalOnProperty, @ConditionalOnResource, @ConditionalOnWebApplication/OnNotWebApplication, @ConditionalOnExpression, @ConditionalOnJava, @ConditionalOnCloudPlatform and @ConditionalOnThreading (Boot 3.2, virtual threads). All are built on Spring's Condition interface, which you can implement for custom logic.

Q11. @ConditionalOnProperty(name="x.enabled", havingValue="true", matchIfMissing=true) — what are the cases?

Property absent → matches (because of matchIfMissing). Property true → matches. Property false or any other value → does not match. Without havingValue, any value except false matches. RefinePoint's OutboxRelay uses exactly this with rp.kafka.enabled, so Kafka is on unless explicitly turned off.

Q12. Why should @ConditionalOnClass not be used on a @Bean method whose return type is the conditional class?

When Spring introspects the configuration class it loads method signatures; if the return type class is missing, introspection throws NoClassDefFoundError before the condition is evaluated. Put the condition at class level or on a nested static configuration class, which isolates the reference.

Q13. How do you find out why an auto-configuration did or did not apply?

Start with --debug (or debug=true) to print the Conditions Evaluation Report with positive matches, negative matches with reasons, exclusions and unconditional classes. At runtime use /actuator/conditions, plus /actuator/beans to see which bean won and /actuator/configprops/env to check the properties that drove the conditions. In tests, ApplicationContextRunner reproduces the scenario in milliseconds.

Q14. How do you disable a specific auto-configuration?

@SpringBootApplication(exclude = X.class) or excludeName for classes not on the classpath, or the spring.autoconfigure.exclude property, which can be profile-specific. Excluding is preferable to defining a dummy bean, which leaves the rest of the auto-configuration active and confusing.

Q15. How do you control auto-configuration ordering, and what does it not control?

@AutoConfiguration(before/after), @AutoConfigureBefore/After and @AutoConfigureOrder control the order in which auto-configurations are parsed, which matters for @ConditionalOnBean. They do not order user configurations and do not decide bean instantiation order — dependencies do (@DependsOn if there is no injection relationship).

Q16. How would you write a custom Spring Boot starter?

Create an autoconfigure module with @AutoConfiguration classes guarded by conditions, a @ConfigurationProperties class with the configuration processor for metadata, register the classes in META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports, use @ConditionalOnMissingBean on every bean so applications can override, and test with ApplicationContextRunner. Then create a starter POM that depends on the autoconfigure module and required libraries. Name it xyz-spring-boot-starter.

Q17. Tell me about a starter you built.

RefinePoint: "We have 13 services and every one needs the same security, tenancy checks, outbox, Kafka settings, observability and OpenAPI. I built ryfn-platform, a shared library with six auto-configurations. Security defines three ordered SecurityFilterChains: public paths (health, docs and the service's own rp.security.public-paths), /internal/** with a shared internal token, and everything else with a Keycloak JWT or an X-API-Key. PlatformWebAutoConfiguration registers OrgAccessInterceptor on /api/v1/organizations/*/** so no controller can forget membership and role checks. Defaults such as the datasource URL with a per-service schema, open-in-view=false, Kafka acks=all and Actuator exposure come from an EnvironmentPostProcessor added with lowest priority. A new service is a main class, its schema name and its business code."

Q18. What is an EnvironmentPostProcessor and when do you use it?

A hook, registered in spring.factories, that can add or modify property sources after the environment is prepared and before the context is created. Use it for defaults shared by many applications, decrypting properties, or deriving properties from others (RefinePoint builds the Kafka SASL JAAS string from KAFKA_USERNAME/KAFKA_PASSWORD). Use addLast for defaults that applications can override, addFirst for values that must win.

Q19. A filter bean in your starter runs twice per request. Why?

Boot auto-registers every jakarta.servlet.Filter bean with the servlet container. If the same filter is also added to a Spring Security chain with addFilterBefore, it runs once in the container chain and once in the security chain. Fix: declare a FilterRegistrationBean for it with setEnabled(false), or do not make it a bean. Extending OncePerRequestFilter only prevents re-execution within the same filter instance's attribute, which helps but is not the real fix.

Q20. What is a starter and how does dependency management work?

A starter is a POM that groups dependencies for one capability, with no code. Versions come from the spring-boot-dependencies BOM, inherited through spring-boot-starter-parent or imported in dependencyManagement. Override a version via the BOM property (<postgresql.version>) so aligned modules move together.

Q21. How does the embedded Tomcat start?

During onRefresh, ServletWebServerApplicationContext asks the ServletWebServerFactory bean for a WebServer; the Tomcat factory creates Tomcat, a connector and a context and runs ServletContextInitializer beans (dispatcher servlet, filters, listeners). The connector is started later, in finishRefresh, by WebServerStartStopLifecycle, after all singletons exist — so the port opens only when the app can serve requests. ServletWebServerInitializedEvent then carries the real port.

Q22. How do you switch from Tomcat to Jetty or Undertow?

Exclude spring-boot-starter-tomcat from spring-boot-starter-web and add spring-boot-starter-jetty. The ServletWebServerFactoryAutoConfiguration imports factory configurations each guarded by @ConditionalOnClass of the server classes, so whichever server is on the classpath wins. Undertow is not supported in Boot 4.

Q23. How do you tune Tomcat for high concurrency?

Size server.tomcat.threads.max (200 default), max-connections (8192) and accept-count (100) together with the database pool and downstream limits; threads beyond what the pool can serve only queue on the pool. Set connection and keep-alive timeouts, enable response compression only where useful, and measure with tomcat.threads.busy and Hikari pending metrics. On Java 21, spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true removes the thread cap for I/O-bound services; then protect downstreams explicitly.

Q24. What changes when you enable virtual threads in Boot 3.2+?

Tomcat (and Jetty) run each request on a new virtual thread; @Async, @Scheduled executors, Kafka listener containers and others use virtual threads where Boot configures them. Blocking calls unmount the virtual thread instead of holding a platform thread. Watch for pinning on synchronized blocks around I/O (fixed in JDK 24, still present on 21), ThreadLocal heavy caches, and the fact that thread pools no longer limit concurrency.

Q25. Explain the property source precedence order.

From lowest to highest: default properties, @PropertySource, config data files (jar then external, base then profile-specific), random.*, OS environment variables, Java system properties, JNDI and servlet parameters, SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON, command-line arguments, then test-specific sources and DevTools global settings. A good one-liner: "the closer to the deployment, the higher the priority".

Q26. A property set in application.yml is ignored in production. How do you debug?

Check /actuator/env/<property.name> — it shows every property source that defines it and which one wins. Common causes: an environment variable with the relaxed name overriding it (SERVER_PORT set by the platform), an external application.yml next to the jar, a profile document overriding it, a typo or wrong prefix (the configuration processor's metadata catches this in the IDE), or @PropertySource being too late for that property.

Q27. How do environment variables map to properties?

Relaxed binding: uppercase, . → _, remove dashes: spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size → SPRING_DATASOURCE_HIKARI_MAXIMUMPOOLSIZE. List elements use _0_ style indices: RP_SECURITY_PUBLICPATHS_0. Map keys keep their case only with bracket notation in properties files, not in env vars.

Q28. What are profiles and profile groups?

Profiles are named sets of configuration and beans activated per environment (spring.profiles.active). Groups let one name activate several: spring.profiles.group.prod=prodDb,prodKafka. Profile-specific documents use spring.config.activate.on-profile; they cannot themselves activate profiles. Use @Profile on beans that should exist only in some environments, like a fake payment gateway for local.

Q29. What is spring.config.import used for?

Loading additional configuration early in config-data processing: extra files (optional:file:./.env[.properties]), directory trees of secrets (configtree:/run/secrets/), Spring Cloud Config (configserver:), Vault or Consul. Because it runs in config-data processing, imported values can affect profiles, logging and anything else, unlike @PropertySource.

Q30. @Value vs @ConfigurationProperties?

@ConfigurationProperties binds a prefix into a typed, validated, immutable object with full relaxed binding and IDE metadata — use it for any group of settings. @Value injects a single value and supports SpEL, but scatters keys across the code, cannot validate and does not support relaxed binding fully. In code review I convert anything with more than one or two related @Values into a properties record.

Q31. How does @ConfigurationProperties binding work and how do you validate it?

ConfigurationPropertiesBindingPostProcessor uses the Binder over relaxed ConfigurationPropertySources and the ConversionService; records and single-constructor classes bind through the constructor, others through setters. Add @Validated and Jakarta constraints (@NotBlank, @Min, @Valid on nested objects); a violation fails startup with a report listing each invalid property. Fail-fast configuration is a production safety net.

Q32. How do you bind durations and sizes?

Use java.time.Duration and org.springframework.util.unit.DataSize fields; values like 30s, 500ms, 2h, 10MB convert automatically. A plain number uses the default unit (milliseconds for Duration, bytes for DataSize), which you can change with @DurationUnit/@DataSizeUnit. This avoids the classic timeout=30 "seconds or millis?" bug.

Q33. What does Actuator provide out of the box, and what is exposed by default?

Health, info, metrics, Prometheus, env, configprops, beans, conditions, mappings, loggers, thread dump, heap dump, startup, scheduled tasks, caches, Flyway, HTTP exchanges, SBOM and shutdown. Over HTTP only health is exposed by default; everything else must be listed in management.endpoints.web.exposure.include. shutdown is also disabled until enabled explicitly.

Q34. How do liveness and readiness probes work in Boot?

Boot tracks LivenessState and ReadinessState via ApplicationAvailability, updated by lifecycle events. With probes enabled (automatic on Kubernetes), /actuator/health/liveness and /actuator/health/readiness are health groups. Readiness becomes ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC only after runners finish and becomes REFUSING_TRAFFIC at shutdown. You can publish AvailabilityChangeEvent yourself, for example to refuse traffic while a large cache reloads.

Q35. Should the database be part of the liveness probe?

No. Liveness failure restarts the pod; if the database is down, restarting every instance does not fix it and causes a thundering-herd restart. Put critical dependencies in readiness (or nowhere, and rely on circuit breakers), and keep liveness about the process itself (deadlock, out of memory).

Q36. How do you write a custom health indicator?

Implement HealthIndicator (or ReactiveHealthIndicator) as a bean; the bean name minus HealthIndicator becomes the component name. Return Health.up()/down() with details. Keep it fast and side-effect-free — health is called frequently; cache expensive checks. Add it to a group with management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.include.

Q37. How do you add custom metrics?

Inject MeterRegistry and register Counter, Timer, Gauge, DistributionSummary or LongTaskTimer, or use @Timed/@Counted (with the aspect bean) or the Observation API (Observation.createNotStarted("recon.run", registry).observe(...)) to get a metric and a span together. Keep tag values bounded, add common tags (application, environment) once via management.metrics.tags.*, and enable histograms for latency SLOs.

Q38. How do you secure Actuator?

Expose only what is needed, run management on a separate internal port if possible, and secure with a dedicated SecurityFilterChain matching EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint(). Health can be public with show-details: when-authorized; Prometheus is scraped with a token or from an internal network; env, configprops and heapdump should never be reachable from the internet. Boot 3 sanitises all env/configprops values by default (show-values: never).

Q39. How do you change a log level in production without a restart?

POST /actuator/loggers/{logger} with {"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}, then reset with null. It is per instance and not persistent. For fleet-wide changes, use a config refresh mechanism or restart with LOGGING_LEVEL_COM_RYFNFLOW=DEBUG. Turn it back off — debug logging on a hot path can halve throughput.

Q40. What is the difference between logback.xml and logback-spring.xml?

logback.xml is loaded by Logback itself before Boot initialises logging, so it cannot use Boot extensions. logback-spring.xml is loaded by Boot's LoggingSystem and supports <springProfile> and <springProperty>. Prefer properties (logging.*, structured logging in 3.4) and add a Spring XML file only for appenders properties cannot express.

Q41. How does graceful shutdown work?

On SIGTERM the JVM shutdown hook closes the context: readiness flips to REFUSING_TRAFFIC, the web server stops accepting new connections and waits for in-flight requests up to spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase (30 s), then other SmartLifecycle beans stop (listeners, schedulers), then singletons are destroyed (@PreDestroy, pools closed). Boot 3.4 makes server.shutdown=graceful the default. Add a preStop sleep on Kubernetes and make background workers stop claiming new work.

Q42. What is inside a Spring Boot fat jar and how does it run?

The manifest's Main-Class is JarLauncher (package org.springframework.boot.loader.launch since 3.2) and Start-Class is your main class. Your classes are in BOOT-INF/classes, dependencies are nested jars in BOOT-INF/lib, plus classpath.idx and layers.idx. The launcher builds a class loader that reads nested jars directly via a custom URL handler and invokes your main. The jars are stored uncompressed so they can be read in place.

Q43. What are layered jars and why use them?

A fat jar split into layers by change frequency (dependencies, spring-boot-loader, snapshot-dependencies, application) recorded in layers.idx. Extract with -Djarmode=tools extract --layers and copy each layer into its own Docker layer. A code change rebuilds and pushes only the few-MB application layer, so builds, pushes and pulls are much faster.

Q44. What were the main challenges migrating Boot 2 to 3?

Java 17 baseline; javax → jakarta namespace across code and every library (third-party libraries without Jakarta versions block you); spring.factories auto-configuration no longer loaded; Spring Security 6 removed WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter and antMatchers; Hibernate 6 query and ID-generation changes; Sleuth replaced by Micrometer Tracing; trailing-slash matching off; property renames. Go via 2.7, use spring-boot-properties-migrator and OpenRewrite, and run the full integration test suite.

Q45. What is Spring AOT and how does it relate to GraalVM native image?

Spring AOT runs during the build, evaluates the context with the build-time classpath and generates source code for bean definitions plus runtime hints. Native image then compiles the app ahead of time under a closed-world assumption, using those hints for reflection, proxies and resources. The result starts in milliseconds and uses far less memory, but conditions and profiles are frozen at build time and peak throughput is usually lower than a JIT-warmed JVM.

Q46. When would you not use a native image?

For long-running, throughput-heavy services (reconciliation engines, batch workers) where startup time is irrelevant and JIT optimisation wins; for apps relying on runtime classpath changes, dynamic class generation or plugins loaded via ServiceLoader from external jars (RefinePoint's connector plugins); and when build-time cost slows the team down. CDS or CRaC give much of the startup gain with fewer constraints.

Q47. What does DevTools do and why is it excluded from production?

It restarts the app quickly using a separate restart class loader for your classes, disables caches, triggers LiveReload and can support remote updates. It is excluded from fat jars (developmentOnly/optional) and disables itself when running from a jar, because restart class loaders and remote update endpoints are a security and stability risk. A known side effect in dev: two class loaders can cause ClassCastException for classes deserialized by libraries loaded in the base loader.

Q48. How would you reduce startup time of a Boot service?

Measure with /actuator/startup or the startup log first. Then exclude unused auto-configurations, narrow scanning, move warm-up work off the startup path, use ddl-auto=validate, avoid eager remote calls in @PostConstruct, and consider CDS, AOT on the JVM, CRaC or native. Lazy initialisation helps in tests and dev, but in production it defers errors and first-request latency.

Q49. What is ApplicationRunner vs CommandLineRunner, and what is a better alternative for warm-up?

Both run after the context starts and before ApplicationReadyEvent; ApplicationRunner receives parsed ApplicationArguments, CommandLineRunner the raw String[]. They block startup and their exceptions fail the app — good for one-off jobs or mandatory checks. For warm-up that should not fail startup or delay readiness, listen to ApplicationReadyEvent and run asynchronously.
