Q50. What does bean definition overriding being disabled mean?

Since Boot 2.1, registering two bean definitions with the same name fails startup (BeanDefinitionOverrideException) instead of silently replacing the first. You can re-enable it with spring.main.allow-bean-definition-overriding=true, but the right fix is a distinct name, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, or @Primary.

Q51. Your service fails with "Parameter 0 of constructor in X required a bean of type Y that could not be found". How do you approach it?

That message comes from a FailureAnalyzer. Check whether Y is in a scanned package (main class package and below), whether an auto-configuration that would create it was skipped (look in the conditions report for Y's auto-configuration and why it did not match), whether a profile or property disabled it, or whether a starter is missing from the classpath. In RefinePoint, for example, OutboxRelay exists only when rp.kafka.enabled is true, so a class injecting it directly would fail exactly like this under KAFKA_ENABLED=false.

Q52. How does Boot decide between a servlet and a reactive application?

WebApplicationType.deduceFromClasspath(): if DispatcherHandler (WebFlux) is present and DispatcherServlet and Jersey are absent → REACTIVE; if servlet classes are present → SERVLET; else NONE. With both MVC and WebFlux on the classpath, SERVLET wins (you can still use WebClient). Override with spring.main.web-application-type.

Q53. How do you test that your auto-configuration backs off correctly?

ApplicationContextRunner with withConfiguration(AutoConfigurations.of(...)), withUserConfiguration(MyOverride.class) and withPropertyValues(...); assert with assertThat(context).hasSingleBean(...), doesNotHaveBean(...) or hasFailed(). Use FilteredClassLoader to simulate a missing class for @ConditionalOnClass cases. Tests run in milliseconds and cover each condition branch.

Q54. How do you share common configuration across many microservices?

Options: a shared starter with auto-configurations and an EnvironmentPostProcessor for defaults (RefinePoint's choice, versioned with the code), a config server or Kubernetes ConfigMaps for environment values, and secrets in a vault/secret store via configtree or config-data loaders. Keep secrets out of the jar; keep defaults overridable; document every property with configuration metadata.

Q55. What do you check before taking a Boot service to production?

Graceful shutdown and probes configured; Actuator exposure locked down; metrics with common tags and latency histograms; structured logs with trace ids; open-in-view=false; ddl-auto=validate with Flyway owning the schema; connection pool sized to the database limit; timeouts on every outbound client; configuration validated at startup; layered jar or buildpack image; JVM container settings (-XX:MaxRAMPercentage). RefinePoint's PlatformDefaults encodes most of this list so no service can forget it.

18. Spring MVC & REST APIs

Senior REST interviews split into two halves. The first is mechanics: what happens between the socket and your controller, why an interceptor cannot change a @ResponseBody, why an exception thrown in a filter skips @ControllerAdvice. The second is design: which status code, how to page a million rows, how to make POST safe to retry. This chapter covers both, then shows how RefinePoint applies them across 13 services.

18.1 The request flow

Tomcat parses the request, runs the servlet filter chain, then calls one servlet: DispatcherServlet, the front controller. Everything after that is Spring's doDispatch method.

The steps in doDispatch, in order:

  1. checkMultipart wraps multipart requests.
  2. getHandler asks each HandlerMapping in order. RequestMappingHandlerMapping holds a registry of every @RequestMapping built at startup and matches path, method, consumes, produces, params and headers. It returns a HandlerExecutionChain: the HandlerMethod plus matching interceptors. No match leads to the resource handler and then a 404.
  3. getHandlerAdapter picks the adapter that can invoke this handler type.
  4. applyPreHandle runs interceptors in order; returning false stops the request.
  5. ha.handle resolves arguments, invokes your method, and processes the return value. For @ResponseBody, the body is serialised and written here.
  6. applyPostHandle runs in reverse order.
  7. processDispatchResult handles any exception via HandlerExceptionResolvers, renders a view if there is one, and calls afterCompletion.

Trap: postHandle cannot reliably change a REST response. The body was already written in step 5, and the response may be committed. To modify bodies use ResponseBodyAdvice; to add headers use a filter, or preHandle.

Matching since Boot 2.6 uses PathPatternParser (parsed patterns, faster than AntPathMatcher). ** is allowed only at the end of a pattern. Boot 3 no longer treats /runs/ as /runs.

18.2 Filters vs interceptors vs AOP

Filter Interceptor AOP aspect
Level Servlet API DispatcherServlet Bean proxy
Runs for Every request, including static and error paths Only requests mapped by MVC Any proxied call, HTTP or not
Sees Request and response, can wrap them Request, response, handler Method args and return value
Can replace the request/response object Yes, by wrapping No No
Exceptions reach @ControllerAdvice No Yes Yes, if under a controller call
Typical use Auth, CORS, tracing, compression Tenant and role checks, per-route logic Transactions, caching, metrics

Rule of thumb: pick the outermost layer that has the information you need. Authentication goes in a filter because it must run before anything else; a check that needs the matched route belongs in an interceptor; a business rule belongs in the service.

RefinePoint: OrgAccessInterceptor is a HandlerInterceptor registered by PlatformWebAutoConfiguration on /api/v1/organizations/*/**. GET and HEAD need any role in the workspace, writes need at least MEMBER, and a locked workspace takes only what WorkspaceLocks allows. Because it is in the shared library, no controller in any service can forget the check. Stricter rules stay on the controller as @PreAuthorize. It is an interceptor rather than a filter because its exceptions must reach GlobalExceptionHandler and become our normal JSON error.

18.3 Controllers, mapping and arguments

@RestController is @Controller + @ResponseBody on every method: return values go through message converters rather than being treated as view names.

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/organizations/{orgCode}/notifications/inbox")
class InboxApi {
    @GetMapping
    ApiResponse<List<Notification>> mine(@PathVariable String orgCode,
                                         @RequestParam(defaultValue = "50") int limit,
                                         @RequestHeader(value = "Accept-Language", required = false) String lang,
                                         @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) { ... }
}

Each parameter is handled by a HandlerMethodArgumentResolver, the first whose supportsParameter returns true:

Annotation / type Source Notes
@PathVariable URI template -parameters compile flag needed if the name is omitted (Boot's parent sets it)
@RequestParam Query or form Required by default; missing gives 400
@RequestHeader, @CookieValue Header, cookie
@RequestBody Body via converter Needs Content-Type a converter accepts, else 415
@RequestPart One multipart part Can be a JSON DTO, unlike @RequestParam
@ModelAttribute (implicit for POJOs) Query and form fields bound to setters Mass-assignment risk
Pageable, Sort page, size, sort params Registered by Spring Data web support
Authentication, Principal Security context

A custom resolver gives a clean signature for a repeated need:

record OrgContext(UUID orgId, OrgRole role) { }

class OrgContextResolver implements HandlerMethodArgumentResolver {
    public boolean supportsParameter(MethodParameter p) { return p.getParameterType() == OrgContext.class; }
    public Object resolveArgument(MethodParameter p, ModelAndViewContainer m, NativeWebRequest req, WebDataBinderFactory f) {
        String code = req.getHeader("X-Org-Code");
        return lookup(code);   // generic sketch, registered through WebMvcConfigurer.addArgumentResolvers
    }
}

18.4 HttpMessageConverters, Jackson and content negotiation

@RequestBody and @ResponseBody are handled by RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor, which picks an HttpMessageConverter by Java type and media type.

For a request, the Content-Type selects the converter (Content-Type: application/xml with no XML converter gives 415). For a response, Accept drives negotiation. Path-extension negotiation (/runs.json) was removed for security reasons; query-parameter negotiation is opt-in.

Boot's JacksonAutoConfiguration builds one ObjectMapper from spring.jackson.* and all Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer beans, with defaults different from plain Jackson: FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES=false, WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS=false, and the JavaTimeModule registered.

Trap: declaring @Bean ObjectMapper om() { return new ObjectMapper(); } backs off Boot's mapper entirely. Instant fields then fail or serialise oddly, and unknown JSON fields start throwing 400s. Use a Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer or spring.jackson.* to adjust rather than replace.

Common settings: @JsonInclude(NON_NULL), @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true) on DTOs read from third parties, @JsonProperty(access = WRITE_ONLY) for passwords, BigDecimal kept as a string or plain number for money (never double).

18.5 Validation

Add spring-boot-starter-validation (it stopped being part of the web starter in Boot 2.3), which brings Hibernate Validator.

public record CreateRuleRequest(
        @NotBlank @Size(max = 200) String name,
        @NotNull @DecimalMin("0.00") BigDecimal tolerance,
        @Valid @NotEmpty List<FieldPair> fields) { }   // @Valid cascades into elements

@PostMapping
ApiResponse<RuleDto> create(@PathVariable String orgCode, @Valid @RequestBody CreateRuleRequest body) { ... }
Where Trigger Exception thrown
@Valid @RequestBody Argument resolver MethodArgumentNotValidException
@ModelAttribute params Binding BindException / MethodArgumentNotValidException (Boot 3)
Constraints directly on @RequestParam, @PathVariable Built-in method validation (Spring 6.1) HandlerMethodValidationException
@Validated on a service class AOP proxy (MethodValidationPostProcessor) ConstraintViolationException

@Valid vs @Validated: @Valid is the Jakarta annotation and cascades into nested objects. @Validated is Spring's: it supports groups and, on a class, turns on method validation through a proxy. Because it is a proxy, self-invocation is not validated.

Groups let one DTO have per-operation rules:

interface OnCreate { }
interface OnUpdate { }
record RuleDto(@Null(groups = OnCreate.class) @NotNull(groups = OnUpdate.class) UUID id, @NotBlank String name) { }

@PostMapping ApiResponse<RuleDto> create(@Validated(OnCreate.class) @RequestBody RuleDto dto) { ... }

Note that a constraint with no groups belongs to Default, which is not checked when you name another group, unless your group extends Default. Separate request records are usually clearer than groups.

Custom constraint:

@Target(FIELD) @Retention(RUNTIME) @Constraint(validatedBy = CurrencyCodeValidator.class)
public @interface CurrencyCode {
    String message() default "must be an ISO 4217 code";
    Class<?>[] groups() default {};
    Class<? extends Payload>[] payload() default {};
}
class CurrencyCodeValidator implements ConstraintValidator<CurrencyCode, String> {
    public boolean isValid(String v, ConstraintValidatorContext c) {
        return v == null || Currency.getAvailableCurrencies().stream().anyMatch(x -> x.getCurrencyCode().equals(v));
    }
}

Validators return true for null by convention, so that @NotNull stays a separate, composable rule. Validators are Spring beans and may inject dependencies.

18.6 Global exception handling

The closest matching exception type wins, and a local @ExceptionHandler in the controller beats any @ControllerAdvice. Advices can be ordered with @Order and limited with basePackages, assignableTypes or annotations.

Filter exceptions skip this. Spring Security translates its own in ExceptionTranslationFilter; for your own filters, either write the response directly or inject the HandlerExceptionResolver bean named handlerExceptionResolver and delegate to it.

ProblemDetail (RFC 7807, updated by RFC 9457) is the standard error body, supported since Spring 6:

@RestControllerAdvice
class Errors extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler {   // handles standard MVC exceptions
    @ExceptionHandler(PlanLimitExceededException.class)
    ProblemDetail limit(PlanLimitExceededException e) {
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.PAYMENT_REQUIRED, e.getMessage());
        pd.setType(URI.create("https://example.com/errors/plan-limit"));
        pd.setProperty("limit", e.limit());
        return pd;      // Content-Type: application/problem+json
    }
}

Setting spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true makes Boot register such an advice for standard exceptions.

RefinePoint: we use our own envelope, not ProblemDetail, so the React client has one shape to handle on success and failure. ApiResponse<T> carries success, data, message, errors and meta (timestamp, requestId). GlobalExceptionHandler in ryfn-platform maps exceptions centrally: EntityNotFoundException to 404, validation and IllegalArgumentException to 400, AccessDeniedException to 403, ConflictException to 409, RateLimitExceededException to 429, PlanLimitExceededException to 402, WorkspaceLockedException to 423. One detail worth telling: a request with Accept: text/event-stream cannot carry a JSON error, and trying to write one fails the handler itself. So a forClient helper returns the status alone for those.

Envelope vs ProblemDetail: an envelope gives clients a uniform parse and room for metadata. Its costs are that it duplicates what HTTP status already says, and generic tools do not understand it. ProblemDetail is the standard and fits public APIs. Either is defensible; being consistent matters more. Never send stack traces, SQL or class names to the client (server.error.include-stacktrace=never, which is the default).

18.7 REST design

REST constraints: client-server, stateless, cacheable, uniform interface, layered system, code on demand (optional). Most "REST" APIs are Richardson level 2: resources + HTTP verbs + status codes. Level 3 adds hypermedia.

Resources are nouns: GET /organizations/acme/runs/42, not /getRun?id=42. For actions that do not map to CRUD, either model the result as a resource (POST /runs/42/exports creates an export) or accept a verb sub-resource (POST /runs/42/retry).

Method Safe Idempotent Cacheable Typical use Success
GET Yes Yes Yes Read 200
HEAD Yes Yes Yes Headers only 200
OPTIONS Yes Yes No Capabilities, CORS preflight 204
POST No No Rarely Create, process 201 + Location, or 202
PUT No Yes No Replace whole resource, or create at a known id 200, 204, 201
PATCH No Not guaranteed No Partial update 200, 204
DELETE No Yes No Remove 204 (or 404 on repeat)

Safe means no intended state change. Idempotent means N identical requests leave the server state the same as one, though the response may differ (a second DELETE can return 404).

Code Meaning Use for
200 / 201 / 202 / 204 OK / created / accepted for async / no body 202 + status URL for long jobs
301 / 302 / 304 / 307 / 308 Redirects / not modified 307, 308 keep the method
400 Malformed or invalid input Validation failure (some teams use 422)
401 Not authenticated Missing or bad token
403 Authenticated, not allowed Wrong role
404 Not found Also to hide existence across tenants
405 / 406 / 415 Wrong method / no acceptable representation / unsupported body type
409 Conflict with current state Duplicate, illegal state transition
412 / 428 If-Match failed / precondition required Optimistic concurrency
422 Well-formed but semantically invalid
429 Rate limited With Retry-After
500 / 502 / 503 / 504 Bug / bad upstream / overloaded / upstream timeout Clients may retry 503, 504

Pagination, sorting, filtering

Style Request Pros Cons
Offset ?page=3&size=50 Jump to any page, simple DB scans and discards OFFSET rows; rows shift under concurrent inserts
Keyset ?after=2026-10-01T12:00:00Z,42&size=50 Stable and fast at any depth with an index No random page jump
Cursor ?cursor=opaque Keyset hidden; can change internally Opaque, cannot share a page number

Return page metadata either in the body or in headers (Link, X-Total-Count). A total count on a big table is expensive; prefer Slice semantics or an approximate count there. Cap size on the server (spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size). Whitelist sort fields: an arbitrary sort can hit an unindexed column and take the database down.

Versioning strategies

Strategy Example Pros Cons
URI /api/v1/runs Obvious, routable, cache-friendly Purists object; version lives in every link
Header X-API-Version: 2 Clean URLs Invisible, harder to test and cache
Media type Accept: application/vnd.rp.v2+json "Most RESTful" Heavy for clients and tools
Query param ?v=2 Easy Messy; caching issues

Prefer additive evolution (new optional fields; clients ignore unknowns) and version only for breaking changes. Publish a deprecation window with Deprecation and Sunset headers.

HATEOAS embeds links so clients discover actions ("_links": {"retry": {"href": ...}}). It suits long-lived public APIs with diverse clients. Most internal APIs skip it because the client is deployed with the server and the contract lives in OpenAPI.

ETags and conditional requests

ShallowEtagHeaderFilter hashes the rendered body: it saves bandwidth, but the server still does all the work. A deep ETag comes from a version column and can skip the work: if (request.checkNotModified(etag)) return null;. If-Match gives optimistic concurrency over HTTP, preventing the lost update when two users edit one resource.

Idempotency keys for POST

POST is not idempotent, but networks fail after the server commits. The client cannot tell, and a retry creates a duplicate payment or run. The client generates a unique key per logical operation and resends it on retry.

Points to raise: the unique constraint is what makes it correct, not a check-then-insert; scope the key by tenant; store the response so the retry gets the same answer; reject a reused key with a different body; expire keys after a retention period.

RefinePoint: recon_runs has an idempotency_key column, and ReconciliationExecutor calls findByOrgIdAndIdempotencyKey before starting a run, returning the existing run for a repeated request. The same thinking sits behind Kafka consumers: ConsumedEvents.firstTime(consumer, eventId) is an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, since at-least-once delivery guarantees repeats.

18.8 File upload, download and streaming

Upload. MultipartFile is backed by StandardServletMultipartResolver. Parts larger than file-size-threshold go to a temp file. Limits default to spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size=1MB and max-request-size=10MB; exceeding them raises MaxUploadSizeExceededException, which should map to 413. Validate the real content rather than the claimed type, never trust the client's file name for a path, and scan if users share files. For large files, a presigned URL straight to object storage keeps application threads free.

Download. Three choices:

Return type Memory Runs on Use for
byte[] Whole file on heap Request thread Tiny files only
Resource (FileSystemResource) Streamed; supports Range Request thread Existing files, resume support
StreamingResponseBody Streamed as you write MVC async executor Generated content: CSV, ZIP 
@GetMapping(BASE + "/export")
public ResponseEntity<StreamingResponseBody> export() {
    return ResponseEntity.ok()
        .contentType(MediaType.parseMediaType("application/zip"))
        .header(HttpHeaders.CONTENT_DISPOSITION, ContentDisposition.attachment().filename(name).build().toString())
        .header(HttpHeaders.CACHE_CONTROL, "private, no-store")
        .body(accounts::export);       // writes to the OutputStream on another thread
}

RefinePoint: that is close to the real AccountController in identity-service, which streams a person's data as a ZIP so its size does not touch the heap. Reconciliation result exports are heavier still, so ExportWorker in run-service prepares them in the background from a FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED queue, and the user downloads the finished file. For large output, an async job beats a long HTTP request.

Traps with StreamingResponseBody: the lambda runs after the controller returned, on another thread. So the @Transactional scope has ended, ThreadLocal context such as SecurityContext needs propagating, and spring.mvc.async.request-timeout can cut the stream. A failure midway cannot change the status (it is already committed), so the client sees a truncated file. The default async executor should be replaced by a bounded one in production.

Server-Sent Events in MVC use SseEmitter: one long-lived connection, server-to-client only.

RefinePoint: InboxController in alert-notify-service streams new notifications with SseEmitter: a hello event with the unread count, then a notification event for each new one, plus periodic comment pings to keep the connection open. It sets X-Accel-Buffering: no so nginx passes each event on at once, and removes the emitter on completion, timeout and error so the map of open streams does not leak.

18.9 CORS

The browser (not the server) enforces the same-origin policy. For a non-simple request it first sends a preflight OPTIONS with Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method; the server answers with Access-Control-Allow-*, and only then is the real request sent. Curl and server-to-server calls ignore CORS entirely, so CORS is not an authorisation mechanism.

Configuration points: @CrossOrigin, WebMvcConfigurer.addCorsMappings, or a CorsConfigurationSource. With Spring Security, enable http.cors(...), otherwise the preflight has no token and gets a 401 before MVC ever sees it. allowCredentials(true) cannot be combined with allowedOrigins("*"); list the origins, or use allowedOriginPatterns.

RefinePoint: CORS is the gateway's job. A service answers browsers directly only when rp.security.allowed-origins is set; otherwise PlatformSecurityAutoConfiguration disables CORS in that service. One place to configure, and no double Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers, which browsers reject.

18.10 Outbound HTTP clients

RestTemplate WebClient RestClient @HttpExchange
Since Spring 3 Spring 5 Spring 6.1 / Boot 3.2 Spring 6
Model Blocking Non-blocking (usable blocking) Blocking, fluent Declarative, on top of a client
API Template methods Fluent, Mono/Flux Fluent, same style as WebClient Annotated interface
Dependency spring-web spring-webflux + reactor spring-web spring-web
Status Maintenance, no new features Active Default for new blocking code Active 
RestClient client = builder.baseUrl("https://api.example.com")
    .defaultStatusHandler(HttpStatusCode::isError, (req, res) -> { throw new UpstreamException(res.getStatusCode()); })
    .build();
Rate rate = client.get().uri("/rates/{pair}", "EURUSD").retrieve().body(Rate.class);

public interface RateApi {                       // HTTP interface
    @GetExchange("/rates/{pair}") Rate rate(@PathVariable String pair);
}
RateApi api = HttpServiceProxyFactory.builderFor(RestClientAdapter.create(client)).build().createClient(RateApi.class);

Inject Boot's auto-configured RestClient.Builder: it carries the Observation registry, so calls emit http.client.requests metrics and propagate traces.

RefinePoint: InternalClient is a RestClient over JdkClientHttpRequestFactory, one per target service, with a 2 s connect timeout and a 10 s read timeout by default. It adds X-Internal-Token and X-Internal-Source, can forward the caller's credentials (asCaller) or call as the service itself (system), and turns non-2xx responses into RemoteCallException through a default status handler, which GlobalExceptionHandler maps back into an HTTP error.

Timeouts and retries

  • Every outbound call needs a timeout. The JDK and RestTemplate defaults can wait forever, and one slow dependency exhausts your thread pool.
  • A read timeout is not a total timeout: a trickling server can keep a call alive indefinitely. Enforce a deadline if it matters.
  • Retry only what is safe: idempotent methods, or POST with an idempotency key; on connection errors, 502, 503, 504, 429; not on 400, 401, 403, 404.
  • Exponential backoff with jitter, otherwise all clients retry in sync and create a retry storm. Honour Retry-After.
  • Retries multiply. Three layers with three attempts each make 27 calls on the bottom service. Retry at one layer only.
  • Pair with a circuit breaker (Resilience4j) so a dead dependency fails fast, and a bulkhead so it cannot consume every thread.

18.11 OpenAPI, security basics and multi-tenant paths

springdoc-openapi generates the OpenAPI 3 document at /v3/api-docs from your mappings, with Swagger UI at /swagger-ui.html. @Operation, @Schema and @Tag add documentation. Code-first keeps docs in step with code; contract-first (write the YAML, generate stubs) fits when several teams must agree before building. Commit the spec and diff it in CI to catch breaking changes.

RefinePoint: PlatformOpenApiAutoConfiguration gives every service Swagger. The docs paths are in the always-public list of the security chain, and Swagger UI signs in against Keycloak using authorization code with PKCE (springdoc.swagger-ui.oauth.use-pkce-with-authorization-code-grant=true).

API security checklist: TLS only; short-lived JWTs validated for signature, issuer, audience and expiry; authorise on every request and every object (IDOR/BOLA is the top API risk: /runs/42 must check that run 42 belongs to the caller's tenant); request size limits; no sensitive data in URLs because they end up in logs; DTOs rather than entities on the wire, which prevents mass assignment and accidental exposure; rate limits; audit logs.

Multi-tenant paths

RefinePoint: most routes carry the workspace in the path, /api/v1/organizations/{orgCode}/..., so it is visible in logs and links and the interceptor can check it uniformly. Routes about "the workspace open in the session" use the X-Org-Code header instead, read by OrgContextService. Either way, the code from the client is only a claim: it is resolved against the caller's membership on the server, and every query then filters on the resolved org_id.

18.12 Rate limiting

Algorithm Behaviour Trade-off
Fixed window Count per minute Simple; allows a burst of double the limit at the boundary
Sliding window Rolling count Accurate; stores more
Token bucket Refill at rate R, capacity B Allows bursts up to B, smooth average
Leaky bucket Constant outflow Smooths traffic, adds queueing

Answer with 429, Retry-After, and ideally X-RateLimit-Limit/Remaining. In-memory counters limit per instance, so N instances allow N times the limit; a shared limit needs Redis with an atomic script. Key by API key or user first and IP second, since many users can share a NAT address.

RefinePoint: RateLimitFilter in api-gateway is an in-memory token bucket in a ConcurrentHashMap: 300 per minute per API key, 900 per user, 1800 per IP address, all configurable. Past the limit it returns 429 with Retry-After, and every answer carries X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining. CORS preflights, health checks and Paddle webhooks are not counted. Inside services, SlidingWindowLimiter protects specific expensive operations. Both are per instance; that is a stated trade-off, a safe floor rather than an exact global limit.

18.13 Testing with MockMvc

Test type Starts Speed Use for
@WebMvcTest(Controller.class) MVC slice, no server; services mocked with @MockitoBean Fast Mapping, validation, status codes, JSON shape
@SpringBootTest + @AutoConfigureMockMvc Whole context, no server Medium Full stack, real security
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT) Real Tomcat Slowest Real HTTP, filters, streaming
@RestClientTest Client slice + MockRestServiceServer Fast Outbound clients 
mvc.perform(post("/api/v1/alert-rules")
        .header("X-Org-Code", "team")
        .with(jwt())                         // spring-security-test: fake authenticated JWT
        .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
        .content(rule))
   .andExpect(status().isOk())
   .andExpect(jsonPath("$.success").value(true));

MockMvc calls DispatcherServlet directly, without a socket. Filters run if registered, but anything async needs asyncDispatch, and real connector behaviour (max-http-header-size, chunking) is not exercised. Spring 6.2 adds MockMvcTester with AssertJ-style assertions; Boot 3.4 replaces @MockBean with @MockitoBean.

18.14 Interview questions and answers

Q1. Explain the Spring MVC request flow.

The container runs the filter chain, then DispatcherServlet.doDispatch finds a handler chain via HandlerMapping, picks a HandlerAdapter, runs interceptor preHandle, resolves arguments, invokes the controller, writes the return value through a converter for @ResponseBody, runs postHandle, handles exceptions through resolvers or renders a view, runs afterCompletion, and the filters unwind. Saying the body is written before postHandle marks you as someone who has debugged this.

Q2. What is the front controller pattern?

One entry point receives all requests and delegates to handlers, centralising routing, error handling and cross-cutting behaviour. DispatcherServlet is Spring's implementation, and it finds its collaborators (mappings, adapters, resolvers) as beans, so each is replaceable.

Q3. How is the DispatcherServlet registered in Boot if there is no web.xml?

DispatcherServletAutoConfiguration creates the servlet bean and a DispatcherServletRegistrationBean, a ServletContextInitializer that the embedded server runs at startup, mapped to spring.mvc.servlet.path (default /). load-on-startup defaults to -1, so it initialises on the first request; setting it to 1 removes that first-call latency.

Q4. @Controller vs @RestController?

@RestController is @Controller + @ResponseBody. With plain @Controller a returned String is a view name, resolved by a ViewResolver. With @RestController it goes through a converter and is written as the body. You can mix by putting @ResponseBody on individual methods.

Q5. Filter vs interceptor vs aspect: when each?

A filter is servlet-level and sees every request, including those MVC never maps, and can wrap the request or response. An interceptor is MVC-level and knows the handler method. An aspect wraps any bean method regardless of HTTP. Use filters for authentication and tracing, interceptors for route-aware checks like tenant access, and aspects for transactions and metrics.

Q6. What order do interceptor callbacks run in?

With interceptors A then B: A.preHandle, B.preHandle, handler, B.postHandle, A.postHandle, B.afterCompletion, A.afterCompletion. If B.preHandle returns false, the handler and postHandles are skipped, and only A.afterCompletion runs, because afterCompletion runs only for interceptors whose preHandle returned true. On an exception, postHandle is skipped but afterCompletion still runs.

Q7. Why doesn't my exception thrown in a servlet filter reach @ControllerAdvice?

Because filters run outside DispatcherServlet, and exception resolvers live inside it. The exception goes to the container, which forwards to /error. Write the error response in the filter, or inject handlerExceptionResolver and delegate to it.

Q8. How do you read the request body twice, for example to log it?

The servlet input stream can be read once. Wrap the request in a filter with ContentCachingRequestWrapper, which caches bytes as they are read; note that it fills only after the body is consumed downstream, so log in the filter after chain.doFilter. Limit the size, and redact sensitive data. For responses use ContentCachingResponseWrapper and call copyBodyToResponse(), or the client gets an empty body.

Q9. How does Spring decide which converter to use?

It looks at the body's Java type and media type. For requests, the Content-Type selects a converter whose canRead is true, else 415. For responses, it intersects Accept with what converters can produce for the return type (narrowed by produces), picks the most specific by quality, else 406. Boot's default for objects is MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter.

Q10. Why would a controller return 406 though the JSON is fine?

The client's Accept has nothing the server can produce: Accept: application/xml with no XML converter, or produces = "application/json" with Accept: text/csv. It also occurs when an error handler tries to write JSON to a client that accepts only text/event-stream, which is exactly the case RefinePoint's forClient handles.

Q11. How do you customise Jackson without losing Boot's defaults?

Use spring.jackson.* properties or a Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer bean; both feed the builder Boot's ObjectMapper is made from. Defining your own ObjectMapper bean disables that. For a one-off, use a dedicated mapper for that use, not the primary bean.

Q12. @RequestParam vs @PathVariable vs @RequestBody?

Path variables identify a resource, query parameters filter or modify a read, and the body carries a representation for create or update. A missing required param gives 400. @RequestBody needs a converter and a compatible Content-Type.

Q13. @Valid vs @Validated?

@Valid is standard Jakarta, triggers validation and cascades into nested objects. @Validated is Spring's: it adds validation groups and, at class level, enables method validation via an AOP proxy. Use @Valid on nested fields and request bodies, @Validated for groups or on services.

Q14. Which exception does validation throw?

@Valid @RequestBody gives MethodArgumentNotValidException. Constraints directly on controller method parameters give HandlerMethodValidationException from Spring 6.1's built-in method validation. Class-level @Validated on a service gives ConstraintViolationException. Handling only the first is a common gap, which lets the others surface as 500s or inconsistent bodies.

Q15. Why is my @NotNull on a nested object not validated?

Validation does not cascade without @Valid on the field. List<@Valid Item> items or @Valid List<Item> items both cascade into elements.

Q16. How do you write a custom validator, and why return true for null?

Define a constraint annotation with message, groups and payload, plus a ConstraintValidator implementation. Return true on null so nullability stays a separate decision via @NotNull, making constraints composable. For rules across fields, put the annotation on the class.

Q17. How does @ControllerAdvice work? What if two handlers match?

At startup ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver collects advice beans. On an exception it checks the controller's own @ExceptionHandler methods first, then advices in @Order order; within one class the closest match in the exception hierarchy wins. Causes are also checked. Advice can be scoped with basePackages, assignableTypes or annotations.

Q18. What is ProblemDetail? Would you use it?

A standard JSON error body (type, title, status, detail, instance plus extensions) from RFC 7807, updated by RFC 9457, with media type application/problem+json. Spring 6 has ProblemDetail and ErrorResponse, and Boot enables it through spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled. I would use it for a public API. In RefinePoint we kept an ApiResponse envelope because one first-party client gets the same parse on success and failure, and I would call that a deliberate trade-off.

Q19. Should a 200 response ever contain an error?

No. Status codes drive retries, caches, gateways, monitoring and alerting. A 200 with {"success": false} makes error rates invisible to all of them. An envelope is fine as long as the status matches, as ours does.

Q20. PUT vs PATCH vs POST?

POST creates or processes, and the server chooses the URI. PUT replaces the full resource at a client-known URI and is idempotent. PATCH partially updates and is not guaranteed idempotent. {"op":"increment"} is a non-idempotent PATCH; JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7386), where null means delete, is usually idempotent. With a partial DTO you must distinguish "absent" from "null", which plain records cannot: use JsonNode, Optional fields or Merge Patch.

Q21. Is DELETE idempotent if the second call returns 404?

Yes. Idempotency concerns server state, not the response. After one or many deletes the resource is gone. Some APIs return 204 on repeats for friendliness; both are valid.

Q22. 401 vs 403? 400 vs 422? 404 vs 403 for another tenant's resource?

401 means we do not know who you are, 403 means we know and you may not. 400 is malformed, 422 is well-formed but semantically invalid; many teams use 400 for both. For another tenant's resource return 404, so that the API does not reveal the id exists.

Q23. How do you model a long-running operation?

POST returns 202 with a Location to a status resource; the client polls or receives a webhook or event. RefinePoint runs work this way: a run is created QUEUED and a RunWorker claims it, while the status lives on the run itself. Holding an HTTP request open for minutes would tie up threads and fail on every proxy timeout.

Q24. Offset vs keyset pagination?

Offset is simple and allows page jumps, but the database reads and discards every skipped row, and concurrent inserts shift pages. Keyset (WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 50) stays fast at any depth with a composite index and is stable, but cannot jump to page 500. Use keyset for feeds, exports and big tables.

Q25. How would you design filtering and sorting?

Simple query params for common fields (?status=FAILED&from=...). Whitelist filter and sort fields, map them to indexed columns, cap page size. A generic filter language is a large surface that can hit unindexed columns, so add one only if needed. Never concatenate field names into SQL.

Q26. How do you version an API? What is a breaking change?

URI versioning for most teams, because it is visible and routable. Breaking changes: removing or renaming a field, changing a type or meaning, adding a required input, tightening validation, changing status codes. Adding an optional field or endpoint is not, provided clients ignore unknown fields (Boot's Jackson default). Run old and new side by side with a deprecation window and usage metrics.

Q27. What is HATEOAS and do you use it?

Hypermedia as the engine of application state: responses include links to the available next actions. It decouples clients from URL structure, but it costs effort and few clients actually navigate by links. I would consider it for a long-lived public API; for first-party clients, OpenAPI is enough.

Q28. What are ETags used for?

Conditional GET: send If-None-Match, get 304, save bandwidth. Optimistic concurrency: If-Match on PUT gets 412 if someone changed the resource. ShallowEtagHeaderFilter saves bandwidth only, since it computes the response before comparing. A version-based ETag can skip the work too.

Q29. How do you make POST idempotent?

A client-generated Idempotency-Key, stored with a unique constraint scoped by tenant in the same transaction as the business change. On repeat, return the stored result. The constraint decides the race between concurrent retries; a check-then-insert alone does not. Also compare a hash of the body, to reject a reused key with a different payload.

Q30. What happens if the client retries while the first request is still in progress?

Without coordination, both run. With a unique constraint, the second blocks or fails on insert. Then it can return 409 ("in progress"), wait for the first result, or return the stored row. Payment APIs typically return 409 for in-flight duplicates and let the client retry later.

Q31. How do you handle a 2 GB file upload?

Do not buffer it: stream it with a multipart temp file, or better, give the client a presigned URL to object storage so the app never handles the bytes. Then process asynchronously via a queue, with checksums and resumable uploads for reliability. Raise spring.servlet.multipart.*, the gateway limit and the proxy limit together, because a request must pass all three.

Q32. StreamingResponseBody vs returning Resource?

Resource suits an existing file: the converter streams it, and handles Range for resume. StreamingResponseBody suits generated content written incrementally; it runs on the MVC async executor. Neither loads everything onto the heap, unlike byte[].

Q33. What can go wrong while streaming a response?

The status is already committed, so a mid-stream error appears as a truncated file: add a trailer record or checksum if integrity matters. Transaction and persistence context have ended by the time the lambda runs. ThreadLocals (security, tenant) are not there unless propagated. Async timeouts cut long streams. Proxies may buffer unless told otherwise.

Q34. How does CORS work and why does a preflight get 401?

For non-simple requests the browser sends OPTIONS first, with no Authorization header. If the security chain runs before CORS handling, it rejects the preflight with 401, and the browser reports a CORS error. Enabling http.cors(...) makes Spring Security's CorsFilter answer it first. In RefinePoint the gateway handles CORS, and the rate limiter deliberately does not count preflights.

Q35. Is CORS a security feature for my API?

It protects browser users from other sites reading responses with their credentials. It does not protect your API: any non-browser client ignores it. Authentication and authorisation still have to be enforced.

Q36. Is CSRF protection needed for a REST API?

Only if the browser sends credentials automatically, as with session cookies. With a bearer token in the Authorization header, a malicious site cannot attach it, so CSRF protection is usually disabled for such stateless APIs, as in our security chains. If you keep tokens in cookies, you need CSRF protection and SameSite.

Q37. RestTemplate vs WebClient vs RestClient?

RestTemplate is blocking and in maintenance. WebClient is non-blocking, needs the Reactor dependency, and is right for reactive stacks or heavy fan-out. RestClient (Spring 6.1) is synchronous with a fluent API: my default for MVC services, particularly with virtual threads. Using WebClient with .block() everywhere pays for Reactor and gains nothing.

Q38. What are HTTP interfaces?

A declarative client: annotate an interface with @GetExchange or @PostExchange, and HttpServiceProxyFactory creates a proxy backed by RestClient, WebClient or RestTemplate. It is Feign's model without the extra dependency. It suits typed clients for stable APIs; a hand-written wrapper suits complex error handling.

Q39. What timeouts do you set on an outbound call?

Connect (1–2 s), read (based on the dependency's p99, well under the caller's own deadline), connection pool acquire, and an overall deadline if a trickling response matters. Our InternalClient defaults to 2 s connect and 10 s read. Missing timeouts are the most common cause of cascading failure: threads pile up waiting on one slow dependency.

Q40. When is retrying harmful?

On non-idempotent calls without a key, since it produces duplicates. On overload, since retries add load (retry storm). When layered, since attempts multiply. And when the total time exceeds the caller's deadline, because the work is wasted. Use backoff with jitter, a retry budget, one retry layer and a circuit breaker.

Q41. A service's latency spiked and all threads are busy. How do you diagnose it?

Check metrics first: tomcat.threads.busy, hikaricp.connections.pending, http.client.requests per dependency, GC pauses. Take a thread dump: threads parked in HikariPool.getConnection mean a pool bottleneck or slow queries, threads in socket read mean a slow dependency without a timeout, many on one monitor mean lock contention. Mitigate with timeouts and bulkheads, then fix the root cause. Raising threads.max usually moves the queue rather than removing it.

Q42. How do you expose a file-processing API without tying up Tomcat threads?

Accept the upload, save it, enqueue, return 202. Workers process from the queue, and the client polls or gets notified. MVC's Callable, DeferredResult or SseEmitter free the container thread while waiting for a result. On virtual threads the thread cost is low, but a queue still gives you retries, durability and backpressure.

Q43. DeferredResult vs Callable vs SseEmitter?

Callable runs your code on the MVC async executor. DeferredResult is completed later by any thread, such as a Kafka listener. SseEmitter and ResponseBodyEmitter send many items over one connection. In each, the container thread goes back to the pool until there is a result to write, and the request is dispatched again to finish.

Q44. SSE vs WebSocket vs polling?

Polling is simple and wasteful. SSE is one-way over plain HTTP, reconnects automatically, and goes through proxies when buffering is off. WebSocket is two-way and needs more infrastructure. Notifications fit SSE: RefinePoint's inbox stream is a text/event-stream with SseEmitter. Each open stream is a held connection, so plan capacity, and with multiple instances the event must reach whichever instance holds the connection.

Q45. How do you enforce tenant isolation at the API layer?

Resolve the tenant from a claim in the request (path or header) against the authenticated user's memberships, on the server, in one central place. Then pass the resolved org_id into every query. RefinePoint does this with OrgAccessInterceptor plus orgs.resolveOrgIdFromCode(orgCode), and BaseOrgEntity makes every tenant row carry org_id. The classic bug is a repository findById(id) that ignores the tenant; use findByOrgIdAndId, and return 404 otherwise.

Q46. Path vs header for the tenant?

A path is visible in logs, bookmarkable, cacheable per tenant, and lets a route-based interceptor check it uniformly. A header keeps URLs clean, suits a "current workspace" session, and needs care in caches (Vary). RefinePoint mostly uses the path, with X-Org-Code for session-scoped routes. Neither is trusted on its own.

Q47. How do you protect against IDOR?

Authorise each object, not just the endpoint. Scope every lookup by tenant and owner, use non-guessable ids (we use UUIDs) as defence in depth rather than as the control, and write tests in which user A requests user B's id and expects 404.

Q48. Why not return JPA entities from controllers?

It exposes the schema and couples the API to the database. Lazy relations trigger extra queries or LazyInitializationException during serialisation, and @RequestBody entities invite mass assignment (a client sets orgId or role). DTOs or records give a stable contract.

Q49. How do you design rate limiting across multiple gateway instances?

In-memory buckets are per instance, so N instances allow N times the limit. For an exact limit, use Redis with an atomic Lua script or a dedicated rate-limit service, adding a network hop and a dependency that needs a fail-open decision. RefinePoint's gateway is in-memory by choice: simple, no dependency, a safe floor. I would add Redis if a contractual per-customer limit required it.

Q50. Token bucket vs sliding window?

Token bucket allows controlled bursts and is cheap: two numbers per key, computed lazily on each request from elapsed time. Sliding window is more exact in its count but stores more. Fixed window is simplest, but lets twice the limit through at a boundary. Our gateway uses a token bucket refilled evenly over a minute; our in-service SlidingWindowLimiter is used where a strict rolling count matters.

Q51. What should a 429 response include?

Retry-After, a machine-readable error, and rate headers so clients can self-throttle. RefinePoint's body uses the same envelope with errors: ["RATE_LIMITED"]. Clients should back off with jitter.

Q52. @WebMvcTest vs @SpringBootTest?

@WebMvcTest loads only the MVC slice with mocked collaborators: quick, for mapping, validation, serialisation and security rules. @SpringBootTest loads everything: for integration through to a real database (with Testcontainers). Keep many slice tests and fewer full tests. Each distinct context configuration costs a new context, so reuse them via the test context cache.

Q53. What does MockMvc not test?

The real network and container: connector limits, header size, chunked behaviour, TLS, and exact error dispatch to /error. Async needs asyncDispatch, and streaming behaviour differs. Use a RANDOM_PORT test for those.

Q54. Why does a trailing slash now return 404 after upgrading to Boot 3?

Spring 6 removed trailing-slash matching by default, so /runs/ no longer matches /runs. Fix clients, or add explicit mappings, or (temporarily) add a filter that redirects. Avoid re-enabling it permanently: differing path interpretation between security rules and handlers has been a source of bypass bugs.

Q55. How do you handle date and money in JSON?

Dates: ISO 8601 with offset (Instant, OffsetDateTime), UTC on the wire, and let the client localise. RefinePoint stores timestamps in UTC, and the UI shows each person's time zone. Money: BigDecimal plus a currency code, never double, and consider serialising as a string, since JavaScript numbers are doubles and silently lose precision on large or precise amounts.

Q56. What is content negotiation and how does it interact with error handling?

Choosing a representation from Accept and produces. If a handler says produces = "text/csv" and throws, Spring removes the producible attribute so the error handler can write JSON (and if the client accepts only CSV, it may fail with 406). So design errors around what your clients accept, and test the error path, including for SSE and file endpoints.

Q57. What makes a good REST API, in your view?

Predictable resource names, correct status codes, consistent errors, pagination everywhere, idempotency for retries, additive evolution, an OpenAPI contract tested in CI, authorisation on each object, timeouts and limits, and traces and metrics per route. Consistency beats cleverness. RefinePoint enforces most of this through ryfn-platform, so each new service inherits it without having to remember it.

Q58. How does the gateway add value over putting everything in each service?

It gives one entry point for routing, TLS, CORS and coarse rate limiting, so services need not repeat them, and clients need only one host. It must stay thin: business logic belongs in services. Authorisation still happens in the services too: RefinePoint's gateway reads the JWT subject only to count requests and does not verify the signature, leaving verification to each service, so nothing depends on the gateway alone.

19. Reactive Programming & Spring WebFlux

The interview question has shifted. It used to be "explain Mono and Flux". Since Java 21 it is "you have virtual threads now, so why would you still use WebFlux?". To answer well you need to know what reactive really gives you (backpressure, composition, fewer threads), what it costs (debugging, context, a coloured API), and how the machinery works: who subscribes, which thread runs what, and why one blocking call can stall thousands of requests. RefinePoint is a good honest case: 12 services are Spring MVC, and exactly one, the gateway, is reactive.

19.1 Why reactive

In thread-per-request, each in-flight request holds a thread for its whole life, including time spent waiting on I/O. A service that spends 95% of a request waiting on the network uses a 1 MB-stack platform thread to do nothing.

Reactive programming is a declarative style for asynchronous data streams with backpressure. You describe a pipeline; when data arrives, the framework runs the next step on whatever thread is available. Benefits:

  • Fewer threads under high concurrency, especially many slow or idle connections (gateways, streaming, fan-out).
  • Backpressure: a slow consumer can limit a fast producer rather than be overwhelmed.
  • Composition: timeouts, retries, parallel calls and fallbacks are one operator each.

Costs, which a senior answer names unprompted:

  • Stack traces become useless without tooling.
  • ThreadLocal context (MDC, security, transactions) does not work the normal way.
  • One blocking call on an event loop stalls every request on that loop.
  • JDBC, JPA and most existing libraries are blocking.
  • Harder to read, write, review and hire for.
  • No throughput gain for CPU-bound work.

Reactive does not make a single request faster. It improves capacity under concurrency.

19.2 Reactive Streams: the specification

Reactive Streams is a small spec of four interfaces, adopted into the JDK as java.util.concurrent.Flow in Java 9. Reactor, RxJava and Akka Streams all implement it.

public interface Publisher<T>  { void subscribe(Subscriber<? super T> s); }
public interface Subscriber<T> {
    void onSubscribe(Subscription s);
    void onNext(T t);
    void onError(Throwable t);
    void onComplete();
}
public interface Subscription  { void request(long n); void cancel(); }
public interface Processor<T, R> extends Subscriber<T>, Publisher<R> { }

Key rules:

  • Nothing happens until subscribe. A pipeline is only a description.
  • Demand flows upstream, data flows downstream. A publisher must not emit more than the total requested. That is backpressure: pull-based flow control over a push-based model.
  • Signal order: onSubscribe onNext* (onError | onComplete)?. At most one terminal signal, and signals to one subscriber are serial (never concurrent).
  • onError and onComplete are terminal; nothing follows them.

Backpressure in practice

source ──► map ──► flatMap ──► subscriber
       ◄── request(32) ◄── request(256) ◄── request(unbounded)

Each operator translates demand. flatMap requests 256 inner publishers by default; each inner prefetches 32. subscribe(consumer) requests Long.MAX_VALUE: no backpressure at all from that subscriber.

If a source cannot slow down (mouse clicks, a hot sink, a Kafka broker you must keep up with), you choose an overflow strategy:

Operator When demand is lacking
onBackpressureBuffer(n) Buffer up to n, then error or apply a strategy
onBackpressureDrop() Discard new items
onBackpressureLatest() Keep only the most recent
onBackpressureError() Signal OverflowException
limitRate(n) Rewrite demand into batches of n

Over HTTP, backpressure maps onto TCP flow control: when the client reads slowly, the socket buffer fills, Netty stops writing, and demand stops propagating. Across a boundary that has no flow control (a plain message broker pushing at you, for instance), it stops being automatic.

19.3 Project Reactor: Mono and Flux

Mono<T> is 0 or 1 item; Flux<T> is 0 to N. Both are publishers, and Reactor is the library behind WebFlux.

Mono<String> a = Mono.just("x");                    // value computed NOW, at assembly
Mono<String> b = Mono.fromCallable(this::load);     // computed at each subscribe
Mono<String> c = Mono.defer(() -> Mono.just(load())); // whole Mono built at each subscribe
Flux<Integer> d = Flux.range(1, 5);
Flux<Long> e = Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(1));

Assembly time vs subscription time. Building a pipeline is assembly; it constructs a chain of operator objects. subscribe walks back up the chain, and data then flows down. Each call to an operator returns a new publisher, and the original is unchanged, so this is a classic bug:

Flux<Integer> f = Flux.just(1, 2, 3);
f.map(x -> x * 2);      // result discarded: no effect at all
f.subscribe(System.out::println);   // prints 1 2 3

Operators you must know

Operator Purpose Ordering / concurrency
map Sync 1:1 transformation Same thread, keeps order
flatMap Async: each item to a publisher, merged Concurrent, order not kept, default 256
concatMap Async, one at a time Sequential, keeps order
flatMapSequential Async, concurrent, output in source order Buffers early finishers
zip Combine latest from each, pairwise Waits for all; ends when any ends
merge Interleave as they arrive Eager subscribe to all
concat One after another Lazy subscribe to next
switchIfEmpty Fallback publisher if empty Argument built at assembly!
defaultIfEmpty Fallback value if empty
onErrorResume Fallback publisher on error Can filter by type
onErrorReturn Fallback value on error
onErrorMap Translate exception
retryWhen Resubscribe with a policy Backoff, jitter, filter
timeout Error if no signal in time Cancels upstream
doOnNext, doOnError, doFinally Side effects Do not change items
collectList Flux to Mono<List> Buffers everything
buffer, window Batches

The flatMap decision is asked constantly. Pick map when the function is synchronous and returns a value; pick flatMap when it returns a Mono/Flux. Using map with an async function gives you Mono<Mono<T>>, and the inner never subscribes, so the call silently never happens.

RefinePoint: the gateway's StatusController builds the public status page with real operators. Each component's check is http.get().uri(part.url()).retrieve().toBodilessEntity().timeout(TIMEOUT).map(...).onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(down)), and the page is Flux.fromIterable(parts).flatMapSequential(this::check).collectList(). flatMapSequential is exactly right: services are checked concurrently, so one slow service does not delay the others, yet the page lists them in a stable order. onErrorResume converts a failure into a "down" value, so one dead service cannot fail the whole page.

Retry with backoff:

webClient.get().uri("/rates").retrieve().bodyToMono(Rate.class)
    .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
    .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(200))
        .jitter(0.5)
        .filter(e -> e instanceof TimeoutException || e instanceof WebClientResponseException.ServiceUnavailable)
        .onRetryExhaustedThrow((spec, signal) -> signal.failure()))
    .onErrorResume(WebClientResponseException.NotFound.class, e -> Mono.empty());

retry works by resubscribing upstream. On a cold HTTP Mono it sends a new request. Put timeout before retryWhen for a per-attempt timeout; put another after for an overall deadline. Retry.backoff by default also retries everything, so always add a filter (no retrying a 400).

Trap: switchIfEmpty(Mono.just(expensive())) or switchIfEmpty(repo.save(x)) builds its argument at assembly, on every request, even when the upstream is not empty. If the argument's construction does work (a method that has side effects before returning its Mono), it runs every time. Wrap with switchIfEmpty(Mono.defer(() -> repo.save(x))). The same applies to Mono.just(load()).

19.4 Cold vs hot

Cold Hot
Data starts At each subscribe, per subscriber Regardless of subscribers
Late subscriber Sees everything from the start Sees only what comes next
Examples WebClient call, Flux.range, R2DBC query Sinks.many(), Flux.interval shared, UI events

Two subscribers to a cold Mono make two HTTP calls. Convert when needed:

Mono<Rate> once = client.fetch().cache();                       // first result replayed to all
Flux<Tick> shared = ticks.share();                              // publish + refCount: multicast while any subscriber
Flux<Tick> replay = ticks.replay(10).autoConnect(1);            // late subscribers get last 10

Sinks.Many<Event> sink = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer();  // push from imperative code
sink.tryEmitNext(event);
Flux<Event> events = sink.asFlux();

19.5 Schedulers: publishOn vs subscribeOn

Reactor is concurrency-agnostic: by default everything runs on the thread that called subscribe, or the thread that emitted the signal. Operators do not imply new threads, except time-based ones (delayElements, timeout, interval, which default to parallel).

Scheduler Threads For
Schedulers.parallel() CPU cores Non-blocking, CPU work
Schedulers.boundedElastic() 10 × cores, with a task queue per thread Wrapping blocking calls
Schedulers.single() 1 Serial work
Schedulers.immediate() Current No hop
Schedulers.fromExecutorService(...) Yours A dedicated pool
  • publishOn changes the thread for signals going downstream from where it is written. Multiple publishOns each apply below themselves.
  • subscribeOn changes the thread on which the subscription travels up and the source runs. Its position does not matter. With several, the one closest to the source wins, but only until a publishOn switches again.
Flux.range(1, 2)
    .map(i -> log("A", i))
    .publishOn(Schedulers.parallel())
    .map(i -> log("B", i))
    .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())
    .subscribe();
// A on boundedElastic-1, B on parallel-1

Wrap blocking calls like this:

Mono<Report> report = Mono.fromCallable(() -> legacyJdbc.load(id))   // blocking
    .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic());                        // moved off the event loop

Reactor 3.6 on JDK 21 can run boundedElastic on virtual threads (-Dreactor.schedulers.defaultBoundedElasticOnVirtualThreads=true).

19.6 The WebFlux stack and the Netty event loop

The names are parallel to MVC: DispatcherHandler, WebFilter, ServerWebExchange (rather than request/response objects) and HttpMessageReader/Writer codecs. Annotated controllers look the same; the alternative is functional RouterFunction + HandlerFunction.

Who subscribes? You do not. The framework subscribes to what your controller returned. Calling subscribe() yourself inside a handler creates a detached pipeline that is unrelated to the request, its errors and its context. That is a common bug.

Event loop model. Reactor Netty runs an event loop group: reactor.netty.ioWorkerCount threads, default max(cores, 4). Each channel is pinned to one event loop for life, and each event loop processes I/O events and tasks from a queue in order.

Event loop reactor-http-nio-2:
  ├─ socket A readable   → decode → run pipeline → WebClient.send → return
  ├─ socket B writable   → write next buffer      → return
  ├─ socket C (backend reply for A) → continue A's pipeline → write → return
  └─ if ANY of these blocks for 200 ms, every channel on this loop waits 200 ms

Blocking in reactive, and BlockHound

Never block an event loop. With 8 event loops, 8 blocked calls stop the service. Symptoms: latency spikes across unrelated endpoints, while CPU is low and thread dumps show reactor-http-nio-* in socket read or Thread.sleep.

Common accidental blockers: JDBC, RestTemplate, file I/O, Thread.sleep, .block(), and logging to a slow synchronous appender.

Calling .block() on a non-blocking thread fails fast with IllegalStateException: block()/blockFirst()/blockLast() are blocking, which is not supported in thread reactor-http-nio-2. For the rest, BlockHound instruments JDK blocking methods and throws if they are called on a thread marked non-blocking. Install it in tests:

@BeforeAll static void setup() { BlockHound.install(); }

BlockHound detects calls such as sleep, socket and file I/O. It does not detect long CPU work, and a tight synchronized block is generally acceptable.

RefinePoint: RateLimitFilter.Bucket has short synchronized methods that do a few double-precision operations. That is fine on an event loop: critical sections take nanoseconds and do no I/O. The bucket map is a ConcurrentHashMap, and idle entries are removed periodically so it cannot grow forever. What would be wrong there is a Redis or JDBC call without a reactive driver.

19.7 WebClient

HttpClient netty = HttpClient.create(ConnectionProvider.builder("rates")
        .maxConnections(100).pendingAcquireTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
        .maxIdleTime(Duration.ofSeconds(30)).build())
    .option(ChannelOption.CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MILLIS, 2000)
    .responseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5));

WebClient client = builder.clientConnector(new ReactorClientHttpConnector(netty))
    .baseUrl("https://api.example.com")
    .codecs(c -> c.defaultCodecs().maxInMemorySize(2 * 1024 * 1024))
    .build();

Mono<Dashboard> dashboard = Mono.zip(
        client.get().uri("/a").retrieve().bodyToMono(A.class),
        client.get().uri("/b").retrieve().bodyToMono(B.class))
    .map(t -> new Dashboard(t.getT1(), t.getT2()));   // concurrent, total time = the slower one

Points interviewers check:

  • retrieve() maps 4xx/5xx to WebClientResponseException and is the default choice. exchangeToMono gives response access but you must consume or release the body, or the connection leaks.
  • The default codec buffer is 256 KB; larger bodies raise DataBufferLimitException. Raise it, or stream.
  • maxIdleTime should be shorter than the server's or load balancer's idle timeout, or you get PrematureCloseException from reusing dead connections.
  • Mono.zip with one empty source completes empty and cancels the rest: that surprises people. .defaultIfEmpty or Optional wrapping avoids it.
  • Build from the injected WebClient.Builder, to get tracing and metrics.

RefinePoint: the gateway's ApiDocsController fetches each service's OpenAPI document with WebClient, timeout(5 s), a 5-minute in-memory cache, and onErrorResume that returns the last good copy, or a 503 if there is none. It raises maxInMemorySize because API documents exceed the default. It is a clean, small example of graceful degradation in one reactive pipeline.

19.8 R2DBC

JDBC is blocking by design, so a truly reactive stack needs R2DBC: a non-blocking SPI with drivers for PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and others. Spring Data R2DBC provides ReactiveCrudRepository, R2dbcEntityTemplate and DatabaseClient.

interface RunRepo extends ReactiveCrudRepository<Run, UUID> {
    Flux<Run> findByOrgId(UUID orgId);
}
Mono<Run> saved = tx.transactional(repo.save(run));   // TransactionalOperator; @Transactional also works

Limitations that matter when deciding:

  • It is not an ORM. No lazy loading, no dirty checking, no relationships, no second-level cache; closer to Spring Data JDBC.
  • Transactions are tied to the Reactor Context, not a ThreadLocal, so they need a ReactiveTransactionManager.
  • Flyway and Liquibase still use JDBC for migrations.
  • Fewer tools and less community experience than JDBC, and the database's connection limit is unchanged: reactive removes thread waits, not database capacity.

Wrapping JDBC in boundedElastic is the pragmatic alternative; it works, but you keep a thread per query, and pool sizes set the limit.

19.9 Context propagation

ThreadLocal relies on a request staying on one thread. In a reactive pipeline it hops between threads, so MDC, SecurityContextHolder and TransactionSynchronizationManager no longer work the normal way.

Reactor Context is an immutable key-value map attached to the subscription, travelling from subscriber up.

Mono<String> greeting = Mono.deferContextual(ctx -> Mono.just("org=" + ctx.get("org")))
    .contextWrite(Context.of("org", "acme"));        // visible to operators ABOVE this line

Because the context travels at subscribe time, from the bottom up, contextWrite affects what is above it. Putting it at the top of a chain does nothing for operators beneath. Spring Security uses this as ReactiveSecurityContextHolder, and reactive transactions do the same.

Bridging to ThreadLocals: Micrometer's context-propagation library defines ThreadLocalAccessors. Hooks.enableAutomaticContextPropagation() (Reactor 3.5.3+), or spring.reactor.context-propagation=auto in Boot 3.2+, restores registered ThreadLocals around each operator, so log lines keep their traceId in MDC. The cost is some overhead per operator.

19.10 Testing and debugging

StepVerifier.create(service.matchAll(orgId))
    .expectNext(first)
    .expectNextMatches(r -> r.rate() > 0.9)
    .verifyComplete();

StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Mono.delay(Duration.ofHours(1)).map(x -> "done"))
    .expectSubscription()
    .thenAwait(Duration.ofHours(1))      // no real wait
    .expectNext("done")
    .verifyComplete();

StepVerifier.create(Flux.range(1, 100), 0)  // demand 0: test backpressure
    .thenRequest(2).expectNext(1, 2).thenCancel().verify();

TestPublisher emits signals on demand and can misbehave deliberately, PublisherProbe checks that a fallback branch was actually subscribed, and WebTestClient tests endpoints. With withVirtualTime the publisher must be created inside the supplier, otherwise real schedulers are already captured.

Debugging. A stack trace shows Reactor's scheduling frames, not your assembly code.

Tool Cost How
checkpoint("loading rates") Low; add at key points Adds description to traces
log() Noisy Prints signals: onSubscribe, request, onNext
Hooks.onOperatorDebug() High: captures a stack at every assembly Dev only
ReactorDebugAgent (reactor-tools) Low: bytecode instrumentation at load time OK in production
name().tag().tap(Micrometer.metrics(registry)) Low Pipeline metrics

Also common is "my pipeline does nothing": the usual causes are no subscriber, a discarded operator result, an empty source hitting a flatMap, or an onErrorResume swallowing the error. Check with log().

19.11 SSE and streaming, e.g. LLM tokens

Reactive suits streaming well, since a stream is simply a Flux:

@GetMapping(value = "/chat", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
Flux<ServerSentEvent<String>> chat(@RequestParam String prompt) {
    return llm.post().uri("/v1/chat").bodyValue(request(prompt))
        .retrieve().bodyToFlux(String.class)        // provider's token stream
        .map(token -> ServerSentEvent.builder(token).event("token").build())
        .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30))            // max gap between tokens
        .onErrorResume(e -> Flux.just(ServerSentEvent.builder("failed").event("error").build()));
}

The best feature is cancellation: when the browser disconnects, cancel travels up and the provider call stops, so you stop paying for tokens no one reads. In MVC you must wire this by hand with SseEmitter.onCompletion.

Practical points: disable proxy buffering (nginx X-Accel-Buffering: no), send heartbeats so idle connections stay up, tag errors as an event because the HTTP status is already sent, and do not hold a DB connection during the stream. MVC controllers can also return Flux and Spring adapts it, so you do not need a full WebFlux app to stream.

RefinePoint: we built this differently, and that is a fair thing to say. LlmClient.complete is a blocking call returning a whole LlmResponse (OpenAiCompatibleClient sends "stream": false), because our AI features produce structured JSON (JsonExtractor parses a reconciliation draft), which is useless half-finished. Live updates that do exist, such as the notification inbox, use MVC's SseEmitter. If I added token streaming to the help assistant, I would return a Flux from an MVC controller or use SseEmitter on a virtual thread instead of converting ai-service to WebFlux.

19.12 Spring Cloud Gateway is WebFlux

Spring Cloud Gateway (reactive variant) runs on Netty and WebFlux, which fits a gateway: tens of thousands of mostly-waiting connections, with no business logic and no JDBC.

A GlobalFilter returns Mono<Void>. Code before chain.filter is "pre", and .then(...) after it is "post":

public Mono<Void> filter(ServerWebExchange exchange, GatewayFilterChain chain) {
    long start = System.nanoTime();
    return chain.filter(exchange)
        .then(Mono.fromRunnable(() -> record(exchange, System.nanoTime() - start)));
}

To reject, set the status and write the body without calling the chain.

RefinePoint: RateLimitFilter implements GlobalFilter, Ordered runs at HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 10. It skips OPTIONS, /actuator and /api/webhooks/, then takes one token from the caller's bucket (API key digest, or the JWT sub) and from the IP bucket. If it is under the limit it returns chain.filter(exchange); otherwise it sets 429, Retry-After, and returns response.writeWith(Mono.just(buffer)) with our standard JSON error. It decodes the JWT payload only to find sub, without checking the signature, because services verify tokens. A forged sub buys nothing, since the IP bucket is still counted. MetricsGuard, a WebFilter, protects the gateway's /actuator/prometheus with a bearer token.

There is also Spring Cloud Gateway Server MVC, a servlet variant for teams that prefer MVC, and it pairs well with virtual threads.

19.13 WebFlux vs MVC + virtual threads

Virtual threads (Java 21) remove the main reason most teams adopted reactive: the cost of a thread waiting on I/O. Write blocking code; the JVM unmounts the virtual thread at each blocking call, and the carrier thread goes on to other work.

Criterion MVC + virtual threads WebFlux
Programming style Plain imperative Declarative pipelines
Stack traces, debugging Normal Need tooling
ThreadLocal, MDC, @Transactional, JPA Work as usual Need Context / R2DBC
Existing blocking libraries Fine Must be isolated
Many concurrent I/O waits Excellent Excellent
Backpressure in the stream Not built in; use semaphores Built in
Streaming, cancellation Possible, manual First class
Composing fan-out, timeouts, retries Structured concurrency (preview in 21) or Resilience4j Operators
Memory per connection Low, some per stack Lowest
Team hiring and maintenance Easy Harder
Blocking the wrong thing Pinning (synchronized on 21) Stalls the event loop

My decision rule:

  • New CRUD or business service with JDBC/JPA: MVC, virtual threads if I/O concurrency is high. 90% of services.
  • Gateway, proxy, streaming fan-out, huge numbers of idle connections: WebFlux.
  • Pipeline where backpressure and cancellation are the actual requirement: Reactor, possibly just the pipeline in an MVC service.
  • Team already expert and stack already reactive: stay; a rewrite buys little.
  • CPU-bound work: neither helps. Use a bounded pool of platform threads.

RefinePoint: 12 services are MVC with JPA and JdbcTemplate; the reactive one is api-gateway, because Spring Cloud Gateway is built on WebFlux, and it does only I/O. The run engine is CPU- and disk-bound work on DuckDB, so reactive would not help at all; capacity is managed by worker slots and queue claims. Mixing paradigms cost us nothing, because services only meet over HTTP.

19.14 Interview questions and answers

Q1. What is reactive programming?

A declarative style for asynchronous streams of data with non-blocking backpressure. You describe a pipeline of transformations; execution is triggered by subscription and driven by data arrival rather than by a thread walking through statements. It serves capacity under I/O concurrency, not single-request speed.

Q2. What are the four Reactive Streams interfaces?

Publisher (emits), Subscriber (receives via onSubscribe, onNext, onError, onComplete), Subscription (request(n), cancel), and Processor (both). Included in the JDK as java.util.concurrent.Flow since Java 9. The spec defines interoperability; it is too low-level to use directly, which is what Reactor is for.

Q3. What is backpressure?

A way for a consumer to tell a producer how much it can handle: the subscriber calls request(n), and the publisher must not exceed the total demand. Without it, a fast producer forces unbounded buffering and eventually an out-of-memory error. Over HTTP it maps to TCP flow control.

Q4. What if the source cannot honour backpressure?

Choose an overflow strategy explicitly: onBackpressureBuffer (bounded), Drop, Latest or Error. Hot sources such as sensor feeds cannot slow down, so you must decide whether to lose data, buffer it, or fail. Dropping is fine for latest-value gauges and wrong for financial events.

Q5. Mono vs Flux? Why have Mono at all?

Mono is 0..1, Flux is 0..N. Mono conveys single-result semantics in the type, and some operators exist only there or are optimised. Mono<Void> represents completion with no value, as in a GlobalFilter.

Q6. What does this print?

Flux<Integer> f = Flux.just(1, 2, 3).map(x -> { System.out.println("m" + x); return x; });
System.out.println("built");

Only built. Nothing runs without a subscriber. If f.subscribe() is called twice, m1 m2 m3 prints twice, because it is a cold publisher.

Q7. map vs flatMap?

map is a synchronous 1:1 function returning a value. flatMap takes a function returning a publisher, subscribes to the inner publishers concurrently and merges their results. Use map for computation, and flatMap for any async call. Using map with an async function produces a nested Mono<Mono<T>>, and the inner never runs.

Q8. flatMap vs concatMap vs flatMapSequential?

flatMap is concurrent (default 256) with no order guarantee. concatMap runs one at a time, keeps order and is slowest. flatMapSequential runs concurrently yet emits in source order by buffering, so a slow first element holds back the output and uses memory. RefinePoint's status page uses flatMapSequential for concurrent checks in stable order.

Q9. How do you limit concurrency of outbound calls?

flatMap(fn, concurrency), for example flatMap(this::call, 10). Otherwise a Flux of 10,000 ids launches 256 calls at once and exhausts the connection pool, or overwhelms the downstream. It is a one-argument bulkhead, one of reactive's nicest features.

Q10. zip vs merge vs concat?

zip pairs one element from each source, waits for all, and ends when any ends. merge interleaves as items arrive, subscribing to all eagerly. concat subscribes to the next only when the previous ends. Use zip to combine parallel calls into one result; merge for fan-in; concat for ordered fallback sequences.

Q11. What happens if one source in Mono.zip is empty?

The result completes empty and the other sources are cancelled, with no error. So a dashboard with one empty section silently returns nothing. Use defaultIfEmpty, or map to Optional with .map(Optional::of).defaultIfEmpty(Optional.empty()).

Q12. What is wrong with switchIfEmpty(callService())?

callService() is evaluated at assembly time on every request, whether or not the upstream is empty. If the method does work before returning its publisher, that work happens regardless. Wrap it in Mono.defer(() -> callService()). Same for Mono.just(load()), where load always runs immediately.

Q13. Mono.just vs Mono.fromCallable vs Mono.defer?

just holds an already-computed value, and if the value is null it throws. fromCallable runs the callable per subscription and treats a null return as empty. defer builds a whole new publisher per subscription. For blocking or costly work, use fromCallable with subscribeOn(boundedElastic).

Q14. How do errors work in a pipeline?

An exception in an operator becomes an onError signal, which skips remaining map-style operators until an error operator or the subscriber. The sequence terminates. onErrorResume swaps in a fallback, onErrorReturn a value, onErrorMap translates, retry resubscribes. onErrorContinue drops an element and continues, but it has confusing semantics; avoid it unless you understand which upstream operators support it.

Q15. What happens if I subscribe() with no error handler?

On an error, Reactor raises ErrorCallbackNotImplemented to the global Hooks.onErrorDropped-style logging. The pipeline ends, and only a log line shows it. In a server handler you should not subscribe anyway; return the publisher.

Q16. Should I ever call subscribe() in a WebFlux handler?

Almost never. The framework subscribes to the returned publisher, tying it to the request lifecycle, context, cancellation and error handling. A manual subscribe is fire-and-forget: no request context, no error path, and it continues after the client disconnects. Compose with flatMap/then. For deliberate background work, use a managed queue.

Q17. Explain publishOn vs subscribeOn.
