publishOn moves execution for operators downstream of it. subscribeOn chooses the thread on which subscription and source emission run, regardless of where it is written. Rule: subscribeOn for a blocking source, publishOn to shift later work elsewhere.

Q18. What thread does each map run on?

Mono.just(1)
    .map(a -> a + 1)
    .publishOn(Schedulers.parallel())
    .map(b -> b + 1)
    .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())
    .map(c -> c + 1)
    .subscribe();

First map on boundedElastic, second and third on parallel. subscribeOn moved the source and everything up to the publishOn; publishOn moved everything after it, regardless of subscribeOn being written later.

Q19. What happens with two subscribeOns?

The one closest to the source controls the source's thread. The other only affects the brief subscription path above it. Library authors use this to guarantee where their own source runs.

Q20. Which scheduler for blocking calls and why not parallel?

boundedElastic: its threads are meant to block, capped at 10 × cores with task queues. parallel has only one thread per core, so blocking one wastes a fixed fraction of capacity, and blocking calls on those threads are also rejected by block() checks.

Q21. What is the event loop model?

A small number of threads (about one per core) each run a loop over a selector, processing ready I/O events and queued tasks, never waiting. Each connection is pinned to one loop. Handlers do small pieces of work and register a continuation for I/O. Concurrency comes from interleaving rather than from thread count, so thousands of connections use only a few threads.

Q22. How many threads does a WebFlux app use?

Reactor Netty I/O workers default to max(cores, 4). Add parallel (one per core) and boundedElastic when used. A thread dump shows reactor-http-nio-N. The WebClient shares the same event loops by default, so one service's slow work also affects its own outbound calls.

Q23. WebFlux latency spikes across all endpoints, CPU is low. What do you check?

A blocked event loop. Take a thread dump and look at reactor-http-nio-* threads stuck in socket read, Thread.sleep, JDBC or lock waits. Confirm with BlockHound in tests and reactor.netty metrics. Check for hidden blockers, like synchronous logging, DNS resolution, or a "reactive" client that blocks internally. Fix by removing the blocking call, or moving it to boundedElastic.

Q24. What is BlockHound?

A Java agent that instruments blocking JDK methods and throws if they are called on non-blocking threads. Install it in tests, with allowBlockingCallsInside for known-safe cases. It catches accidental blocking early, though it cannot catch slow CPU work on an event loop. Note that on JDK 13+ it needs -XX:+AllowRedefinitionToAddDeleteMethods.

Q25. Why does .block() throw in WebFlux?

Reactor marks event-loop threads as NonBlocking, and block() checks and throws IllegalStateException to prevent the deadlock in which a thread waits for a result that only it could deliver. Blocking is allowed on boundedElastic or on non-Reactor threads, but it is usually a design smell.

Q26. Cold vs hot publishers?

A cold publisher starts its work for each subscriber, so every subscriber gets all data and two subscribers make two HTTP calls. A hot one emits regardless of subscribers, and late subscribers miss earlier items. share, publish, cache and replay convert; Sinks creates a hot source.

Q27. Two subscribers to a WebClient Mono: how many HTTP calls?

Two, because it is cold. Use .cache() if the result should be shared. A sneaky version: Mono<User> u = client.getUser(); Mono.zip(u.map(a), u.map(b)) makes two calls, and cache() fixes that. A cache() with no TTL holds its value as long as the reference lives.

Q28. How do you implement a retry with backoff, and what mistakes do people make?

retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(200)).jitter(0.5).filter(isTransient)). Mistakes: no filter, so 400s retry; retrying non-idempotent POSTs; timeout in the wrong place (per attempt or overall); no jitter, which makes synchronised storms; and hiding the original error, which onRetryExhaustedThrow fixes.

Q29. How does timeout work?

If no signal arrives in the duration, it cancels upstream and emits TimeoutException. On a Flux, it is the time between items, plus the first, not total duration. It runs on parallel. Cancellation closes the HTTP connection, so the work on the far side may still complete.

Q30. What does cancellation do, and why does it matter?

cancel travels upstream through every operator, closing connections and stopping sources. If a client disconnects, the whole pipeline stops, saving DB and API costs. Cancel can be seen with doOnCancel, and doFinally handles all outcomes. Do not assume a cancelled DB write rolled back without checking how the driver treats it.

Q31. How does WebClient differ from RestTemplate under load?

RestTemplate holds a thread per call, so 1000 concurrent calls need 1000 threads. WebClient uses a few event loops and a bounded connection pool, so 1000 calls wait on sockets, not threads, and pending acquires are limited. With virtual threads, RestClient closes much of the gap, and is simpler for a blocking service.

Q32. What are WebClient's common production problems?

DataBufferLimitException (default 256 KB buffer); PrematureCloseException (idle connection closed by the server; set maxIdleTime); PoolAcquireTimeoutException (too few connections, or a leak); leaks from exchangeToMono without consuming the body; no timeouts by default; and building a new WebClient or HttpClient per call, which loses the pool. RefinePoint's gateway keeps one WebClient per controller and sets explicit timeouts.

Q33. What is R2DBC, and is it worth it?

A non-blocking database driver SPI. It removes thread waits on the DB in an already reactive stack, with Spring Data R2DBC on top. But it is no ORM, and the database's capacity limits are the same. If you need JPA, stay on MVC. With virtual threads, JDBC's blocking is cheap, which weakens the case further.

Q34. Can I use JPA with WebFlux?

Technically, by wrapping each call in fromCallable().subscribeOn(boundedElastic), but you get the worst of both. Lazy loading and @Transactional depend on ThreadLocals, so transactions and sessions do not span operators, and your concurrency is limited by the elastic pool and JDBC pool. If most of the service is JPA, use MVC.

Q35. How do transactions work in reactive?

@Transactional on a method returning Mono/Flux uses ReactiveTransactionManager and keeps the connection in the Reactor Context, committing on complete, rolling back on error, and rolling back on cancel by default. TransactionalOperator is the programmatic form. A subscriber must exist: returning the publisher is what matters, because without a subscribe nothing happens, not even the transaction.

Q36. Why doesn't ThreadLocal work, and what replaces it?

A pipeline hops threads, so a value set at one operator is absent at the next, and can leak to another request on that thread. Reactor Context, an immutable map bound to the subscription, replaces it. Micrometer's context-propagation bridges to ThreadLocals when libraries need them.

Q37. Why must contextWrite come after the operators that read it?

Context is populated during subscription, which flows from the bottom of the chain to the top. So contextWrite is visible to operators above it. People who write it at the top see NoSuchElementException or empty context. In web apps a WebFilter adds it around chain.filter, which puts it at the outermost level, visible to all handlers.

Q38. How do you log a trace id in a reactive app?

Enable automatic propagation (spring.reactor.context-propagation=auto, Boot 3.2+) with Micrometer Tracing, so MDC is restored per operator and normal logging gets traceId. Before that, people used a doOnEach helper that read from Context and set MDC by hand.

Q39. How do you unit test a Flux?

StepVerifier.create(flux).expectNext(...).verifyComplete(), expectError, thenCancel. withVirtualTime for delays without real waits. An initial demand of 0 plus thenRequest for backpressure tests. TestPublisher for controlled or badly-behaved sources. PublisherProbe to assert that a fallback was subscribed to.

Q40. How do you debug a reactive stack trace?

checkpoint("description") at boundaries for a cheap marker. ReactorDebugAgent.init() for assembly info in production, at low cost. Hooks.onOperatorDebug() in dev only, because it captures a stack at every operator. log() to see signals. Name pipelines and export metrics to see where time goes.

Q41. A pipeline never emits and never errors. How do you approach it?

Add log() at several points to see which signals pass. Candidates: nobody subscribed, a result was discarded, the source is empty so flatMap never fires, request was never made, a connection pool is exhausted, or an onErrorResume returned Mono.empty(). Add a timeout so a hang becomes a visible error.

Q42. How do you stream LLM tokens to a browser?

Use WebClient.bodyToFlux on the provider's stream, map to ServerSentEvent, return Flux with text/event-stream. Disable proxy buffering, heartbeat, set a per-token timeout, and send errors as an event. Client disconnect propagates cancel, which stops the upstream call. For structured output that must parse whole, streaming adds little: that is why RefinePoint's LlmClient returns the full response.

Q43. SseEmitter vs Flux<ServerSentEvent>?

SseEmitter is MVC's imperative API: you call send from any thread and must handle completion, timeout and error callbacks and clean up your registry. Flux is declarative and propagates cancellation automatically, and works from WebFlux or from an MVC controller. RefinePoint's inbox uses SseEmitter because a Kafka-driven service pushes to a registry of open connections, and it fits the MVC stack.

Q44. Why is Spring Cloud Gateway built on WebFlux?

A gateway is nearly pure I/O: accept, route, proxy, stream both ways, with many concurrent and long-lived connections. A non-blocking model keeps memory and threads low, and streaming bodies pass through with backpressure. The rule that follows: never put blocking code in a gateway filter.

Q45. How do pre and post filters work in a GlobalFilter?

Work before chain.filter(exchange) is pre-filter; chain.filter(exchange).then(Mono.fromRunnable(...)) is post-filter, once downstream completes. Filters run by Ordered value, lowest first, with post logic in reverse. Our rate limiter is at HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 10, so it rejects a request before anything else is spent on it.

Q46. How would you add rate limiting to Spring Cloud Gateway?

Use the built-in RequestRateLimiter filter with Redis for a shared limit, or a custom GlobalFilter for no dependency. RefinePoint chose the second: token buckets in a ConcurrentHashMap with API-key, user and IP keys, evicting idle entries, and returning 429 with Retry-After. The trade-off: each gateway instance counts separately.

Q47. Is synchronized allowed on the event loop?

Yes, for very short critical sections with no I/O. It does stall that loop if contended, so keep it to a few instructions. RateLimitFilter.Bucket does exactly that. A ConcurrentHashMap is fine too, though avoid expensive computeIfAbsent functions, since they hold a bin lock while running.

Q48. Are virtual threads replacing WebFlux?

For most services, yes: the main motivation, cheap waiting, is now available with plain blocking code, with normal stack traces and ThreadLocals. WebFlux keeps its place where backpressure, cancellation and stream composition are the requirement: gateways, streaming, or large fan-out pipelines. Do not rewrite a working reactive service only for that reason.

Q49. What do virtual threads not give you that Reactor does?

Backpressure as a protocol, cancellation that propagates automatically, and declarative stream operators (buffer, window, zip, retryWhen). Thread limits also vanish, so you need explicit semaphores to protect downstreams. Structured concurrency helps with fan-out and cancellation, though it was still a preview feature in Java 21.

Q50. What about the reverse: what does Reactor not give you that virtual threads do?

Readable sequential code, normal debugging, stack traces and profilers, full compatibility with JDBC/JPA and ThreadLocal-based libraries, and no "function colouring", where everything that calls reactive code must become reactive too.

Q51. Would you use WebFlux for a new service? Give your decision process.

I would first ask where time goes and what the concurrency looks like. Mostly DB CRUD on JPA: MVC. High I/O concurrency with blocking libraries: MVC with virtual threads. Proxying, streaming, thousands of idle connections or stream processing with backpressure: WebFlux. CPU-bound: neither; bound the pool. I also count team experience, since a reactive codebase nobody can debug is a production risk.

Q52. Does reactive reduce the load on the database?

No. It only reduces threads waiting on it. The DB still has the same number of connections, locks and I/O. Unlimited concurrency in the app can make the DB worse, so you still need pool limits and bounded flatMap concurrency.

Q53. Can a reactive app have higher latency than blocking?

Yes. At low concurrency, operator overhead and thread hops add latency compared with a direct call. An imperative app is often as fast or faster until concurrency exhausts its thread pool. Reactive's advantage is holding latency steady at high concurrency, not reducing it at low concurrency.

Q54. How do you call a blocking library from WebFlux safely?

Mono.fromCallable(() -> blocking()).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()). Consider a dedicated bounded scheduler so one slow library cannot exhaust the shared elastic pool. Add timeout, but note that it cannot interrupt the underlying blocking call unless that call is interruptible.

Q55. How is Flux.interval or delayElements different in threading?

They emit from a timer on the parallel scheduler, even if you called from another thread, so downstream operators run there unless you publishOn. Blocking in such a pipeline blocks a parallel thread. It surprises people who expect their calling thread.

Q56. What is Mono<Void> and why does then() matter?

A signal of completion or error with no value. then() ignores elements and completes when upstream completes; then(other) continues with another publisher. Use it to sequence side effects, as in repo.save(x).then(notify(x)). Remember doOnNext(x -> send(x)) with a Mono-returning send never subscribes to it: use flatMap for async side effects.

Q57. What is flatMap's prefetch and why do you see 32 and 256?

Queues.SMALL_BUFFER_SIZE (256) is the default flatMap concurrency, and XS_BUFFER_SIZE (32) the default prefetch per inner source. They explain why a Flux subscribed with flatMap takes 256 items upfront, and why log() shows request(256). They can be tuned per operator, and by system properties.

Q58. How do you convert Flux<DataBuffer> for large downloads and avoid leaks?

Pass the Flux<DataBuffer> straight through, exchange.getResponse().writeWith(flux), or use DataBufferUtils.write to a file. Buffers are reference-counted Netty memory, so any operator that drops one without releasing it leaks direct memory; use DataBufferUtils.release, and enable Netty's leak detector during tests. Never collectList a large body, since that defeats streaming.

Q59. How did you use reactive in your project?

RefinePoint: "Only where it earns its keep. The gateway is Spring Cloud Gateway, so reactive by nature. I wrote a RateLimitFilter as a GlobalFilter with in-memory token buckets, and small WebClient pipelines for the status page and API docs, using flatMapSequential, timeout and onErrorResume so one dead service degrades a page rather than breaking it. The other services are MVC with JPA and JdbcTemplate, since they are transactional and CPU-heavy, where reactive would add complexity and no capacity. Live notifications use SseEmitter."

20. Spring Data JPA & Hibernate Internals

JPA questions are where senior candidates are most often caught out, because JPA looks simple until production: a page that issues 400 queries, an update that silently does nothing, a LazyInitializationException in a JSON serializer, a batch insert that turns out to be 100,000 round trips. Interviewers probe the persistence context, because almost every JPA surprise is explained by it. This chapter builds that model first, then covers mapping, fetching, locking and multi-tenancy, and closes with when to stop using JPA, which RefinePoint does deliberately on its hot paths.

20.1 JPA vs Hibernate vs Spring Data JPA

Layer What it is You use it for
JPA (jakarta.persistence) Specification: interfaces and annotations Portable mapping and EntityManager API
Hibernate The most common JPA provider, plus its own extras @BatchSize, @JdbcTypeCode, @SoftDelete, filters, statistics
Spring Data JPA Abstraction over JPA Repositories without implementations, paging, Specifications, auditing

Session extends EntityManager in Hibernate 6, so entityManager.unwrap(Session.class) gives you the native API when you need it. Boot 3.4 ships Hibernate 6.6.

20.2 The persistence context

The persistence context is a map of (entity type, id) → managed instance plus a snapshot of each instance's state as it was loaded. One EntityManager owns one persistence context. In Spring, the transaction-scoped EntityManager you inject is a shared proxy that binds the real one to the current transaction (through TransactionSynchronizationManager), so one transaction means one persistence context.

It gives three things:

  1. First-level cache / identity guarantee. em.find(Run.class, id) twice in one transaction returns the same object and runs one SELECT. Within a context, one row maps to exactly one Java object.
  2. Automatic dirty checking. At flush, Hibernate compares each managed entity with its snapshot and generates UPDATEs for what changed. You do not call save to update a managed entity.
  3. Write-behind. INSERTs, UPDATEs and DELETEs are queued in an action queue and sent at flush, which allows ordering and JDBC batching.

Flush and flush modes

Flush means "synchronise the queued changes to the database"; it is not commit. Flush happens:

Trigger Mode AUTO (default) Mode COMMIT
Transaction commit Yes Yes
Before a JPQL/HQL query whose tables have pending changes Yes No
Before a native SQL query Yes, when bootstrapped through JPA (Hibernate cannot tell which tables it touches) No
Explicit em.flush() Yes Yes

Hibernate's native API adds MANUAL (only explicit flush) and ALWAYS.

Trap: "I set a field, but the native SELECT in the same transaction did not see it." If the flush mode is COMMIT, or the query goes through JdbcTemplate (a different API that knows nothing about the persistence context), pending changes are invisible. JdbcTemplate uses the same connection inside a Spring transaction, but Hibernate does not flush for it. Call em.flush() before mixing.

Dirty checking cost

Each managed entity costs memory for the instance plus its snapshot, and each flush compares every managed entity, field by field. Loading 100,000 entities in one transaction makes every flush slow and the heap large. Remedies:

  • @Transactional(readOnly = true): Spring sets the Hibernate session to read-only and flush mode MANUAL, so no snapshots are kept and no dirty check runs.
  • Projections (DTOs) instead of entities for reads.
  • In batch jobs, flush() and clear() every N rows.
  • Bytecode enhancement with dirty tracking, so Hibernate records which fields changed instead of comparing.

20.3 Entity lifecycle

State In persistence context? Has DB row? Changes saved automatically?
Transient No No No
Managed Yes Yes, or will at flush Yes
Detached No Yes No
Removed Yes, scheduled for delete Until flush Delete at flush

EntityManager operations

Operation Does Edge cases
persist(e) Makes a transient instance managed; INSERT at flush (immediately with IDENTITY) On a detached instance: EntityExistsException / "detached entity passed to persist"
merge(e) Copies state of e onto a managed instance (loaded by SELECT if needed) and returns that instance e itself stays detached; keep using the return value. Hibernate 6.6: merging a detached entity with a generated id that no longer exists throws an optimistic lock exception instead of inserting
find(cls, id) Context first, then SELECT; null if absent
getReference(cls, id) Returns an uninitialised proxy without SQL EntityNotFoundException on first access if absent. Ideal for setting a foreign key
remove(e) Schedules DELETE Must be managed; detached gives IllegalArgumentException
detach(e), clear() Evicts one or all Pending unflushed changes to them are lost
refresh(e) Reloads state from DB, overwriting changes
flush() Executes queued SQL Inside the transaction; still rollback-able

What Spring Data's save really does

@Transactional
public <S extends T> S save(S entity) {          // SimpleJpaRepository
    if (entityInformation.isNew(entity)) { em.persist(entity); return entity; }
    else { return em.merge(entity); }
}

isNew is true if the id is null (or a primitive 0), or if a wrapper @Version field is null, or as decided by Persistable.isNew(). Consequences:

  • An entity with an id assigned by the application (id = UUID.randomUUID() in the constructor) is "not new", so save calls merge, which issues a SELECT first to see if the row exists. Implement Persistable or add a @Version field to avoid it.
  • Calling save on a managed entity is harmless but useless; dirty checking already handles it.
  • Always use the return value of save; with merge it is a different object.

RefinePoint: BaseEntity uses @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.UUID), so the id is null until persist, isNew is true, and save takes the cheap persist path. The UUID is generated in the JVM, so unlike IDENTITY no round trip is needed to learn it.

20.4 Spring Data repositories

At startup, @EnableJpaRepositories (auto-configured by Boot from the AutoConfigurationPackages base package) scans for repository interfaces and registers a JpaRepositoryFactoryBean for each.

Query derivation parses method names with PartTree at startup: findTop30ByOrgIdOrderByStartedAtDesc, countByOrgIdAndStatusIn, existsBy..., deleteBy.... A reference to a property that does not exist fails application startup, which is a nice safety net. Keywords: And, Or, Between, LessThan, In, IsNull, Like, StartingWith, IgnoreCase, OrderBy, Top/First, Distinct.

RefinePoint: ReconRunRepository shows the full range: Page<ReconRun> findByOrgIdAndProcessIdOrderByStartedAtDesc(UUID orgId, UUID processId, Pageable pageable), findByOrgIdAndIdempotencyKey, findFirstByProcessIdAndStatusInOrderByRunNumberDesc (is a run already going?), and countByOrgIdAndQueuedAtGreaterThanEqualAndStatusNot, which counts a workspace's runs for plan limits. When a name gets past readability, like "latest completed run per process", it becomes an @Query JPQL with a correlated subquery.

@Query:

@Query("""
    SELECT r FROM ReconRun r
    WHERE r.orgId = :orgId AND r.status = 'COMPLETED' AND r.resultTable IS NOT NULL
      AND r.completedAt = (SELECT max(x.completedAt) FROM ReconRun x
                           WHERE x.orgId = :orgId AND x.processId = r.processId AND x.status = 'COMPLETED')
    """)
List<ReconRun> findLatestCompletedPerProcess(@Param("orgId") UUID orgId);

@Query(value = "SELECT * FROM recon_runs WHERE org_id = :org AND status = 'FAILED'",
       countQuery = "SELECT count(*) FROM recon_runs WHERE org_id = :org AND status = 'FAILED'",
       nativeQuery = true)
Page<ReconRun> failed(@Param("org") UUID org, Pageable p);

@Modifying(clearAutomatically = true, flushAutomatically = true)
@Query("DELETE FROM ErrorRecord r WHERE r.datasourceId = :ds AND r.status = 'OPEN'")
int deleteOpen(@Param("ds") UUID datasourceId);

JPQL is validated at startup; native SQL is not. Bulk @Modifying queries bypass the persistence context: managed entities in memory keep stale values, @Version is not incremented, cascades and lifecycle callbacks do not run. clearAutomatically clears the context afterwards, and flushAutomatically flushes pending changes first.

Projections

Kind Example SQL selects Notes
Entity List<ReconRun> All columns Managed, dirty checked
Closed interface interface RunSummary { UUID getId(); String getStatus(); } Only those columns Proxy-backed
Open interface @Value("#{target.matched + target.unmatched}") All columns SpEL needs the whole entity
DTO / record record RunRow(UUID id, String status) Constructor args Derived queries support records; JPQL uses SELECT new com.x.RunRow(r.id, r.status)
Dynamic <T> List<T> findByOrgId(UUID org, Class<T> type) Depends on type Caller chooses
Tuple List<Tuple> As written Flexible, untyped

DTO projections are the most effective single performance improvement for read endpoints: no snapshots, no dirty checking, no lazy loading surprises, fewer columns.

Specifications and Criteria

For dynamic filters (any combination of optional criteria), concatenating JPQL strings is error-prone and an injection risk. JpaSpecificationExecutor<T> takes composable predicates built on the Criteria API:

static Specification<ReconRun> inOrg(UUID org)        { return (r, q, cb) -> cb.equal(r.get("orgId"), org); }
static Specification<ReconRun> status(String s)        { return s == null ? null : (r, q, cb) -> cb.equal(r.get("status"), s); }
static Specification<ReconRun> since(LocalDateTime t)  { return t == null ? null : (r, q, cb) -> cb.greaterThanOrEqualTo(r.get("startedAt"), t); }

Page<ReconRun> page = repo.findAll(Specification.where(inOrg(org)).and(status(s)).and(since(t)), pageable);

null specifications are ignored, which makes optional filters simple. The JPA static metamodel (ReconRun_.status) makes them type-safe. Querydsl and jOOQ are alternatives with more readable syntax.

20.5 Pagination

Page<T> runs the content query and a count query; Slice<T> fetches size + 1 rows to know if there is a next page, without counting; List<T> with a Pageable does neither.

Page Slice Keyset (Window / ScrollPosition)
Total count Yes, extra query No No
Deep pages OFFSET scans skipped rows Same Constant cost with an index
Stable while inserting No No Yes
UI fit Numbered pages "Load more" Infinite scroll, exports, APIs 
-- offset: page 2000 reads and throws away 100,000 rows
SELECT * FROM recon_runs WHERE org_id = ? ORDER BY started_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 50 OFFSET 100000;
-- keyset: an index range scan from where the last page ended
SELECT * FROM recon_runs WHERE org_id = ? AND (started_at, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY started_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 50;

Spring Data 3.1 added Window<T> findFirst50ByOrgIdOrderByStartedAtDescIdDesc(UUID org, ScrollPosition pos) with ScrollPosition.keyset(). Always include a unique tie-breaker (id) in the sort, or rows with equal timestamps get skipped or duplicated between pages. For a Page over a complex @Query, provide countQuery explicitly; the derived count of a query with joins can be wrong or very slow.

20.6 Relationships and mapping

Owning side is the side whose mapping controls the foreign key column. In a bidirectional @OneToMany/@ManyToOne, the @ManyToOne side (the table with the FK) owns it; the collection side says mappedBy and is ignored when writing.

@Entity class ReconProcess extends BaseOrgEntity {
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "process", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
    private Set<FieldMapping> mappings = new HashSet<>();

    public void addMapping(FieldMapping m)    { mappings.add(m); m.setProcess(this); }   // keep both sides in sync
    public void removeMapping(FieldMapping m) { mappings.remove(m); m.setProcess(null); }
}
@Entity class FieldMapping extends BaseOrgEntity {
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "process_id")
    private ReconProcess process;              // OWNING side: this writes process_id
}

Rules worth stating in an interview:

  • Adding to the inverse collection only (process.getMappings().add(m)) without setting m.process writes nothing to the FK. Use helper methods that sync both sides.
  • Unidirectional @OneToMany without @JoinColumn creates a join table, and updating it can delete and reinsert all rows. Prefer bidirectional or unidirectional @ManyToOne.
  • Cascade propagates operations (PERSIST, MERGE, REMOVE, ALL) from parent to child. Cascade on @ManyToOne towards a parent is almost always wrong: deleting a child would delete the parent.
  • orphanRemoval = true deletes a child removed from the collection. CascadeType.REMOVE only deletes children when the parent is deleted.
  • @ManyToMany: use a Set (with a List, Hibernate deletes and reinserts all join rows on change), and as soon as the link needs attributes (who added it, when), replace it with an explicit join entity and two @ManyToOnes.
  • equals/hashCode on entities in Sets must be stable across persist (see chapter 1, Q31).

RefinePoint: we map almost no associations. Entities hold foreign keys as plain values (ReconRun.processId is a UUID, not a @ManyToOne ReconProcess), and code loads what it needs explicitly. Each service owns its own schema and aggregates are small, so object graphs add little and cost us N+1 risks, cascades and lazy loading. Referencing other aggregates by id is also standard DDD advice, and it is the only option across service boundaries anyway.

20.7 Fetching and the N+1 problem

Association JPA default fetch
@ManyToOne, @OneToOne EAGER
@OneToMany, @ManyToMany LAZY

Make every association LAZY and fetch explicitly per use case. EAGER cannot be turned off for one query, and with JPQL it still causes N+1, because the query loads the parents and Hibernate then fetches each eager association separately.

N+1: one query loads N parents, then accessing a lazy association on each parent issues one more query each.

List<ReconProcess> processes = repo.findByOrgId(org);           // 1 query
for (ReconProcess p : processes) p.getMappings().size();         // + N queries

Diagnosis: enable hibernate.generate_statistics or log SQL (logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG, org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=TRACE for parameters in Hibernate 6), look for repeated identical statements per request, count queries per request in integration tests (datasource-proxy or Hypersistence's SQLStatementCountValidator), and use APM traces that show 100 spans of the same SQL.

Fixes:

Fix How Good for Watch out
JOIN FETCH SELECT p FROM ReconProcess p JOIN FETCH p.mappings WHERE p.orgId = :org One use case, one collection Duplicated parents (Hibernate 6 deduplicates entities automatically); pagination applied in memory (warning HHH90003004)
@EntityGraph @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "mappings") List<ReconProcess> findByOrgId(UUID org) Derived queries Same pagination caveat
Batch fetching @BatchSize(size = 50) or hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=50 Global safety net N/50 + 1 queries instead of 1
@Fetch(FetchMode.SUBSELECT) Second query with the original query as subselect Collections of all loaded parents Re-runs the parent query
DTO projection SELECT new ... with explicit joins Read endpoints Not managed
Two queries Load parents page, then children WHERE process_id IN (:ids) Pagination + collections Manual assembly

Fetching two List collections in one query throws MultipleBagFetchException; even with Sets it produces a Cartesian product (10 mappings × 10 rules = 100 rows per process). Fetch one collection per query and batch the rest.

LazyInitializationException and open-in-view

LazyInitializationException: could not initialize proxy - no Session happens when an uninitialised proxy or collection is touched after its persistence context closed: typically in a controller or the JSON serializer after the @Transactional service returned.

Open Session in View (OSIV), spring.jpa.open-in-view, is true by default in Boot (with a startup warning). OpenEntityManagerInViewInterceptor keeps the EntityManager open for the whole web request, so lazy loading works in the view. The price: a DB connection may be held during rendering and slow serialisation, and lazy loads during serialisation run outside any transaction, silently generating N+1 queries in the JSON layer.

Fix properly: turn it off, fetch what each use case needs inside the service (fetch join, entity graph, DTO), and return DTOs.

RefinePoint: PlatformDefaults sets spring.jpa.open-in-view=false for all 13 services. A lazy access outside the service layer fails loudly in development instead of turning into hidden queries in production.

20.8 Second-level cache and query cache

The second-level cache is shared across sessions (and, with a distributed provider, across instances). Enable it with a JCache provider (Ehcache 3, Caffeine via JCache, Hazelcast, Infinispan): hibernate.cache.use_second_level_cache=true, a region factory, and @Cacheable + @org.hibernate.annotations.Cache(usage = READ_WRITE) on entities. It caches entity state by id (dehydrated, not object references). Concurrency strategies: READ_ONLY (immutable reference data), NONSTRICT_READ_WRITE, READ_WRITE (soft locks), TRANSACTIONAL.

The query cache stores ids of a query's results and is invalidated whenever any row in a table involved changes. For frequently written tables it adds overhead and gives almost nothing. It only helps alongside the entity cache.

Use the L2 cache for read-mostly reference data. Pitfalls: bulk updates and native SQL bypass it (Hibernate invalidates whole regions on native writes it cannot analyse), stale data across instances with local caches, memory, and changes made by other applications.

RefinePoint: we do not enable the Hibernate L2 cache. Services run as several instances, and most hot data (runs, breaks) is written constantly. For the few read-mostly values (remote API key checks, workspace lookups across services), ryfn-platform has a small TtlCache with explicit expiry, where staleness is a stated, bounded choice.

20.9 ID generation

Strategy How the id is produced JDBC batch inserts Notes
IDENTITY DB auto-increment at INSERT Disabled for inserts Hibernate must execute the INSERT immediately at persist to learn the id
SEQUENCE nextval before insert Yes allocationSize (default 50) with the pooled optimizer: one nextval gives 50 ids in memory
TABLE Emulated sequence in a table Yes Row lock contention; avoid
UUID (JPA 3.1) Generated in the JVM Yes No round trip; 16 bytes
AUTO Provider chooses Hibernate 6: SEQUENCE for numbers, UUID generator for UUID 
Pooled optimizer, allocationSize = 50, INCREMENT BY 50 in the DB sequence:
  nextval → 101   app hands out 52..101 from memory
  nextval → 151   app hands out 102..151
  Multiple instances each get their own block → no collisions, gaps are normal

The DB sequence's INCREMENT BY must match allocationSize, or ids collide or Hibernate fails validation. Hibernate 6 also changed the default sequence name to one per entity (<entity>_seq) instead of a shared hibernate_sequence, a classic Boot 3 migration surprise.

UUID trade-offs: random UUIDv4 keys insert into random positions of a B-tree index, causing page splits and poor cache locality on large tables; they are also 16 bytes against 8 for bigint. Time-ordered UUIDv7 keeps the generate-anywhere benefit with sequential locality. Benefits of UUIDs: ids can be created before persist, safe across services and in URLs (not enumerable), and easy to merge between environments.

20.10 Batch inserts and updates

spring:
  jpa:
    properties:
      hibernate:
        jdbc.batch_size: 50
        order_inserts: true          # group INSERTs by entity so batches are not broken
        order_updates: true
        jdbc.batch_versioned_data: true
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://host/db?reWriteBatchedInserts=true   # driver rewrites to multi-row INSERT
@Transactional
void importRows(List<Row> rows) {
    for (int i = 0; i < rows.size(); i++) {
        em.persist(toEntity(rows.get(i)));
        if (i % 50 == 49) { em.flush(); em.clear(); }    // bound memory and dirty-check cost
    }
}

What breaks batching: IDENTITY ids, interleaving entity types without order_inserts, a flush triggered by a query in the loop, and saveAll on entities with assigned ids (each merge SELECTs first). Even working, JPA batching still builds one entity and snapshot per row; for real bulk loads, JdbcTemplate.batchUpdate or PostgreSQL COPY is several times faster.

20.11 Locking

Optimistic: @Version

@Version private long version;

Every UPDATE becomes UPDATE ... SET ..., version = 8 WHERE id = ? AND version = 7. Zero rows updated means someone else changed it: Hibernate throws OptimisticLockException, which Spring translates to ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException. Handle it by retrying the whole read-modify-write, or by returning 409 to the user. It prevents lost updates without holding locks, best when conflicts are rare. Over HTTP it pairs with ETag/If-Match (chapter 18).

Pessimistic

@Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)                                     // SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
@QueryHints(@QueryHint(name = "jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout", value = "3000"))
@Query("select s from OrgSubscription s where lower(s.pendingEmail) = lower(:email) and s.orgId is null")
List<OrgSubscription> lockPendingByEmail(@Param("email") String email);
Mode PostgreSQL SQL Use
PESSIMISTIC_READ FOR SHARE Others may read-lock, nobody may write
PESSIMISTIC_WRITE FOR UPDATE Exclusive until commit
PESSIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT FOR UPDATE + version bump
Lock timeout 0 / -2 (Hibernate) NOWAIT / SKIP LOCKED Fail fast / queue workers

Locks are held until the transaction ends, so keep those transactions short, lock rows in a consistent order to avoid deadlocks, and never hold a row lock across a remote call.

RefinePoint: billing-service's OrgSubscriptionRepository.lockPendingByEmail is @Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE): the welcome page and sign-up can both try to claim a pending Paddle purchase at the same moment, and the lock makes sure the purchase is applied, or cancelled and refunded, exactly once. The work queues use FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED through JdbcTemplate, because there the point is that concurrent workers skip locked rows instead of waiting.

20.12 Inheritance mapping

Strategy Tables Polymorphic query Pros Cons
SINGLE_TABLE (default) One, with a discriminator column One SELECT, no joins Fastest Subclass columns must be nullable; wide table
JOINED Parent + one per subclass Joins (outer joins for polymorphic) Normalised, NOT NULL possible Join cost grows with depth
TABLE_PER_CLASS One per concrete class, full columns UNION ALL No joins for concrete queries Polymorphic queries slow; no IDENTITY
@MappedSuperclass No table for parent Not possible Share columns and mapping only Parent is not an entity

@MappedSuperclass is for code reuse of mapping, not a type hierarchy you query. You cannot write SELECT b FROM BaseEntity b or have a @ManyToOne BaseEntity.

RefinePoint: BaseEntity (id as a generated UUID, createdAt with @CreationTimestamp, updatedAt with @UpdateTimestamp) and BaseOrgEntity (adds org_id NOT NULL) are @MappedSuperclasses. Every tenant table gets the same columns from one place, and nobody ever needs "all entities of any type" polymorphically.

20.13 Auditing, soft delete and JSON columns

Auditing. Two ways to fill timestamps:

Hibernate Spring Data
Annotations @CreationTimestamp, @UpdateTimestamp @CreatedDate, @LastModifiedDate, @CreatedBy, @LastModifiedBy
Setup None @EnableJpaAuditing + @EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class)
"Who" No AuditorAware<T> bean, from the security context

Neither keeps history. For a history of changes, use Hibernate Envers (an _AUD table per entity) or domain audit events.

RefinePoint: entities use Hibernate's timestamps through BaseEntity, with hibernate.jdbc.time_zone=UTC so stored times are UTC. Who did what is a business record, not a column: services emit audit events (AuditTrail, via the outbox) that audit-service stores, which is what an auditor of a financial system actually asks for.

Soft delete. Hibernate 6.4+ has @SoftDelete (a boolean or timestamp column, filtered automatically). Before that: @SQLDelete(sql = "UPDATE x SET deleted = true WHERE id = ?") plus @SQLRestriction("deleted = false") (6.3, replacing @Where). Consequences: unique constraints must become partial indexes (WHERE deleted = false), every index and native query must remember the flag, and data grows. Consider an archive table, or event history, instead.

JSON columns. @JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON) on a Map or record maps it to PostgreSQL jsonb without custom types in Hibernate 6. RefinePoint's AuditLog and PaymentOrder use exactly that.

20.14 Multi-tenancy approaches

Discriminator (org_id) Schema per tenant Database per tenant
Isolation Logical; one missed filter leaks data Strong Strongest
Cost per tenant Near zero Medium High
Migrations Once N times N times
Cross-tenant reporting Easy Harder Hardest
Noisy neighbours Shared Shared Separate
Hibernate support @TenantId (6.0+), filters MultiTenantConnectionProvider + CurrentTenantIdentifierResolver Same, or AbstractRoutingDataSource
Fits SaaS with many small tenants Tens to hundreds of tenants with compliance needs Few large or regulated tenants

Enforcing a discriminator automatically:

  • Hibernate @TenantId: a field filled from CurrentTenantIdentifierResolver, added to every query of that entity.
  • Hibernate filters: @FilterDef(name = "org", parameters = @ParamDef(name = "orgId", type = UUID.class)) + @Filter(name = "org", condition = "org_id = :orgId"), enabled per session (session.enableFilter("org").setParameter(...)). Filters do not apply to find by id or native SQL.
  • PostgreSQL row-level security: policies USING (org_id = current_setting('app.org')::uuid), enforced by the database even for native SQL. Requires setting the variable on every connection checkout, and testing that pooling cannot leak it.

RefinePoint: we use the discriminator column. BaseOrgEntity makes org_id mandatory, OrgAccessInterceptor resolves the workspace code to an org id after checking membership, and repositories take the org id explicitly: findByOrgIdAndProcessIdOrderByStartedAtDesc, findByOrgIdAndIdempotencyKey. Explicit parameters are visible in code review; a method without OrgId in its name stands out. Separately, each service owns one PostgreSQL schema (currentSchema=${rp.schema}, hibernate.default_schema), which is service isolation, not tenant isolation.

20.15 When to use JdbcTemplate instead

JPA is good at loading an aggregate, changing it and saving it. It is the wrong tool for set-based work.

Use JPA for Use JdbcTemplate / JdbcClient / jOOQ for
CRUD on aggregates with invariants Bulk insert, upsert (ON CONFLICT), COPY
Dirty checking, cascades, optimistic locking Queue claims with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and RETURNING
Paged lists with filters Reporting, window functions, CTEs
Moderate data volumes Millions of rows, streaming result sets
Dynamic tables (names decided at runtime) 
jdbc.batchUpdate("""
    INSERT INTO lookup_rows (id, table_id, key, range_from, range_to, row_values, position)
    VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?::jsonb, ?)
    ON CONFLICT (table_id, key) WHERE key IS NOT NULL DO UPDATE SET row_values = EXCLUDED.row_values
    """, batch);

RefinePoint: we use both in the same services, in the same transactions. JPA repositories cover configuration and entities: processes, runs, subscriptions, settings. JdbcTemplate covers the hot paths: RunWorker claims runs with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE OF r SKIP LOCKED and marks them RUNNING with a heartbeat; a reaper resets stale runs with UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) RETURNING id; lookup-service imports rows with a batched ON CONFLICT upsert; BreakEvents and data-quality checks insert with batchUpdate; consumers dedupe with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. Reconciliation results themselves live in result tables processed by DuckDB, which no ORM could map.

Spring 6.1's JdbcClient is a fluent wrapper: jdbc.sql("SELECT ... WHERE id = :id").param("id", id).query(Run.class).optional().

20.16 Flyway migrations

Flyway applies versioned SQL scripts in order and records each in flyway_schema_history with a checksum.

db/migration/
  V1__baseline.sql             versioned: runs once, in order
  V2__break_management.sql
  V14__run_queue.sql
  R__views.sql                 repeatable: re-runs when its checksum changes, after versioned ones

Boot runs Flyway before the EntityManagerFactory is created (the factory depends on the Flyway initialiser), so ddl-auto=validate checks the migrated schema. At startup Flyway validates checksums of applied scripts: editing a script that has already run fails startup, deliberately. Never edit an applied migration; add a new one. (flyway repair realigns checksums when a change was intentional, for example a comment-only edit.)

Zero-downtime changes use expand/contract, because old and new versions run side by side during a rolling deploy:

Renaming a column in one migration breaks the old instances still running. Large backfills should not run inside the startup migration (they hold locks and delay startup); CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run in a transaction, so it needs its own non-transactional migration.

RefinePoint: every service owns one schema and its migrations. PlatformDefaults sets spring.flyway.schemas=${rp.schema}, create-schemas=true and ddl-auto=validate, so Hibernate never changes the schema; it only checks that mappings match. Each service starts from V1__baseline.sql and applies its numbered changes in order (run-service is past V14 already).

20.17 Interview questions and answers

Q1. What is the difference between JPA, Hibernate and Spring Data JPA?

JPA is the specification: annotations plus the EntityManager API. Hibernate is an implementation of it with many extras. Spring Data JPA sits on top and generates repository implementations, query derivation, paging and auditing. You can use JPA without Spring Data, but Spring Data JPA cannot work without a JPA provider.

Q2. What is the persistence context?

The set of managed entity instances for one EntityManager, keyed by type and id, with a snapshot of each. It guarantees one object per row per context, serves repeated lookups without SQL, detects changes at flush (dirty checking), and queues writes. In Spring, it is normally scoped to the transaction.

Q3. What is the first-level cache? Can it be disabled?

It is the persistence context itself. It cannot be disabled, because it is how JPA tracks identity. It is per transaction and not shared, so it does not cause staleness across requests. In long batch transactions it grows, so clear() it periodically.

Q4. What does this print?

@Transactional void test(UUID id) {
    ReconRun a = repo.findById(id).orElseThrow();
    ReconRun b = repo.findById(id).orElseThrow();
    System.out.println(a == b);
}

true, with one SELECT. Both lookups hit the same persistence context. Without @Transactional (and with OSIV off), each repository call runs in its own transaction, so it prints false and issues two SELECTs.

Q5. I changed an entity's field and never called save. Why was it updated?

It was managed: loaded inside a transaction. At commit, dirty checking compared it with its snapshot and issued an UPDATE. That is by design. To avoid it, change a detached copy or a DTO, use readOnly = true transactions, or do not mutate entities you only meant to read.

Q6. Why did my update not get saved?

Usually the entity was detached (loaded in a different transaction, or no transaction at all), so nothing tracked it. Or the method was not transactional because of self-invocation, or it was readOnly, or an exception rolled back the transaction, or the update was a @Modifying query whose effect was then overwritten by a later flush of stale managed state. Check the transaction boundaries first.

Q7. When does Hibernate flush?

At commit, before a JPQL query that touches tables with pending changes (in AUTO mode), before native queries when bootstrapped via JPA, and on explicit flush(). Flush sends SQL; commit makes it durable. A flushed change can still be rolled back.

Q8. What are the entity states?

Transient (new, unknown to JPA), managed (in a persistence context and tracked), detached (has an id and row, but no longer tracked), removed (scheduled for delete). persist makes transient managed, merge copies detached onto managed, closing the context detaches, remove marks it removed.

Q9. persist vs merge?

persist makes the given instance managed; it is for new entities and returns nothing. merge copies the state of the given instance onto a managed instance, loading it if needed, and returns that managed one; the argument stays detached. Using merge for new entities costs an extra SELECT; using persist on a detached entity throws.

Q10. What does Spring Data's save() do?

It calls persist if isNew (id null, or version null, or Persistable.isNew()), else merge, and returns the result. So with application-assigned ids, every save is a merge with a SELECT first. Always use the return value.

Q11. findById vs getReferenceById?

findById hits the context then the DB, and returns Optional (empty if absent). getReferenceById returns a lazy proxy with no SQL; the first access to a non-id field loads it, and throws EntityNotFoundException if the row is missing. Use the reference to set a foreign key without loading the parent: child.setProcess(repo.getReferenceById(processId)).

Q12. How are Spring Data repository implementations created?

At startup, repository interfaces are found by scanning, and for each a factory bean creates a JDK proxy whose target is SimpleJpaRepository (CRUD), plus an interceptor that executes query methods. Query methods are parsed into PartTree or @Query objects at startup, and fail startup if invalid. Custom fragments (XxxRepositoryCustom plus Impl) are mixed in. The proxy adds transactions and exception translation.

Q13. Are repository methods transactional?

Yes. SimpleJpaRepository is @Transactional(readOnly = true) at class level, with @Transactional on write methods. Derived query methods you declare inherit the read-only default. For several calls to share one context and commit atomically, the service method must be @Transactional itself.

Q14. How does query derivation fail?

At startup, with PropertyReferenceException or a query creation error, when a method name refers to a property that does not exist. That is a benefit: renaming a field breaks the build or startup, not production. Long names are a readability smell; past three or four criteria, use @Query or a Specification.

Q15. What does @Modifying do, and what are the pitfalls?

It marks an @Query as an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE executed with executeUpdate. It bypasses the persistence context: managed entities keep stale values, and later flushes can overwrite the bulk change. @Version, cascades and entity callbacks are skipped. Use clearAutomatically and flushAutomatically, and it must run in a writable transaction.

Q16. JPQL vs native query?

JPQL is written against entities, validated at startup, portable, and understood by Hibernate (flush decisions, caches). Native SQL gives full database features (window functions, ON CONFLICT, SKIP LOCKED, jsonb operators), but is not validated, needs a manual count query for paging, and can confuse the cache. Use native where it adds something you need.

Q17. What projection types does Spring Data support?

Closed interface projections (select only the getters' columns), open interface projections (SpEL, so the full entity is loaded), class/record DTOs (constructor expressions), dynamic projections (a Class<T> parameter) and Tuple. For read-heavy endpoints, DTO and closed projections avoid entity overhead.

Q18. How do you write a dynamic search with optional filters?

JpaSpecificationExecutor with small composable Specifications, where each returns null when its filter is absent; or Querydsl, or the Criteria API directly. Avoid string concatenation of JPQL. Whitelist sortable fields and make sure filter columns are indexed.

Q19. Page vs Slice?

Page runs an extra count query to give total elements and pages. Slice fetches one extra row to know whether a next page exists, and is cheaper on big tables. For deep paging, use keyset (Window, ScrollPosition) instead of either.

Q20. Why is deep offset pagination slow?

OFFSET 100000 makes the database produce and discard 100,000 rows before returning 50. Keyset pagination (WHERE (started_at, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY started_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 50) uses an index range scan and costs the same at any depth. Include a unique tie-breaker.

Q21. What is the owning side of a relationship?

The side whose mapping writes the foreign key: the @ManyToOne side, or the side with @JoinColumn / @JoinTable. The mappedBy side is inverse and ignored for writes. Changing only the inverse collection does not change the database.

Q22. Why do we need helper methods for bidirectional associations?

Because both sides are Java references that JPA does not sync for you. If you add a child to the parent's collection without setting the child's parent field, the in-memory graph is inconsistent and the FK is not written. addMapping/removeMapping set both sides in one place.

Q23. CascadeType.REMOVE vs orphanRemoval?

Cascade REMOVE deletes children when the parent is removed. orphanRemoval also deletes a child as soon as it is removed from the parent's collection, or reassigned. Use orphanRemoval for true composition (the child cannot exist alone). Never cascade from child to parent.

Q24. What are the problems with @ManyToMany?

With a List (a bag), Hibernate deletes all join rows and reinserts them on every change. Extra attributes on the link cannot be mapped. Cascading REMOVE can delete shared entities. Use a Set, and replace with an explicit join entity once the link has its own data.

Q25. Default fetch types, and what should you use?

@ManyToOne/@OneToOne are EAGER by default; collections are LAZY. Make everything LAZY, then fetch explicitly per use case, because an EAGER association cannot be made lazy for a single query and causes extra queries in JPQL.

Q26. What is the N+1 problem?

One query loads N rows, then N more queries load an association for each. It hides in loops, in mappers and in JSON serialisation. It is invisible at 10 rows and severe at 10,000, since every round trip costs network latency.

Q27. How do you detect N+1 in an application?

Log SQL in dev (org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG) and look for repeated statements, enable Hibernate statistics, assert query counts in integration tests, and use APM traces in production, which show many identical queries in one request. Also watch for slow endpoints whose DB time far exceeds a single query's.

Q28. How do you fix N+1? Compare the options.

JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph load in one query for a given use case. @BatchSize/default_batch_fetch_size turns N queries into N/size queries as a global safety net. SUBSELECT fetch loads all children with one extra query. DTO projections select exactly what the view needs. For paginated parents with collections: page the parent ids, then fetch children with IN.

Q29. What happens if you JOIN FETCH a collection with pagination?

Hibernate cannot apply LIMIT to joined rows without cutting a parent's children, so it fetches all rows and paginates in memory, logging HHH90003004. On a big table this is an out-of-memory risk. You can make it fail instead with hibernate.query.fail_on_pagination_over_collection_fetch=true. Fix by paging ids first.

Q30. What is MultipleBagFetchException?

Thrown when you fetch-join two List (bag) collections in one query, because Hibernate cannot tell duplicates apart in a Cartesian product. Switching to Set stops the exception but keeps the Cartesian explosion. Fetch one collection per query and batch-fetch the others.

Q31. What causes LazyInitializationException, and how do you fix it properly?

Touching an uninitialised lazy proxy or collection after the persistence context closed, usually in the web layer or serializer. Proper fixes: fetch needed data inside the transactional service (fetch join, entity graph, DTO) and return DTOs. Workarounds to avoid: OSIV, enable_lazy_load_no_trans (a new session and connection per lazy load), and making associations EAGER.

Q32. What is open-in-view and why disable it?

spring.jpa.open-in-view=true (Boot's default) keeps the EntityManager open for the whole HTTP request, so lazy loading works in controllers and serializers. It hides N+1 queries in serialisation, holds a connection longer, and blurs where data access happens. RefinePoint disables it platform-wide in PlatformDefaults.

Q33. What is the second-level cache, and when would you use it?

A shared cache of entity state by id across sessions, with pluggable providers and per-entity concurrency strategies. Use it for read-mostly reference data looked up by id. Avoid it for frequently written data and when other systems write to the database, and use a distributed or invalidating provider with multiple instances.

Q34. Why is the query cache rarely worth it?

It stores result ids keyed by query and parameters, and it is invalidated whenever any table in the query changes. On tables with regular writes, it is invalidated constantly and adds overhead. It also needs the entity cache, otherwise each cached id becomes a separate SELECT, which is worse than the original query.

Q35. Why does IDENTITY disable batch inserts?

Hibernate must know the id as soon as an entity becomes managed, and with IDENTITY only the INSERT itself produces it. So each persist executes its INSERT immediately and individually. SEQUENCE (with a pooled allocation) or a UUID gets ids without inserting, so INSERTs can be queued and batched.

Q36. How does the pooled sequence optimizer work?

With allocationSize = 50 and the sequence INCREMENT BY 50, one nextval reserves a block of 50 ids that the JVM hands out from memory. Each instance reserves its own blocks, so ids never collide and only one round trip happens per 50 inserts. Gaps are normal after restarts. A mismatch between allocation size and the increment causes duplicates or validation failure.

Q37. UUID vs bigint primary keys?

UUIDs can be generated anywhere (before persist, across services, offline), are not enumerable in URLs, and merge cleanly across environments. They cost 16 bytes against 8, and random v4 values fragment B-tree indexes on large tables. Use UUIDv7 for time-ordered locality. RefinePoint uses GenerationType.UUID everywhere, which fits the many services and public URLs.

Q38. How do you make batch inserts fast with Hibernate?

hibernate.jdbc.batch_size (30–100), order_inserts/order_updates, a non-IDENTITY id, reWriteBatchedInserts=true for PostgreSQL, and flush() + clear() every batch to bound the context. Avoid saveAll with assigned ids. For millions of rows use JdbcTemplate.batchUpdate or COPY.

Q39. Optimistic vs pessimistic locking?

Optimistic (@Version) detects conflicts at write time without holding locks: high concurrency, rare conflicts, user edits, and it works across requests via a version or ETag. Pessimistic (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) blocks others until commit: high contention or must-not-fail critical sections such as claiming a payment. Pessimistic needs short transactions and consistent lock ordering.

Q40. What happens on an optimistic lock failure, and how do you handle it?

The UPDATE matches zero rows because the version changed, so Hibernate throws OptimisticLockException (Spring: ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException), and the transaction is marked for rollback. Retry the whole unit of work in a new transaction (Spring Retry or a loop), or return 409 to the user to reload. Retrying only the save inside the same transaction does not work.

Q41. How do you implement a job queue with JPA?

Native or @Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) with lock timeout -2 (SKIP LOCKED in Hibernate) to claim rows, then commit the claim straightaway so the lock is not held during processing. In RefinePoint we do it with JdbcTemplate: SELECT ... LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED in a short TransactionTemplate, then UPDATE status = 'RUNNING', instance = ?, heartbeat_at = now(). A reaper re-handles rows whose heartbeat went stale.

Q42. What inheritance strategies exist, and which do you choose?

SINGLE_TABLE is fastest with nullable subclass columns; JOINED is normalised with joins; TABLE_PER_CLASS uses UNIONs for polymorphic queries. Default to SINGLE_TABLE for small hierarchies queried polymorphically, JOINED when subclasses differ a lot and integrity matters. If you never query polymorphically, use @MappedSuperclass, or composition.

Q43. @MappedSuperclass vs @Entity inheritance?

@MappedSuperclass shares mapped fields with subclasses but is not an entity: it has no table, cannot be queried, and cannot be a relationship target. Entity inheritance creates a polymorphic type you can query and reference. RefinePoint's BaseEntity/BaseOrgEntity are mapped superclasses, because we want the same columns everywhere, not a queryable hierarchy.

Q44. How do you add auditing columns?

Either Hibernate's @CreationTimestamp/@UpdateTimestamp (no setup), or Spring Data's @CreatedDate, @LastModifiedDate, @CreatedBy, @LastModifiedBy with @EnableJpaAuditing, AuditingEntityListener and an AuditorAware bean. Neither covers bulk updates. For full change history, use Envers or domain audit events; RefinePoint does the latter through audit-service.

Q45. How do you implement soft delete, and what does it cost?

Hibernate 6.4's @SoftDelete, or @SQLDelete + @SQLRestriction before that. Costs: unique constraints become partial indexes, native queries must remember the filter, related entities need consistent rules, and tables grow. An archive table, or keeping deletions as events, is often cleaner.

Q46. What multi-tenancy approaches does Hibernate support?

Discriminator (@TenantId in Hibernate 6, or filters), schema per tenant and database per tenant (both through MultiTenantConnectionProvider plus CurrentTenantIdentifierResolver). Choose by tenant count, isolation and compliance needs, and operational cost. Many SaaS products use a discriminator, optionally backed by PostgreSQL row-level security.

Q47. How did you implement multi-tenancy?

RefinePoint: "A discriminator column. Every tenant entity extends BaseOrgEntity, so org_id is NOT NULL by construction. The request's workspace code is resolved to an org id by OrgAccessInterceptor after a membership check, and repositories take it explicitly, like findByOrgIdAndIdempotencyKey, so a query without a tenant is visible in review. I chose explicit parameters over Hibernate filters because filters do not apply to find by id or native SQL, and a lot of our hot-path SQL is native through JdbcTemplate."

Q48. What are the risks of Hibernate filters for tenancy?

They must be enabled on every session (one missing place leaks data), they do not apply to find/getReference by id, to native queries, or to bulk operations in all cases, and they are easy to forget in background jobs that run without a request. Defence in depth: row-level security in PostgreSQL, plus tests that try cross-tenant access.

Q49. When would you use JdbcTemplate instead of JPA?

For set-based or database-specific work: bulk inserts and upserts, SKIP LOCKED queue claims, reporting queries with CTEs and window functions, streaming large results, and dynamic table names. JPA stays for aggregates with invariants and moderate volume. They mix safely in one Spring transaction; just flush the persistence context before JDBC reads entity tables you changed.

Q50. How do JPA and JdbcTemplate share a transaction?

JpaTransactionManager binds the JDBC connection of the EntityManager to the transaction, and JdbcTemplate obtains its connection via DataSourceUtils, which returns that same bound connection. So both commit or roll back together. Hibernate does not know what JDBC changed, though: entities already loaded may be stale, and pending JPA changes are not visible to JDBC until a flush.

Q51. How do Flyway and Hibernate cooperate at startup?

Boot runs Flyway migrations before building the EntityManagerFactory, then Hibernate's ddl-auto=validate checks that mappings match the migrated schema and fails startup if not. Never use ddl-auto=update in shared environments: it cannot drop or rename, and it changes schemas without review. RefinePoint sets validate in the platform defaults.

Q52. Someone edited an applied migration and the service won't start. What happened and what now?

Flyway validates checksums at startup and found a mismatch with flyway_schema_history. If the change was meant to alter the schema, revert the file and add a new versioned migration. If it was cosmetic, run flyway repair to update the checksum. Applied migrations are immutable history.

Q53. How do you rename a column with zero downtime?

Expand/contract: add the new column, deploy code that writes both and reads the old, backfill in batches, deploy code that reads the new, and later drop the old column. A one-step rename breaks the old instances still running during a rolling deploy.

Q54. A list endpoint got slow as data grew. Walk me through your investigation.

Measure first: count queries per request and time per query from traces. N+1 shows as many identical queries, so fix with fetch joins, batching or a DTO. One slow query: run EXPLAIN ANALYZE, check for a missing index on the filter and sort columns (org_id, started_at), deep OFFSET, a count(*) behind Page. Huge result sets: paginate, project fewer columns, and use readOnly transactions. Then load-test the fix.

Q55. What does @Transactional(readOnly = true) do for JPA?

Spring sets the Hibernate session to read-only and the flush mode to MANUAL, so no snapshots are kept, no dirty checking runs, and no accidental updates happen. The JDBC connection is also marked read-only, which some drivers and routing data sources use to send queries to replicas. It is a real optimisation for large reads, not only documentation.

Q56. How does Hibernate map a JSON column?

In Hibernate 6, @JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON) on a Map, List or record field maps it to json/jsonb using the configured JSON format mapper (Jackson if present). RefinePoint's AuditLog details and billing's PaymentOrder use it. For querying inside JSON, native SQL with jsonb operators and a GIN index works best.

Q57. Why can a JPA entity's equals/hashCode break a Set?

If they use the generated id, the hash changes from null to a value at persist, so the entity is "lost" in its hash bucket. If they use all fields, lazy proxies and mutable fields cause the same problem. Use a stable business key, or id-based equals with a constant hashCode, and compare classes with Hibernate-proxy awareness.

Q58. How do you stream a large result set without running out of memory?

Use a Stream<T> repository method inside a read-only transaction with a fetch size hint (@QueryHints(@QueryHint(name = HINT_FETCH_SIZE, value = "1000"))), process each row, and detach or clear as you go. PostgreSQL only streams with autocommit off and a fetch size set. Or use JdbcTemplate with a RowCallbackHandler, which avoids entity overhead entirely.

Q59. What changed for JPA when moving to Boot 3?

javax.persistence became jakarta.persistence, Hibernate 5 became 6 (new SQM query parser, stricter HQL, @Where replaced by @SQLRestriction, per-entity default sequence names, @Type changes replaced by @JdbcTypeCode), and query result deduplication for fetch joins became automatic. Boot 3.4 brings Hibernate 6.6, which also refuses to merge a detached entity whose generated id no longer exists. Run the integration suite against a real PostgreSQL (Testcontainers) when upgrading.

Q60. How would you explain your data-access design in an interview?

RefinePoint: "Every service owns one PostgreSQL schema, migrated by Flyway with ddl-auto=validate. Entities extend BaseOrgEntity, so each has a UUID id, UTC timestamps and org_id. We map associations as ids rather than object graphs, so there are no cascades or N+1 surprises, and open-in-view is off platform-wide. Spring Data repositories cover CRUD and paging with org-scoped derived queries. Billing claims use a PESSIMISTIC_WRITE lock. Everything set-based or hot goes through JdbcTemplate: SKIP LOCKED work queues, ON CONFLICT upserts, batched inserts and idempotent consumer inserts. Each tool is used where it is strongest."

21. Transactions in Depth

Transactions are where senior interviews separate people who have used @Transactional from people who know what it does. The questions go deep fast: which connection does the inner method use, why did the outer method throw UnexpectedRollbackException, why did the pool run dry under load, how do you keep a database write and a Kafka message consistent without XA. This chapter goes from ACID down to the ThreadLocal that holds your connection, then up to sagas and the transactional outbox we run in production.

21.1 ACID — what each letter really costs

Letter Promise How PostgreSQL delivers it What breaks it in application code
Atomicity All statements commit or none do Every row version carries the creating transaction id (xmin); an aborted transaction's versions are simply invisible Doing non-transactional side effects (HTTP call, Kafka send, file write) inside the transaction
Consistency Constraints hold before and after NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE, FOREIGN KEY, deferred constraints checked at commit Invariants kept only in Java ("never more than 5 seats") without a constraint or a lock
Isolation Concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-done work MVCC snapshots + row locks + predicate locks (SERIALIZABLE) Choosing READ COMMITTED and writing read-modify-write logic
Durability Committed data survives a crash Write-ahead log (WAL) flushed (fsync) at commit, replayed on recovery synchronous_commit = off (trades last few ms of commits for speed)

The C is the odd one out: atomicity, isolation and durability are database guarantees; consistency is a joint responsibility. The database enforces declared constraints; your code enforces everything else, and it can only do so correctly if A, I and D hold.

PostgreSQL never overwrites a row in place: an UPDATE writes a new tuple version and marks the old one dead (xmax). Rollback is therefore nearly free (just mark the transaction aborted in the commit log), and readers never block writers. The price is vacuum: dead versions must be cleaned up, and a long-running transaction prevents that cleanup because its snapshot might still need old versions. This is one of several reasons long transactions are harmful (§21.9).

21.2 How a Spring local transaction actually works

@Transactional is AOP. The bean you inject is a proxy (JDK dynamic proxy for interfaces, CGLIB subclass otherwise; Boot defaults to CGLIB). The proxy's advice is TransactionInterceptor, which delegates to a PlatformTransactionManager.

Key internals:

  1. TransactionDefinition — propagation, isolation, timeout, readOnly, name. Built from the annotation by AnnotationTransactionAttributeSource (it caches attributes per method).
  2. PlatformTransactionManager — three methods: getTransaction(def), commit(status), rollback(status). Implementations: DataSourceTransactionManager / JdbcTransactionManager (plain JDBC, JdbcTemplate), JpaTransactionManager (JPA, also covers JdbcTemplate on the same DataSource), JtaTransactionManager (XA), KafkaTransactionManager. Reactive code uses ReactiveTransactionManager (R2dbcTransactionManager) and the Reactor context instead of thread locals.
  3. TransactionSynchronizationManager — a set of ThreadLocals: resources (a map from DataSource/EntityManagerFactory to the holder of the current connection/EntityManager), synchronizations (callbacks like afterCommit), current transaction name, read-only flag, isolation level and actualTransactionActive.
  4. Resource lookup — JdbcTemplate calls DataSourceUtils.getConnection(ds), which first checks the thread-local map. If a transaction bound a connection, you get that connection; otherwise a fresh auto-commit connection. Spring Data repositories use a shared EntityManager proxy that does the same lookup. That is how two repositories called from one service method share one database transaction without passing anything around.
Thread "http-nio-8080-exec-7"
 └── ThreadLocal resources
       ├── HikariDataSource@1a2b      → ConnectionHolder(conn#4, autoCommit=false)
       └── EntityManagerFactory@9f0e  → EntityManagerHolder(em, tx active)
 └── ThreadLocal synchronizations     → [TransactionalEventListener adapters, afterCommit callbacks]
 └── currentTransactionReadOnly       → false

Consequences you must be able to state: the transaction is bound to the thread. Code on another thread (an @Async method, a CompletableFuture.supplyAsync, a parallel stream, a new virtual thread) does not see it.

Proxy rules that follow from AOP

  • Self-invocation bypasses the proxy: this.save() inside the same bean calls the real method, so its @Transactional is ignored.
  • Annotate public methods. Since Spring 6.0, protected and package-private methods are also intercepted on CGLIB proxies, but private methods and final methods never are (CGLIB cannot override them).
  • @Transactional on an interface method works only with interface-based proxies; put it on the class.
  • The proxy wraps the bean, so calling the method on an object you created with new gets no transaction.

21.3 Propagation — all seven levels

Propagation answers: "a transactional method is called; is there already a transaction on this thread, and what should I do about it?"

Propagation Existing transaction present No transaction present Typical use
REQUIRED (default) Join it Start a new one Almost everything
REQUIRES_NEW Suspend it, start an independent one (new connection) Start a new one Audit/error logging that must survive the caller's rollback; claiming a work item
NESTED Create a savepoint inside it Behave like REQUIRED Optional sub-step whose failure should roll back only itself
SUPPORTS Join it Run non-transactionally Read helpers that do not care
NOT_SUPPORTED Suspend it, run without Run without Long non-DB work called from a transactional method (e.g., calling an LLM)
MANDATORY Join it Throw IllegalTransactionStateException Repository-like methods that must never run alone (e.g., EventPublisher.publish)
NEVER Throw Run without Guard: method must not be called inside a transaction

REQUIRED: one physical transaction, many logical scopes

Each @Transactional method creates a logical transaction scope, but with REQUIRED they all map to one physical transaction. Only the outermost scope commits. If any inner scope fails, it cannot roll back alone: it sets the shared transaction's rollback-only flag. That is the root of UnexpectedRollbackException (§21.6).

REQUIRES_NEW: a second connection

Suspension unbinds the outer resources from the thread-local map and stores them in a SuspendedResourcesHolder; the inner method gets a new connection, commits, and the outer resources are re-bound. Use cases:

  • Audit or failure logs that must persist even if the business transaction rolls back ("user tried to approve and failed").
  • Claiming work so the claim is visible immediately to other workers.
  • Sequence/number allocation that must not be held locked for the outer transaction's duration.

Costs: two connections per thread at the same time (pool deadlock risk, §21.9), the inner transaction cannot see the outer one's uncommitted rows, and if the inner one updates a row the outer one has locked, the thread deadlocks with itself (inner waits for the outer's lock; the outer waits for the inner to return).

RefinePoint: we chose the opposite of REQUIRES_NEW for audit. AuditTrail.record(...) writes the entry to the service's outbox in the same transaction as the change, and Kafka delivers it to audit-service. The audit log can never claim something that was rolled back, and an audit-service outage never blocks the action. The trade-off: a rolled-back attempt leaves no audit entry. If you must also record failed attempts, that is when REQUIRES_NEW earns its place. Know both patterns and be able to say which question each answers ("what changed" vs "who tried").

NESTED: savepoints

NESTED issues SAVEPOINT sp1 on the same connection. If the nested method throws, Spring runs ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp1 and the outer transaction continues; if it succeeds, RELEASE SAVEPOINT. Nothing is durable until the outer transaction commits, which is the difference from REQUIRES_NEW.

@Transactional
public ImportResult importRows(List<Row> rows) {
    for (Row row : rows) {
        try { rowImporter.importOne(row); }          // NESTED: a bad row rolls back only itself
        catch (DataIntegrityViolationException e) { result.reject(row, e); }
    }
    return result;                                   // good rows commit together
}

@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.NESTED)
public void importOne(Row row) { ... }

Support: DataSourceTransactionManager/JdbcTransactionManager yes (JDBC 3 savepoints). JpaTransactionManager supports it only for JDBC access through the same connection: the database rolls back to the savepoint but Hibernate's persistence context still holds the entities you changed, so mixing NESTED with JPA entity changes is unreliable. JtaTransactionManager does not support it. In PostgreSQL a failed statement aborts the whole transaction (current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block), so savepoints are the only way to continue after an error inside one transaction.

21.4 Isolation levels and the anomalies they prevent

The anomalies, with timelines

Dirty read — reading another transaction's uncommitted write.

T1: UPDATE acct SET bal = 0 WHERE id=1     (not committed)
T2:                                         SELECT bal → 0   ← dirty
T1: ROLLBACK                                T2 acted on a value that never existed

Non-repeatable read — the same row read twice gives different values because someone committed in between.

T1: SELECT status FROM run WHERE id=7 → QUEUED
T2:                                         UPDATE run SET status='RUNNING' WHERE id=7; COMMIT
T1: SELECT status FROM run WHERE id=7 → RUNNING   ← changed under T1

Phantom read — the same predicate returns a different set of rows.

T1: SELECT count(*) FROM breaks WHERE run_id=7 → 10
T2:                                         INSERT INTO breaks (run_id ...) VALUES (7 ...); COMMIT
T1: SELECT count(*) FROM breaks WHERE run_id=7 → 11   ← phantom row

Lost update — two read-modify-write cycles overlap; one write overwrites the other.

T1: SELECT bal → 100                 T2: SELECT bal → 100
T1: UPDATE bal = 100 - 30 → 70       T2: UPDATE bal = 100 - 50 → 50 (waits for T1's row lock)
T1: COMMIT                           T2: proceeds, writes 50; COMMIT  ← T1's -30 is lost

Write skew — two transactions read an overlapping set, each writes a different row, and together they violate an invariant neither violated alone.

Rule: at least one approver must stay on duty
T1: SELECT count(*) WHERE on_duty → 2     T2: SELECT count(*) WHERE on_duty → 2
T1: UPDATE approver SET on_duty=false WHERE id=A
                                          T2: UPDATE approver SET on_duty=false WHERE id=B
T1: COMMIT                                T2: COMMIT   → zero approvers on duty
