No row was written by both, so row locks never conflict. Only SERIALIZABLE (or explicit locking of the rows read) prevents it.

The matrix

Level Dirty read Non-repeatable Phantom Lost update Write skew
READ UNCOMMITTED (SQL std) possible possible possible possible possible
READ COMMITTED prevented possible possible possible possible
REPEATABLE READ (SQL std) prevented prevented possible prevented* possible
REPEATABLE READ (PostgreSQL) prevented prevented prevented prevented (error 40001) possible
SERIALIZABLE prevented prevented prevented prevented prevented

*Depends on implementation. MySQL InnoDB REPEATABLE READ (its default) uses next-key/gap locks for locking reads but plain SELECT reads a snapshot, so lost updates are still possible there without FOR UPDATE.

PostgreSQL specifics you should quote

  • Default is READ COMMITTED. READ UNCOMMITTED is accepted but behaves as READ COMMITTED — PostgreSQL never shows dirty data.
  • In READ COMMITTED each statement gets a fresh snapshot. Two SELECTs in one transaction can disagree.
  • When an UPDATE/DELETE/SELECT FOR UPDATE finds a row that a concurrent transaction is changing, it waits for that transaction. If it commits, PostgreSQL re-reads the newest version and re-checks the WHERE clause on it (the "EvalPlanQual" recheck), then updates that version. That is why UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - 30 is safe under READ COMMITTED while read-then-write in Java is not.
  • REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation: one snapshot for the whole transaction, taken at the first statement. If you try to update a row someone else changed after your snapshot, you get ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update (SQLSTATE 40001). The application must retry the whole transaction.
  • SERIALIZABLE is Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI): snapshot isolation plus tracking of read/write dependencies (SIRead predicate locks). It aborts one transaction of a dangerous cycle with 40001. Overhead is moderate; the real cost is that you need retry logic everywhere.
@Retryable(retryFor = CannotAcquireLockException.class, maxAttempts = 3, backoff = @Backoff(delay = 50, multiplier = 2))
@Transactional(isolation = Isolation.SERIALIZABLE)
public void goOffDuty(UUID approverId) { ... }

Spring translates 40001 into CannotAcquireLockException/PessimisticLockingFailureException subclasses (both TransientDataAccessException). The retry must wrap the outside of the transaction — a retry inside a rolled-back transaction is useless. With Spring Retry, put @Retryable on the same method and make sure the retry advice runs before the transaction advice (it does by default because @EnableRetry uses a higher precedence), or call the transactional method from a separate retrying bean.

Interview tip: when asked "which isolation level do you use?", the senior answer is: "READ COMMITTED (the PostgreSQL default) plus targeted locking — atomic UPDATE ... SET x = x + 1, conditional updates, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the rows that guard an invariant, and unique constraints for 'only one' rules. @Version optimistic locking fits user edits with long think time. I would not raise the global isolation level; I would raise it per transaction where an invariant spans rows."

21.5 readOnly, timeout and rollback rules

readOnly = true

It is a hint whose effect depends on the transaction manager and driver:

Layer Effect
Spring Sets TransactionSynchronizationManager.isCurrentTransactionReadOnly() — usable for routing to a read replica (AbstractRoutingDataSource + LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy)
JpaTransactionManager + Hibernate Session flush mode set to MANUAL and session default read-only: no dirty-checking snapshots kept, no flush at commit — less memory and CPU for big reads
JDBC Connection.setReadOnly(true); with JdbcTransactionManager.setEnforceReadOnly(true) Spring also executes SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY
PostgreSQL A read-only transaction rejects writes (cannot execute UPDATE in a read-only transaction) and can use cheaper paths for SERIALIZABLE (READ ONLY DEFERRABLE never aborts)

Common pattern: @Transactional(readOnly = true) on the service class, @Transactional on write methods. Spring Data's SimpleJpaRepository does exactly this.

Trap: readOnly on an outer REQUIRED transaction is inherited by inner methods. An inner @Transactional write method joining a read-only transaction will not flush its JPA changes (flush mode MANUAL) — changes silently disappear. Spring logs nothing by default.

timeout

@Transactional(timeout = 30) sets a deadline in seconds. It is not a thread interrupt: Spring checks the deadline when a statement is prepared (JdbcTemplate applies Statement.setQueryTimeout with the remaining time, JPA applies the query timeout hint), and throws TransactionTimedOutException if the deadline has passed. A loop that spends 5 minutes in Java code between queries will not be stopped mid-loop. For a database-side guarantee, set PostgreSQL statement_timeout, lock_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout.

Rollback rules

Default: roll back on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException) and Error; commit on checked exceptions. Historical reason: EJB treated checked exceptions as "business outcomes".

@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)                 // roll back on checked too
@Transactional(noRollbackFor = DuplicateBreakException.class) // keep the tx despite this runtime exception

Spring Framework 6.2 (Boot 3.4) adds a global switch: @EnableTransactionManagement(rollbackOn = RollbackOn.ALL_EXCEPTIONS). Rollback rules match by exception type and its subclasses; the string form (rollbackForClassName) matches by name pattern.

The decision is made when the exception leaves the proxy. An exception caught inside the method never reaches the interceptor, so the transaction commits — unless an inner REQUIRED method already marked it rollback-only.

21.6 Exceptions and the rollback-only trap

The inner method did not start the physical transaction, so it cannot roll it back; it can only vote. The outer method swallowed the exception and asked to commit, which contradicts the vote, so Spring rolls back and throws UnexpectedRollbackException: Transaction silently rolled back because it has been marked as rollback-only.

Fixes, depending on intent:

  1. The inner failure is really fatal → do not catch it.
  2. The inner step is optional → make it REQUIRES_NEW (independent outcome) or NESTED (savepoint), or noRollbackFor that exception.
  3. The inner method should not be transactional at all (pure validation) → remove @Transactional from it, so throwing does not touch the transaction.

You can also mark rollback without throwing: TransactionAspectSupport.currentTransactionStatus().setRollbackOnly(), or status.setRollbackOnly() inside TransactionTemplate.

The full list of "my @Transactional did nothing" causes

Cause Why
Self-invocation (this.method()) Proxy bypassed
Private / final method Proxy cannot intercept
Bean created with new or not a Spring bean No proxy
Checked exception thrown Default rules commit
Exception caught inside the method Interceptor never sees it
Wrong transaction manager (two DataSources) Transaction on DS A, query on DS B (auto-commit)
Work done on another thread Thread-local binding
MySQL MyISAM table Engine is not transactional
@Transactional from jakarta.transaction vs Spring's Both work in Spring, but jakarta has no readOnly/isolation/propagation nuances beyond TxType

21.7 Programmatic transactions

Declarative is the default; programmatic is better when the transaction boundary is smaller than a method or chosen at runtime (loops, schedulers, batches).

// TransactionTemplate: callback style, uses the same PlatformTransactionManager
Integer sent = tx.execute(status -> sendBatch());            // commit on return, rollback on RuntimeException
tx.executeWithoutResult(status -> { if (bad) status.setRollbackOnly(); });

// Custom settings per template
var requiresNew = new TransactionTemplate(txManager);
requiresNew.setPropagationBehavior(TransactionDefinition.PROPAGATION_REQUIRES_NEW);
requiresNew.setTimeout(10);

RefinePoint: OutboxRelay (in ryfn-platform) is a @Scheduled method that loops: do { sent = tx.execute(status -> sendBatch()); } while (sent == BATCH);. Each batch of 100 is its own short transaction: lock rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, send each to Kafka, mark it sent, commit. If we had put @Transactional on relay(), one transaction would cover the whole backlog, keep thousands of rows locked, and lose all progress on failure. JobScheduler.claim() and RunWorker.claim() use TransactionTemplate the same way: a few-millisecond transaction to claim work, and the long work itself runs outside any transaction.

Lowest level: PlatformTransactionManager directly (getTransaction / commit / rollback in try/finally) — only in framework code.

21.8 Transaction-bound events

@Transactional
public void complete(UUID runId) {
    run.complete();
    events.publishEvent(new RunCompleted(runId));   // ApplicationEventPublisher
}

@TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)
public void onCompleted(RunCompleted e) { notifier.email(e); }
Phase Runs Use for
BEFORE_COMMIT During commit(), before the database commit, inside the transaction Last-moment writes/validation that must be atomic with the transaction
AFTER_COMMIT (default) After a successful commit Emails, cache eviction, WebSocket pushes
AFTER_ROLLBACK After rollback Compensation logging, metrics
AFTER_COMPLETION After either Cleanup

Internals: publishing inside a transaction registers a TransactionSynchronization in the thread-local list; the transaction manager calls beforeCommit, afterCommit, afterCompletion on it. If there is no active transaction, the event is dropped unless fallbackExecution = true.

Pitfalls:

  • In AFTER_COMMIT, the old transaction's resources are still bound but already committed. A write with plain REQUIRED joins a finished transaction and is never committed. Spring 6.1+ refuses to start if a @TransactionalEventListener method is annotated @Transactional with anything other than REQUIRES_NEW or NOT_SUPPORTED.
  • AFTER_COMMIT is not durable: if the JVM dies after the commit and before the listener runs, the email is never sent. For anything that must happen, use the outbox (§21.11).
  • Listeners run synchronously on the same thread unless you add @Async.

21.9 Transactions, threads, virtual threads and pool exhaustion

Why a transaction pins a connection: from BEGIN to COMMIT the connection belongs to that thread. Anything slow inside the method — an HTTP call, an LLM request, generating a report, waiting on a lock — keeps it borrowed. With 10 connections and 200 request threads, ten slow transactions stop the whole service; every other request waits connectionTimeout (30 s by default) and fails with Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms.

Rules to follow:

  1. No remote calls inside a transaction. Fetch first, transact briefly, call afterwards (or use the outbox).
  2. Short claim transactions, long work outside (the run-queue pattern).
  3. spring.jpa.open-in-view=false (ryfn-platform's PlatformDefaults sets it for every RefinePoint service) — Open Session In View keeps the persistence context, and with Hibernate's default connection handling the connection too, until the view is rendered.
  4. Size the pool for the database, not for threads: a few dozen connections per database server, divided across instances. HikariCP's formula connections = cores * 2 + effective spindles is a starting point.
  5. Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout in PostgreSQL to kill sessions a crashed or buggy app left open.
  6. REQUIRES_NEW needs two connections per thread: if all N threads are in the outer transaction and all need an inner one, nobody can proceed — a pool deadlock until timeout.

@Async and executors: the task runs on another thread, outside the caller's transaction. If the caller passes an entity id and the async task reads it before the caller commits, the task does not find the row. Publish async work from AFTER_COMMIT or the outbox.

Virtual threads (Java 21): TransactionSynchronizationManager uses ThreadLocal, and each virtual thread has its own thread locals, so declarative transactions work unchanged on virtual threads (spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true). Two caveats: (a) virtual threads make it cheap to have 10,000 concurrent requests but the pool still has 10 connections, so requests now queue on getConnection() instead of on the Tomcat thread pool — limit concurrency with a semaphore or by pool size; (b) in Java 21 a virtual thread blocked inside a synchronized block pins its carrier thread; older JDBC drivers and pools used synchronized heavily. PostgreSQL JDBC 42.6+ and HikariCP 5 replaced most of it with ReentrantLock, and JDK 24 (JEP 491) removes pinning for synchronized.

Reactive: WebFlux + R2DBC keeps transaction state in the Reactor Context, not thread locals; @Transactional works with R2dbcTransactionManager because the operators carry the context across threads.

21.10 Locking: optimistic vs pessimistic

Optimistic Pessimistic
Idea Detect conflict at write time Prevent conflict by locking at read time
Mechanism @Version column: UPDATE ... SET version = 6 WHERE id = ? AND version = 5 SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (row lock held until commit)
On conflict 0 rows updated → OptimisticLockException → retry or tell the user Second transaction waits (or fails with NOWAIT / skips with SKIP LOCKED)
Best for Low contention, long "think time" (user edits a form for 5 minutes) High contention on few rows, short transactions, queues
Cost Retry logic, wasted work on conflict Blocking, deadlock risk, held connections 
@Entity
class Invoice {
    @Version private long version;    // Hibernate adds "AND version = ?" and increments it
}

public interface TaskRepository extends JpaRepository<Task, UUID> {
    @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)                       // SELECT ... FOR NO KEY UPDATE / FOR UPDATE
    @QueryHints(@QueryHint(name = "jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout", value = "-2"))  // -2 = SKIP LOCKED, 0 = NOWAIT
    @Query("select t from Task t where t.status = 'QUEUED' order by t.createdAt")
    List<Task> claimNext(Pageable one);
}

For REST APIs, optimistic locking extends to HTTP: return the version as an ETag, require If-Match on PUT, answer 412 Precondition Failed on mismatch. This stops two finance users silently overwriting each other's rule edits.

FOR UPDATE, NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED

Clause Behaviour when the row is locked by someone else
FOR UPDATE Wait until the other transaction ends (bounded by lock_timeout)
FOR UPDATE NOWAIT Fail immediately: ERROR 55P03 could not obtain lock on row
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED Pretend the row is not there; return the next unlocked rows

PostgreSQL also has weaker row locks: FOR NO KEY UPDATE (what a normal UPDATE takes when key columns do not change; does not block foreign-key checks), FOR SHARE and FOR KEY SHARE (taken by FK checks).

RefinePoint: run-service, job-service (JobScheduler), the export worker and the datasource refresh worker are all PostgreSQL work queues. RunWorker.claim() runs in a TransactionTemplate: it takes pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('run-queue')) so per-workspace concurrency caps are checked by one claimer at a time (the claim lasts milliseconds), selects one queued run FOR UPDATE OF r SKIP LOCKED, marks it RUNNING with the instance name and a heartbeat, and commits. The run itself executes outside the transaction. A reaper finds runs whose heartbeat is older than two minutes with UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) RETURNING id, so only one instance fails each orphaned run. Scaling is "start another instance" — no leader election, no ZooKeeper.

Deadlocks

Two transactions lock rows in opposite order. PostgreSQL detects the cycle after deadlock_timeout (1 s) and aborts one with 40P01 deadlock detected; Spring maps it to DeadlockLoserDataAccessException (deprecated alias) / CannotAcquireLockException. Prevention: lock rows in a consistent order (ORDER BY id ... FOR UPDATE), keep transactions short, avoid lock upgrades (read with FOR SHARE then update), retry the loser.

21.11 Distributed transactions: the dual-write problem, 2PC, sagas and the outbox

The dual-write problem

@Transactional
public void completeRun(UUID id) {
    runRepo.markCompleted(id);
    kafka.send("run.completed", id.toString(), json);   // not part of the DB transaction
}

Four failure windows: Kafka send succeeds and DB commit fails (consumers act on a run that is not completed); DB commits and the process dies before send (event lost); send times out but was actually written (unknown); send after commit fails (event lost). There is no ordering of two independent writes that is safe. You need either one transaction spanning both systems (2PC) or a design where only one system is written transactionally (outbox).

Two-phase commit (XA)

Why we avoid it in microservices:

  • Blocking: a participant that voted yes must hold locks until it hears the decision; if the coordinator dies, those rows stay locked ("in-doubt" transactions) until manual recovery.
  • Availability: the transaction succeeds only if every participant is up — availability multiplies down.
  • Support: Kafka does not support XA; many cloud databases and HTTP APIs cannot participate at all. PostgreSQL supports it (PREPARE TRANSACTION) but ships with max_prepared_transactions = 0.
  • Latency and coupling: extra round trips, shared coordinator, tight runtime coupling between services that should be independent.

2PC is still valid inside one boundary (an app server writing to two databases you own, using Atomikos or Narayana with JtaTransactionManager).

Sagas

A saga is a sequence of local transactions, each publishing an event or command that triggers the next; on failure, earlier steps are undone by compensating transactions. You give up isolation (other transactions see intermediate states) to gain availability.

Choreography Orchestration
Control Each service reacts to events One component tells each service what to do
Coupling Services know event types only Orchestrator knows every participant
Visibility Flow is implicit, hard to see Flow is explicit in one state machine
Good for 2–4 steps, simple flows Many steps, branching, timeouts, human approvals
Tools Kafka topics Temporal, Camunda, a hand-written state table

Design rules: each step is a local ACID transaction; compensations must be idempotent and must be possible (you cannot "un-send" an email — send it last, the "pivot transaction" idea); use semantic locks (status PENDING) so other flows know a record is mid-saga; every message is published with the outbox.

The transactional outbox

The service writes the event as a row in the same local transaction as the business change. Atomicity is now a database guarantee: both or neither. A separate relay reads unsent rows and publishes them. Two relay styles:

  • Polling publisher (what we use): a scheduled query. Simple, no extra infrastructure, adds up to one polling interval of latency.
  • Transaction log tailing / CDC: Debezium reads the PostgreSQL WAL through a logical replication slot and publishes rows. Lower latency, no polling load, but another moving part to operate (and a replication slot that retains WAL if Debezium stops).

RefinePoint: EventPublisher.publish(topic, key, type, payload) builds an EventEnvelope (event id UUID, type, source service, timestamp, payload) and inserts it into outbox_events using the caller's transaction. OutboxRelay sends rows oldest first (ORDER BY seq), waits for each Kafka ack (.get(10, SECONDS)), sets sent_at, and on the first failure records attempts/last_error and stops the batch so later events never overtake an earlier one. Because a commit can fail after Kafka acknowledged, or a relay can crash between send and update, delivery is at least once. Every consumer calls ConsumedEvents.firstTime(consumer, eventId) — an INSERT INTO consumed_events (consumer, event_id) VALUES (?, ?) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING that returns whether one row was inserted — inside its own business transaction, so "record that I handled it" and "do the work" commit or roll back together. A purge job deletes sent events after 7 days and consumed ids after 30.

Idempotency

At-least-once delivery + idempotent consumer = effectively exactly-once processing. Ways to make an operation idempotent:

Technique Example
Dedup table keyed by message id consumed_events (consumer, event_id) primary key
Natural idempotence UPDATE run SET status = 'COMPLETED' WHERE id = ? AND status = 'RUNNING' — second call changes 0 rows
Unique business key UNIQUE (org_id, paddle_subscription_id) + upsert
Idempotency-Key header on APIs Store key + request hash + response; replay the stored response for repeats
Version check Apply event only if event.version > row.version

Kafka's own "exactly-once semantics" (idempotent producer + transactions + read_committed consumers) covers Kafka-to-Kafka pipelines. It does not include your database, which is why the outbox and dedup table are still needed.

21.12 Interview questions and answers

Q1. What is a transaction and what does ACID mean?

A transaction is a unit of work that the database executes as all-or-nothing, isolated from concurrent work and durable once committed. Atomicity: all statements commit or none do. Consistency: declared constraints hold before and after. Isolation: concurrent transactions behave (to a chosen degree) as if run one after another. Durability: a committed change survives a crash because the WAL is flushed at commit. Add the senior nuance: consistency is shared with the application — the database only enforces the rules you declared.

Q2. How does PostgreSQL implement atomicity and isolation without blocking readers?

MVCC. Each row version records the transaction that created it (xmin) and the one that deleted or replaced it (xmax). A snapshot is a list of which transactions were committed when it was taken; a reader sees only versions created by committed-before-snapshot transactions. Writers create new versions, so readers never wait for writers. Rollback just marks the transaction aborted in the commit log. Vacuum later removes dead versions.

Q3. What happens internally when a method annotated with @Transactional is called?

The call hits the Spring proxy, whose TransactionInterceptor reads the method's transaction attributes, asks the PlatformTransactionManager for a transaction (borrowing a connection, setAutoCommit(false), binding it to the thread through TransactionSynchronizationManager), invokes the real method, then commits or rolls back according to the rollback rules, runs synchronization callbacks, unbinds the resources and returns the connection to the pool. Repositories and JdbcTemplate find the bound connection through the thread-local map.

Q4. Which PlatformTransactionManager does Spring Boot configure?

With spring-boot-starter-data-jpa: JpaTransactionManager (which also exposes the JDBC connection, so JdbcTemplate on the same DataSource joins the same transaction). With only JDBC: JdbcTransactionManager (a DataSourceTransactionManager that also translates commit exceptions). With JTA libraries on the classpath: JtaTransactionManager. With R2DBC: R2dbcTransactionManager. If you define several, mark one @Primary or name it in @Transactional("ordersTx").

Q5. What is TransactionSynchronizationManager?

The thread-local registry of the current transaction: bound resources (DataSource → ConnectionHolder, EntityManagerFactory → EntityManagerHolder), registered TransactionSynchronization callbacks, the transaction name, read-only flag, isolation level and whether a real transaction is active. You rarely call it directly, but isActualTransactionActive() and registerSynchronization(...) (for an afterCommit hook) are useful in framework code.

Q6. Why does @Transactional not work when I call the method from the same class?

Because this.method() calls the target object directly, not the proxy, so the interceptor never runs. Fixes: move the method to another bean (cleanest), inject the bean into itself lazily (@Lazy self-reference), use TransactionTemplate around the code, or use AspectJ weaving mode (@EnableTransactionManagement(mode = ASPECTJ)) which weaves the advice into the class bytecode.

Q7. Does @Transactional work on private methods?

No. Proxies (JDK or CGLIB) cannot intercept private methods; CGLIB also cannot override final methods. Since Spring 6.0, protected and package-private methods are intercepted on class-based proxies, but public remains the convention. AspectJ weaving works on any method.

Q8. Should @Transactional go on the controller, service or repository?

The service layer — the transaction boundary is the use case. Controllers should not hold transactions (they do HTTP and serialization work and would keep connections longer); repositories alone are too small (each call would be a separate transaction). Spring Data repositories already have @Transactional(readOnly = true) on reads and @Transactional on writes, which join the service's transaction.

Q9. Explain the seven propagation levels in one breath each.

REQUIRED: join or create. REQUIRES_NEW: always create, suspending any current one. NESTED: savepoint inside the current one, or create. SUPPORTS: join if present, else run without. NOT_SUPPORTED: suspend and run without. MANDATORY: must join, else exception. NEVER: must not be in one, else exception.

Q10. What is the difference between REQUIRES_NEW and NESTED?

REQUIRES_NEW is a separate physical transaction on a separate connection: it commits independently and survives the outer rollback; it cannot see the outer one's uncommitted data. NESTED is a savepoint on the same connection: its rollback undoes only its work, but nothing commits until the outer transaction commits, so an outer rollback undoes the nested work too, and it sees everything the outer transaction did.

Q11. Give real use cases for REQUIRES_NEW.

Audit or security logs that must persist even if the business operation fails ("login failed", "approval rejected by rule"); persisting a failure status for a job before rethrowing; allocating numbers from a counter table without holding the counter lock for the whole outer transaction; claiming a queue item so it is visible immediately. Each one should be short and must not touch rows the outer transaction has locked.

Q12. What can go wrong with REQUIRES_NEW?

Pool deadlock: each thread needs two connections; under load all connections are held by outer transactions and nobody gets an inner one. Self-deadlock: the inner transaction updates a row the outer one locked and waits until lock_timeout. Inconsistency: the inner commit survives an outer rollback, which may be wrong for business data. And it is silently ignored under self-invocation, like every other attribute.

Q13. When does NESTED not work?

With JtaTransactionManager (no savepoints), with JpaTransactionManager when you rely on entity changes (the database rolls back to the savepoint but the persistence context keeps the modified entities and may flush them later), and with drivers that lack savepoint support. With JdbcTransactionManager and plain SQL it is reliable.

Q14. What happens if an inner REQUIRED method throws and the outer method catches the exception?

The inner scope marks the shared transaction rollback-only. The outer method continues and returns normally, the interceptor tries to commit, sees the flag, rolls back and throws UnexpectedRollbackException. The caller sees an exception from a method that "succeeded". Fix by not catching, or by making the inner call REQUIRES_NEW or NESTED, or by removing @Transactional from the inner method if it only validates.

Q15. Which exceptions trigger rollback by default, and why are checked exceptions different?

RuntimeException and Error roll back; checked exceptions commit. The convention comes from EJB: checked exceptions were "application exceptions" (expected outcomes such as InsufficientFundsException), unchecked were system failures. Use rollbackFor = Exception.class, or in Spring 6.2 the global rollbackOn = RollbackOn.ALL_EXCEPTIONS on @EnableTransactionManagement, if your codebase uses checked exceptions for failures.

Q16. Predict the outcome.

@Transactional
public void save(Run r) throws IOException {
    repo.save(r);
    throw new IOException("disk full");
}

The run is committed and the caller gets IOException. Checked exception, default rules. A frequent production bug in file-import code.

Q17. Predict the outcome.

@Transactional
public void approveAll(List<UUID> ids) {
    for (UUID id : ids) {
        try { approver.approve(id); }          // approve() is @Transactional (REQUIRED) and throws for one id
        catch (RuntimeException e) { log.warn("skip {}", id); }
    }
}

Nothing is approved and UnexpectedRollbackException is thrown at the end. The first failure marked the whole transaction rollback-only. To skip bad items, give each item its own transaction (REQUIRES_NEW, or a TransactionTemplate per item called from a non-transactional loop) or use NESTED with JDBC.

Q18. What does readOnly = true actually do?

It is a hint. Spring exposes it as a thread-local flag (useful for routing to replicas). With Hibernate it sets flush mode MANUAL and read-only sessions, so no dirty-check snapshots are kept and nothing is flushed — real memory and CPU savings for large reads. The JDBC connection is set read-only, and with enforceReadOnly Spring issues SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY, after which PostgreSQL rejects writes. It does not lock anything.

Q19. How would you route read-only transactions to a replica?

Use an AbstractRoutingDataSource whose determineCurrentLookupKey() returns replica when TransactionSynchronizationManager.isCurrentTransactionReadOnly() is true, wrapped in a LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy so the physical connection is fetched only at the first statement — after the transaction attributes are known. Warn about replication lag: a user who just saved and immediately reads may not see the change (read-your-writes), so pin those reads to the primary.

Q20. How does the transaction timeout work, and why did my long loop not time out?

Spring stores a deadline and checks it whenever a statement is created through Spring-managed resources (it sets the JDBC query timeout to the remaining time and throws TransactionTimedOutException once exceeded). It never interrupts Java code, so CPU work or an HTTP call between statements is not stopped. For hard limits use PostgreSQL statement_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, and timeouts on the HTTP client itself.

Q21. What isolation level does PostgreSQL use by default, and what does it mean in practice?

READ COMMITTED. Every statement sees a snapshot of data committed before that statement started; two reads in one transaction may differ; rows you update are re-checked against the newest committed version if someone changed them concurrently. Dirty reads never happen in PostgreSQL at any level.

Q22. Explain dirty read, non-repeatable read and phantom read.

Dirty: reading uncommitted data of another transaction. Non-repeatable: reading the same row twice and getting different committed values. Phantom: running the same predicate query twice and getting a different set of rows because of inserts or deletes committed in between. Non-repeatable is about one row's content; phantom is about the membership of a result set.

Q23. What is a lost update and how do you prevent it?

Two transactions read the same value, each computes a new value in the application, and the later write overwrites the earlier one. Prevent with: an atomic SQL update (SET balance = balance - :amt), a pessimistic lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before reading), optimistic locking (@Version), or REPEATABLE READ in PostgreSQL (the second writer gets a serialization error and retries).

Q24. What is write skew? Which isolation level prevents it?

Two transactions read an overlapping set of rows, then each updates a different row so that a combined invariant breaks (two approvers both go off duty; two bookings for the same room inserted after both checked "no overlap"). Snapshot isolation (PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ) allows it because there is no write-write conflict. SERIALIZABLE (SSI) prevents it; so do explicit locks on the rows that represent the invariant, or a constraint (an exclusion constraint for overlapping ranges).

Q25. How does PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ differ from the SQL standard and from MySQL?

The standard allows phantoms at REPEATABLE READ; PostgreSQL does not, because it uses one snapshot for the whole transaction. On a write-write conflict PostgreSQL raises 40001 instead of overwriting. MySQL InnoDB's REPEATABLE READ (its default) gives consistent snapshots for plain reads, but locking reads and updates see the latest data and use gap locks; lost updates are possible with plain read-then-write.

Q26. How does SERIALIZABLE work in PostgreSQL and what must the application do?

It uses Serializable Snapshot Isolation: transactions run on snapshots as in REPEATABLE READ, while PostgreSQL tracks read-write dependencies with predicate (SIRead) locks; when it detects a pattern that could produce a non-serializable result, it aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40001. The application must retry the whole transaction, outside the transactional method. Declaring READ ONLY DEFERRABLE for long reports avoids aborts for them.

Q27. Why can't you retry inside the @Transactional method?

After a serialization failure or deadlock, PostgreSQL has aborted the transaction; every further statement fails with "current transaction is aborted". The retry must start a new transaction, so it belongs in a layer above the proxy: a retrying caller, @Retryable ordered outside the transaction advice, or a loop around TransactionTemplate.execute.

Q28. When would you change the isolation level of a single method?

When an invariant spans several rows and you cannot express it as a constraint or a single atomic statement — for example "total allocated must not exceed budget" across many allocation rows. Options: SERIALIZABLE with retry for that method, or lock the parent budget row with FOR UPDATE and stay at READ COMMITTED. The second is usually simpler and more predictable.

Q29. Can @Transactional(isolation = ...) change the level in the middle of an existing transaction?

No. Isolation applies when a transaction starts. A REQUIRED method joining an existing transaction runs at the outer level; Spring ignores the inner setting (with validateExistingTransaction = true on the manager it throws instead). Use REQUIRES_NEW if the inner work truly needs a different level.

Q30. What is the difference between optimistic and pessimistic locking? When do you use each?

Optimistic: no lock; a version column checked at update time; conflict detected late and handled by retry or by asking the user. Use for low contention and long user think time. Pessimistic: lock the row when reading (FOR UPDATE); conflicts wait. Use for hot rows with short transactions, counters, queues. Many systems use both: optimistic for UI edits, pessimistic for background workers.

Q31. How does @Version work in Hibernate?

Hibernate adds AND version = :old to the UPDATE and sets version = old + 1. If the update count is 0, someone changed or deleted the row: Hibernate throws OptimisticLockException (Spring: ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException). Version can be numeric or a timestamp; numeric is safer. LockModeType.OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT bumps the version even without changes, useful to version an aggregate root when a child changes.

Q32. How do you implement optimistic locking across a REST API?

Return the version as an ETag (or a version field) on GET; the client sends it back in If-Match on PUT/PATCH; the service compares before applying (or sets it on the entity so Hibernate checks it) and returns 412 Precondition Failed or 409 Conflict on mismatch. Without this, two users editing the same reconciliation rules in separate tabs silently overwrite each other — the version check inside one transaction alone does not help because each request loads fresh data.

Q33. Explain SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED.

FOR UPDATE locks the selected rows until the transaction ends; other lockers wait. NOWAIT fails immediately with a lock error instead of waiting — good for user actions where you would rather say "someone else is editing". SKIP LOCKED silently skips rows locked by others — ideal for work queues where any free item will do. SKIP LOCKED gives an inconsistent view by design, so never use it for reports.

Q34. How do you build a job queue on PostgreSQL with multiple instances?

Table of jobs with a status. Each worker, in a short transaction: SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'QUEUED' ORDER BY created_at LIMIT n FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, update them to RUNNING with its instance id and a heartbeat, commit. Run the work outside the transaction. On completion update the status. A reaper requeues or fails rows whose heartbeat is stale. Add an index on (status, created_at); a partial index WHERE status = 'QUEUED' is even better.

RefinePoint: this is exactly run-service and job-service. JobScheduler claims as many due jobs as it has free workers (... AND running_execution_id IS NULL AND (next_run_at <= now() OR retry_at <= now()) ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED), marks each running, and moves its next due time; a watchdog handles timeouts and stale instances; failed attempts retry with doubling backoff. We scale by adding instances.

Q35. Why not do the actual work inside the claim transaction?

The row lock and the connection would be held for the whole run — minutes for a large reconciliation. That pins a pool connection per running job, holds back vacuum, and if the instance dies the lock disappears but nobody can tell whether the work half-happened. Short claim + status column + heartbeat gives visibility and recovery.

Q36. What causes deadlocks and how do you handle them?

Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, usually because they lock the same rows in different orders. PostgreSQL detects the cycle (after deadlock_timeout, default 1 s) and aborts one with 40P01. Handle: lock in a consistent order (sort ids, ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE), keep transactions short, avoid read-then-upgrade patterns, and retry the aborted transaction. Monitor with log_lock_waits = on.

Q37. What is the difference between a row lock and an advisory lock?

Row locks protect rows and are taken by UPDATE, DELETE and FOR UPDATE. Advisory locks are application-defined locks on an arbitrary 64-bit key (pg_advisory_xact_lock(key) released at transaction end, pg_advisory_lock released at session end or explicitly). Use them to serialize an operation that does not map to a single row — RefinePoint's RunWorker takes pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('run-queue')) so only one claimer at a time evaluates per-workspace concurrency caps. Prefer the transaction-scoped form; session-scoped locks leak with pooled connections.

Q38. How does TransactionTemplate compare to @Transactional?

Same transaction manager and semantics; different style. @Transactional is declarative, method-sized and proxy-based (self-invocation pitfalls). TransactionTemplate is explicit, can wrap any block, can be called in a loop to make many small transactions, and its settings can be chosen at runtime. Use it in schedulers, batch loops and infrastructure code; use the annotation for services.

Q39. Why does RefinePoint's OutboxRelay use TransactionTemplate instead of @Transactional?

Because the transaction must be per batch, not per invocation. relay() loops calling tx.execute(status -> sendBatch()) until a batch comes back smaller than 100. Each batch locks at most 100 rows briefly and commits its progress; a failure loses at most one batch's sent_at updates (those events are re-sent — at-least-once). One method-level transaction would lock the whole backlog and roll back all progress on any failure.

Q40. What are the phases of @TransactionalEventListener and their pitfalls?

BEFORE_COMMIT, AFTER_COMMIT (default), AFTER_ROLLBACK, AFTER_COMPLETION. Pitfalls: events published without a transaction are dropped unless fallbackExecution = true; writes in AFTER_COMMIT need REQUIRES_NEW (Spring 6.1 enforces this at startup); AFTER_COMMIT is not durable — a crash between commit and listener loses the side effect; listeners are synchronous unless @Async, so a slow listener delays the HTTP response even though the data is already committed.

Q41. When would you use AFTER_COMMIT listeners instead of the outbox?

For side effects that are cheap to lose or that are local and best-effort: evicting a cache, pushing a WebSocket refresh, incrementing an in-memory metric. Anything another service depends on, or that money or compliance depends on, goes through the outbox.

Q42. Does a transaction propagate to an @Async method or a CompletableFuture?

No. The transaction is bound to the calling thread. The async method runs on a pool thread with no transaction (or its own, if annotated). It may also run before the caller commits, so it might not see the caller's data. Trigger async work after commit (AFTER_COMMIT listener or outbox) and pass ids, not managed entities — entities are tied to the caller's persistence context.

Q43. Do transactions work with virtual threads?

Yes. Thread locals are per virtual thread, so TransactionSynchronizationManager works unchanged. The bottleneck moves to the connection pool: thousands of virtual threads compete for a handful of connections, so add a concurrency limit and keep transactions short. On Java 21, watch for carrier pinning inside synchronized blocks in older drivers; current pgJDBC and HikariCP avoid most of it, and JDK 24 removes the problem for synchronized.

Q44. A service starts failing with "Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms". How do you investigate?

Hikari's pool is exhausted. Check Hikari metrics (hikaricp_connections_active, hikaricp_connections_pending, usage histograms) and enable leakDetectionThreshold to log stack traces of connections held too long. In PostgreSQL, SELECT pid, state, xact_start, query FROM pg_stat_activity ORDER BY xact_start shows long or idle in transaction sessions. Usual culprits: remote calls inside @Transactional, Open Session In View, REQUIRES_NEW under load, a lock wait (one blocked transaction holds a connection and everyone behind it queues), or a pool too small for instances × concurrency. Fix the cause; increasing the pool only moves the bottleneck to the database.

Q45. Why are long transactions harmful in PostgreSQL specifically?

They hold a connection, hold row locks (blocking writers), keep their snapshot's xmin horizon old so vacuum cannot remove dead tuples anywhere in the database (table and index bloat, slower queries), and raise the chance of serialization failures and deadlocks. An idle in transaction session from a buggy client is the worst case. Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and alert on transactions older than a few minutes.

Q46. What is Open Session In View and why disable it?

Spring Boot's default spring.jpa.open-in-view=true registers an interceptor that opens the EntityManager at the start of a web request and closes it at the end, so lazy associations can load during JSON serialization. It hides N+1 queries in the view layer and keeps the persistence context (and typically its connection) for the whole request, including slow serialization or remote calls. Disable it and fetch what the response needs inside the service (fetch joins, entity graphs, DTO projections).

Q47. What is the dual-write problem?

Writing to two systems (database and Kafka, database and a search index, database and another service's API) without a shared transaction. Any ordering leaves a window where one write succeeds and the other does not: events lost, or events describing changes that were rolled back. Solve it by writing to only one system transactionally (outbox, CDC) and propagating asynchronously and idempotently.

Q48. What is 2PC and why do microservices avoid it?

Two-phase commit: a coordinator asks every participant to prepare (durably promise to commit, holding locks), then tells all to commit if all voted yes. It gives atomicity across resources but is blocking (participants hold locks while waiting for the coordinator; a coordinator crash leaves in-doubt transactions), reduces availability (all participants must be up), adds latency, and many systems — Kafka, most SaaS APIs, many managed databases — cannot take part. Microservices prefer eventual consistency with sagas and outboxes.

Q49. Explain the saga pattern. Choreography vs orchestration?

A saga splits a business transaction into local transactions, each followed by an event or command; a failure triggers compensating transactions for completed steps. Choreography: services react to each other's events — low coupling, but the flow is implicit and hard to follow beyond a few steps. Orchestration: a central coordinator (a persisted state machine, or a workflow engine like Temporal or Camunda) sends commands and handles replies, timeouts and compensations — explicit and testable, at the cost of a component that knows every step.

Q50. What are compensating transactions and what makes them hard?

Business-level undo: refund a charge, release a reservation, mark an order cancelled. They are not rollbacks — the original change was visible and may have triggered other effects. They must be idempotent and retryable; some actions cannot be compensated (an email sent, cash dispensed), so order steps so that irreversible ones come last, and use semantic locks (status PENDING) to keep other processes from acting on half-finished data.

Q51. Describe the transactional outbox pattern end to end.

In the same local transaction as the business change, insert the event into an outbox table. A relay (poller or CDC) reads unsent events in order, publishes them to the broker, and marks them sent. Consumers deduplicate by event id because delivery is at least once. You get atomicity between state and event without 2PC, durability of events while the broker is down, and ordering per relay.

Q52. Tell me about the outbox in your project.

"Every RefinePoint service publishes through EventPublisher, which inserts an envelope into outbox_events using the caller's transaction — if the transaction rolls back, there is no event; if Kafka is down, events wait in the table. OutboxRelay runs every second on every instance, locks up to 100 oldest unsent rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so instances never double-send, sends each and waits for the ack, marks it sent, and on the first failure records the error and stops the batch so a later event in that batch cannot overtake an earlier one. Consumers call ConsumedEvents.firstTime(consumer, eventId) — an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING into consumed_events — inside the handler's transaction, so duplicates are ignored atomically. A purge removes sent events after a week and consumed ids after a month. Trade-offs we accepted: up to about a second of latency, at-least-once delivery, and no strict global order — with several instances, relays can hold adjacent batches at the same moment, so consumers must not assume one."

Q53. Why must the dedup insert be in the same transaction as the business update?

If you record the event id in one transaction and do the work in another, a crash between them either loses the work (id recorded, work not done — the redelivery is ignored) or duplicates it (work done, id not recorded). In one transaction both happen or neither does, which is what makes at-least-once delivery safe.

Q54. Polling outbox vs Debezium CDC?

Polling: simple, no extra infrastructure, works with any database, adds polling latency and some query load; ordering and locking are your responsibility. CDC: reads the WAL through a logical replication slot, near-real-time, no polling, preserves commit order, but adds Kafka Connect and Debezium to operate, and a stopped connector makes the slot retain WAL until the disk fills. For a small team, polling is the pragmatic choice.

Q55. What is idempotency and how do you design idempotent APIs?

An operation is idempotent if repeating it has the same effect as doing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by HTTP semantics; POST is not. For POST (payments, run creation), accept an Idempotency-Key header, store it with a hash of the request and the response under a unique constraint, return the stored response for repeats, and reject the same key with a different body. Internally, prefer conditional updates (WHERE status = 'RUNNING') and unique business keys so retries are harmless.

Q56. How do you handle a webhook (e.g., Paddle) that may be delivered twice or out of order?

Verify the signature, then deduplicate by the provider's event id (unique constraint), and apply state changes only if they move the record forward (compare the event's occurred_at or a version with what is stored). Respond 2xx quickly and process asynchronously if processing is slow, since providers retry on timeouts. This is the same idempotent-consumer idea as for Kafka.

Q57. Can Kafka transactions replace the outbox?

No. Kafka transactions make a consume-transform-produce loop atomic within Kafka (offsets and produced messages commit together). They cannot include a PostgreSQL commit. Spring's old ChainedTransactionManager (deprecated) committed the DB and Kafka one after the other, which still leaves a window. The outbox makes the database the single source of truth.

Q58. How do you test transactional behaviour?

Integration tests against a real PostgreSQL (Testcontainers), because H2 differs in locking and isolation. Test rollback paths explicitly (throw from a mocked collaborator and assert nothing was written). Be careful with @Transactional on test classes: Spring rolls the test transaction back at the end, which hides commit-time behaviour (deferred constraints are never checked, AFTER_COMMIT listeners never fire, REQUIRES_NEW writes are not rolled back). For concurrency, start two threads with a CountDownLatch and assert one gets a lock or version conflict.

Q59. Two DataSources in one service — how do transactions work?

Each needs its own transaction manager; @Transactional("reportingTx") picks one. A method annotated for one does not cover statements on the other (those run in auto-commit). There is no atomicity across the two without JTA. Usually the right design avoids needing it: one database per service, or an outbox-style handoff between them.

Q60. "Our nightly import sometimes leaves half the rows and sometimes rolls everything back. Design it properly."

Split the work into chunks with their own short transactions (TransactionTemplate per chunk of 500–1000 rows); track progress in an import-run table (status, last committed chunk, counts, errors); make each chunk idempotent (upsert by business key, or delete-and-reinsert by import id) so a restart can resume; collect bad rows into an error table instead of failing the chunk (or use savepoints per row with JDBC); and publish "import completed" through the outbox only when the final status commits. Spring Batch implements this chunk-oriented pattern with a JobRepository if you want a framework.

22. Spring Security, OAuth2, JWT & Keycloak

A senior security interview rarely stops at "how do you configure JWT in Spring". It moves to where the filter sits, why a request got 401 rather than 403, what the signature on a token proves and does not prove, how you stop tenant A reading tenant B's data, and how you revoke something designed not to be revocable. This chapter builds from the servlet filter upward and ends with OWASP and production practice.

22.1 Architecture: from servlet container to your controller

Spring Security is a chain of servlet filters. The servlet container knows nothing about Spring beans, so a bridge is needed.

  • DelegatingFilterProxy is a plain servlet Filter that looks up a Spring bean by name and delegates to it. It lets a bean take part in the servlet lifecycle.
  • FilterChainProxy holds a list of SecurityFilterChains. It picks the first one whose securityMatcher matches and runs only that chain, then clears the SecurityContext when finished. It also applies HttpFirewall (rejects //, encoded slashes, bad methods).
  • SecurityFilterChain is an ordered list of filters for one kind of request.

The order of the filters that matter:

Order Filter Job
1 SecurityContextHolderFilter Loads the context from the repository (session, or nothing when stateless)
2 HeaderWriterFilter Security headers
3 CorsFilter Answers preflight, adds CORS headers (must come before authentication, preflights carry no credentials)
4 CsrfFilter Checks CSRF token on unsafe methods
5 LogoutFilter Handles logout URL
6 UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter, BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter Authentication mechanisms
7 AnonymousAuthenticationFilter Puts an anonymous token in the context if nobody authenticated
8 ExceptionTranslationFilter Turns security exceptions into 401 (AuthenticationEntryPoint) or 403 (AccessDeniedHandler)
9 AuthorizationFilter Final URL rule check (authorizeHttpRequests)

401 vs 403: AuthenticationException or an access denial for an anonymous user produces 401, meaning "I don't know who you are". AccessDeniedException for an authenticated user produces 403, meaning "I know you, and you may not". Exceptions thrown from a controller or @PreAuthorize must pass back up through ExceptionTranslationFilter; a @ControllerAdvice that catches Exception will swallow them and turn 403 into 500.

SecurityContextHolder

SecurityContextHolder holds a SecurityContext that holds an Authentication (principal, credentials, authorities). The storage strategy decides where:

Strategy Behaviour
MODE_THREADLOCAL (default) One context per thread
MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL Child threads copy it at creation; unsafe with pools because a pooled thread keeps its old context
MODE_GLOBAL One context for the JVM; desktop apps only

Because the default is a thread local, @Async methods and executors lose the user. Wrap the executor in DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor, or use a TaskDecorator that copies and clears the context. WebFlux keeps it in the Reactor context (ReactiveSecurityContextHolder).

22.2 Authentication flow

  • AuthenticationManager has one method: authenticate(Authentication).
  • ProviderManager is the usual implementation. It asks each AuthenticationProvider whose supports(tokenClass) is true; the first success wins. If none succeeds, it tries its parent manager, then throws. It erases credentials from the result.
  • DaoAuthenticationProvider loads a UserDetails and compares the password through PasswordEncoder. To resist username enumeration by timing, it hashes the presented password even when the user does not exist.

Password storage

Never store plain, encrypted or fast-hashed (MD5, SHA-256) passwords. Use a slow, salted, adaptive function.

@Bean PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
    return PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder(); // stores {bcrypt}$2a$10$...
}

A bcrypt string $2a$10$N9qo8uLOickgx2ZMRZoMye... contains the version, the cost (10 means 2^10 rounds) and a 22-character salt, followed by the hash. So no separate salt column is needed. Bcrypt only reads the first 72 bytes of input. OWASP currently prefers Argon2id (memory-hard, resists GPUs) with bcrypt acceptable for existing systems. DelegatingPasswordEncoder stores the algorithm id in {...}, so you can upgrade: verify with the old one, re-hash on next login (UserDetailsPasswordService). Tune the cost so one hash takes about 250 ms on your hardware.

RefinePoint: we store no passwords at all. Keycloak owns credentials, password policy and MFA; our services only see tokens. Reducing what you must protect is the strongest design choice available.

22.3 Authorization

Two layers: URL rules at the filter level and method rules at the proxy level.

@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity
class SecurityConfig {
    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http, KeycloakJwtConverter converter) throws Exception {
        http
            .cors(Customizer.withDefaults())
            .csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable)
            .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/health").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/api/v1/admin/**").hasRole("admin")
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(j -> j.jwtAuthenticationConverter(converter)));
        return http.build();
    }
}

Boot 3 and Security 6 changes interviewers ask about: WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter is gone (declare SecurityFilterChain beans); antMatchers became requestMatchers; authorizeRequests became authorizeHttpRequests (uses AuthorizationManager); @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity became @EnableMethodSecurity with prePostEnabled on by default; lambda DSL replaces .and() chains; the security context is no longer saved automatically (SecurityContextHolderFilter).

hasRole vs hasAuthority: hasRole('admin') looks for the authority ROLE_admin; hasAuthority('ROLE_admin') is the exact string. A role is simply an authority with the prefix.

Method security

Annotation When Example
@PreAuthorize Before the method, SpEL @PreAuthorize("hasRole('admin') or #userId == authentication.name")
@PostAuthorize After, can use returnObject @PostAuthorize("returnObject.ownerId == authentication.name")
@PreFilter / @PostFilter Filter collections @PostFilter("filterObject.public") — loads then filters; use a query instead
@Secured, @RolesAllowed Simple role lists Older or JSR-250

Method security is AOP, so all the proxy rules apply: self-invocation skips the check. SpEL can call any bean with @beanName.method(...), and that is how real permission logic is written. Annotations can be composed into meta-annotations.

@PreAuthorize("@orgAuth.isAdmin()")
@Retention(RUNTIME) @Target(METHOD)
public @interface CanManageOrganization {}

@PreAuthorize("@orgAuth.can('breaks.resolve')")
public void resolve(UUID breakId) { ... }

For object-level rules, the classic extension point is PermissionEvaluator with hasPermission(#id, 'Break', 'resolve'). A named bean like @orgAuth does the same job with less ceremony.

22.4 CSRF, CORS, sessions

CSRF exploits the browser attaching cookies automatically: a malicious page submits a form to your site and the browser adds the session cookie. Defence: a token the attacker's page cannot read (synchroniser token or double-submit cookie), and SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies. Disable it only when the API authenticates with something browsers do not attach automatically, such as Authorization: Bearer or X-API-Key. Keep it on for session cookies, and also if you put a JWT in a cookie, since the cookie brings the same problem back.

CORS relaxes the browser's same-origin policy. The browser sends a preflight OPTIONS for non-simple requests, and the server answers with allowed origin, methods and headers. CORS protects users' browsers, not your server: curl ignores it entirely, so it is not access control. allowedOrigins("*") with allowCredentials(true) is rejected by Spring and browsers. Configure it in Spring Security through .cors(...) so preflights pass before authentication.

Sessions vs stateless:

Server session (JSESSIONID) Stateless token (JWT)
State On server (or Redis) In the token
Revocation Instant: delete the session Hard: valid until expiry
Scale Needs sticky sessions or shared store Any instance can validate
Browser attack surface CSRF XSS if stored in JS-readable storage
Size Small cookie 1–2 KB on every request

22.5 OAuth2 and OpenID Connect

OAuth2 is delegated authorization: letting a client act on a resource with limited rights, without giving it the user's password. Roles: resource owner (the user), client (the app), authorization server (Keycloak), resource server (our API).

Authorization code + PKCE

The default for every user-facing client, including SPAs and mobile apps.

PKCE defeats code interception: a stolen code is useless without the verifier, which never left the client. state stops login CSRF. nonce ties the ID token to this login and stops replay. OAuth 2.1 requires PKCE for all authorization-code clients.

Client credentials

No user. A machine authenticates as itself.

Other grants

Grant Status Note
Authorization code + PKCE Use it Users on any client type
Client credentials Use it Service to service
Device code Use it TVs, CLIs without a browser
Refresh token Use it Rotation: each use issues a new one and invalidates the old; reuse detection kills the family
Implicit Deprecated Tokens in URL fragments leak through history and referrers
Password (ROPC) Deprecated The client sees the password; no MFA

OIDC

OpenID Connect is an authentication layer on OAuth2. With scope=openid the token response also has an ID token: a JWT for the client saying who logged in (sub, name, email, nonce, aud = the client). The access token is for the resource server. Never send an ID token to an API as a credential, and never read user identity in the client from an access token. OIDC also standardises discovery (/.well-known/openid-configuration), the UserInfo endpoint, and JWKS.

22.6 JWT

eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6ImFiYyJ9 . eyJzdWIiOiI0MiIsImV4cCI6MTcwMDAwMDAwMH0 . MEUCIQDf...
└──────────── header ──────────────┘   └────────────── payload ──────────────┘   └ signature ┘
{"alg":"RS256","kid":"abc"}            {"sub":"42","iss":"https://sso/realms/rp",  sign(base64url(header)
                                        "aud":"account","exp":1700000000,                + "." +
                                        "realm_access":{"roles":["admin"]}}              base64url(payload))

It is base64url-encoded, not encrypted: anyone can read it. Signing gives integrity and authenticity, not secrecy. Never put secrets or personal data you would not show the user in it. JWE is the encrypted variant, rarely needed.

HS256 RS256 / ES256
Key One shared secret Private key signs, public key verifies
Who can forge Every service that can verify Only the authorization server
Distribution Secret copied everywhere Public keys over JWKS
Use One service issuing to itself Anything with several services

JWKS (/protocol/openid-connect/certs in Keycloak) publishes public keys, each with a kid. The decoder reads kid from the header, finds the key in its cache, and refetches on an unknown kid. That is how rotation works without downtime: publish a new key, start signing with it, keep the old one until its tokens expire.

Attacks to name: alg: none (accept unsigned tokens); RS256-to-HS256 confusion (attacker signs with the public key as HMAC secret); weak HMAC secrets brute-forced offline; missing aud check, so a token for another API is accepted; kid or jku used to load attacker-controlled keys. Defend by pinning the expected algorithm and validating iss, aud, exp. Spring's NimbusJwtDecoder is keyed to an algorithm and validates exp/nbf with 60 s clock skew and iss when configured through issuer-uri; audience must be added.

The revocation problem: a signed JWT is valid until exp, because no one consults a server. Options, in order of use:

  1. Short access token (5–15 minutes) + refresh token rotation: disabling the user stops refresh, so the exposure is bounded by the access token's life.
  2. Deny-list of jtis in Redis, checked per request, for emergencies. This reintroduces a lookup, but only for a small set.
  3. Token introspection (RFC 7662) or opaque tokens: a server call per request gives instant revocation at a latency and availability cost.
  4. Per-user "tokens valid after" timestamp compared with iat.

Resource server configuration

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://auth.example.com/realms/refinepoint   # discovery, iss validation
          jwk-set-uri: https://auth.example.com/realms/refinepoint/protocol/openid-connect/certs
          audiences: refinepoint

22.7 Keycloak

Concept Meaning
Realm An isolated space of users, clients, roles and keys
Client An application. Public (SPA, no secret, PKCE) or confidential (has a secret; can have a service account for client credentials)
Realm role / client role Global role vs a role scoped to one client; composite roles group others
Group Set of users that inherits roles and attributes
Protocol mapper Decides what goes into tokens: audience, attributes, role claims
Identity brokering Log in through Google, Azure AD, or a corporate SAML/OIDC provider

Roles appear at realm_access.roles and resource_access.<client>.roles. Spring knows neither by default: it maps scope to SCOPE_* authorities only. So you write a converter.

@Component
public class KeycloakJwtConverter implements Converter<Jwt, AbstractAuthenticationToken> {
    @Override public AbstractAuthenticationToken convert(Jwt jwt) {
        return new JwtAuthenticationToken(jwt, extractRealmRoles(jwt));   // realm_access.roles → ROLE_x
    }
}

The old Keycloak Spring adapters are deprecated and removed. Use Spring's standard resource server support and keep services independent of Keycloak's libraries; to them it is just an OIDC provider.

22.8 Multi-tenant authorization

Being logged in says nothing about which workspace you may touch. Broken access control across tenants is the top risk of any SaaS.

RefinePoint: the org code is in the URL (or X-Org-Code on older endpoints). Membership is enforced in one place, OrgAccessInterceptor, so no controller can forget it: reads need any role, writes need at least MEMBER. OrgRole is ordered VIEWER, MEMBER, ADMIN, OWNER with atLeast(...). Finer rules use @PreAuthorize("@orgAuth.can('breaks.resolve')") against the Permissions catalogue, where workspaces can define custom roles and scope process permissions to a group. Realm roles cannot express this, because workspace owners hold no realm role at all. The access decision sits behind a WorkspaceAccess port: identity-service implements it over its tables, every other service uses RemoteWorkspaceAccess, which asks identity-service and caches the answer briefly.

IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference): GET /organizations/ACME/breaks/77, where break 77 belongs to another tenant. The interceptor passes because the caller really is in ACME. The fix is that every query filters by tenant: findByIdAndOrgId(id, orgId), never findById(id). BaseOrgEntity gives every tenant table an org_id. Additional depth: unguessable UUIDs (obscurity only, not a control), PostgreSQL Row-Level Security or a Hibernate @Filter/@TenantId as a safety net. Return 404, not 403, so a caller cannot probe which ids exist.

22.9 API keys, service-to-service auth, webhooks

API keys for machines. Random, high-entropy secret shown once, stored hashed.

RefinePoint: ApiKeyAuthenticationFilter (before BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter) reads X-API-Key. Sending both a key and a bearer token gets a 400. ApiKeyPaths allows workspace endpoints only and forbids /members, /api-keys, /billing, /export and /team, so a leaked key cannot grant itself more access. A valid key becomes a synthetic JwtAuthenticationToken for the creator, limited to the key's workspace and role with no realm roles, so everything downstream works as for a person. Keys are stored as key_hash (SHA-256) plus a key_prefix such as rpk_... for recognising them in lists, with expires_at, last_used_at and revoked_at. A key's role can never exceed its creator's.

Why SHA-256 rather than bcrypt here: passwords are low-entropy, so hashes must be slow to resist guessing. A random 256-bit key cannot be guessed, and it is verified on every request, so a slow hash would only hurt latency.

Service-to-service options:

Option How Trade-off
Shared internal token Header compared in constant time Simple; one secret, no per-service identity
Client credentials Each service gets a JWT from the authorization server Per-service identity and scopes; token management
Forwarding the user token Pass the bearer on Keeps user identity; audience gets broad
mTLS Both sides present certificates (often through a service mesh) Strong identity at transport level; certificate operations

RefinePoint: /internal/** is never routed by the gateway, and InternalTokenFilter requires X-Internal-Token, compared with MessageDigest.isEqual. InternalClient adds it. This is defence in depth on a private network. Client credentials or mTLS would be the upgrade if services stopped sharing a trusted host network.

Webhook signatures. A webhook URL is public, so anyone can POST to it. Verify an HMAC over the raw body before parsing.

// Paddle-Signature: ts=1700000000;h1=<hex> — several h1 values while a secret rotates
if (Math.abs(Instant.now().getEpochSecond() - signedAt) > 300) throw new SecurityException("replay");
String expected = hmacSha256(ts + ":" + payload);
if (signatures.stream().noneMatch(h -> constantTimeEquals(expected, h))) throw new SecurityException("bad signature");

The timestamp inside the signed data stops replays; constant-time comparison stops timing attacks; accepting multiple h1 values allows secret rotation with no downtime.

22.10 OWASP Top 10 for Java developers

OWASP 2021 Java example Defence
A01 Broken access control IDOR, missing tenant filter, @PreAuthorize skipped by self-invocation Deny by default, central checks, scoped queries
A02 Cryptographic failures MD5 passwords, secrets in logs, HTTP bcrypt/Argon2, TLS, AES-GCM
A03 Injection String-concatenated SQL/JPQL, log injection, Log4Shell Bind parameters, whitelist identifiers
A04 Insecure design No rate limit on OTP, no tenant model Threat modelling
A05 Misconfiguration Actuator exposed, default passwords, verbose errors Expose health only, generic errors
A06 Vulnerable components Old Jackson, Log4j, Spring SBOM, Dependabot, dependency-check
A07 Auth failures Weak sessions, no MFA, no lockout OIDC provider, MFA
A08 Integrity failures Native deserialization, unsigned updates Avoid ObjectInputStream, sign artefacts
A09 Logging failures No audit of denials, tokens in logs Audit trail, masking
A10 SSRF Server fetches user URL → 169.254.169.254 cloud metadata Allow-lists, block internal ranges

(The 2025 edition reorders these, folds SSRF into access control and adds supply-chain failures; the 2021 numbering is what most interviewers still quote.)

SQL injection. Parameter binding sends the value separately from the statement, so it is never parsed as SQL. Identifiers (ORDER BY columns) cannot be bound; whitelist them.

jdbc.queryForList("SELECT * FROM breaks WHERE org_id = ? AND status = ?", orgId, status); // safe
"... ORDER BY " + sortParam                                                               // injectable

JPQL string concatenation is equally injectable. Rule languages deserve the same care: compiling user rules to SQL must bind values and validate identifiers, as our SqlCompiler must for DuckDB.

XSS. Untrusted data rendered as HTML runs in the user's session. React escapes by default, except dangerouslySetInnerHTML. Add a strict CSP. For JSON APIs, return the correct Content-Type plus X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.

SSRF.

RefinePoint: users configure webhook URLs and SFTP or database hosts, which the server then contacts. OutboundUrlValidator.requireSafe demands HTTPS, refuses embedded credentials, resolves the host and rejects loopback, private, link-local (the cloud metadata range), multicast, carrier-grade NAT and reserved addresses. The class documents its residual risk, DNS rebinding between check and send: the sender disables redirects, and egress filtering on the host is the complete fix.

Deserialization. ObjectInputStream.readObject instantiates classes before you can check them, so gadget chains on the classpath give remote code execution. Avoid native serialization; use JSON. If forced, ObjectInputFilter (JEP 290) allow-lists classes. In Jackson never use enableDefaultTyping or @JsonTypeInfo(use = CLASS) on untrusted input; use @JsonSubTypes with explicit names. Disable DTDs in XML parsers to stop XXE.

Secrets management. Never in Git or images. Inject through environment or a secret store (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Kubernetes Secrets with encryption at rest), and rotate. Run gitleaks in CI. Treat a committed secret as compromised: rotate first, then clean history.

Rate limiting and brute force. Limit by IP and by identity. Add login lockout or progressive delay, and enable Keycloak's brute-force detection.

RefinePoint: the gateway's RateLimitFilter keeps token buckets in a ConcurrentHashMap, per IP and per caller; a bucket holds a minute's requests and refills evenly; past it comes 429 with Retry-After. Sensitive endpoints add a SlidingWindowLimiter, such as SSO domain lookups at 30 per minute. Both count per instance, which is a safe floor, not an exact global limit. Health checks, preflights and Paddle webhooks are not counted. Address buckets use the connection's remote address, and AuditTrail reads only the X-Real-IP set by nginx; neither reads X-Forwarded-For, which a client can forge.

Security headers. Spring adds by default: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Cache-Control: no-store, X-Frame-Options: DENY, Strict-Transport-Security (HTTPS only). Add yourself: Content-Security-Policy, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy.

22.11 Testing security

@WebMvcTest(BreakController.class)
@Import(SecurityConfig.class)
class BreakControllerTest {
    @Test @WithMockUser(roles = "admin")
    void adminAllowed() throws Exception { mvc.perform(post("/x").with(csrf())).andExpect(status().isOk()); }

    @Test
    void jwtWithRole() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(get("/x").with(jwt().authorities(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_viewer"))))
           .andExpect(status().isForbidden());
    }

    @Test void anonymousRejected() throws Exception { mvc.perform(get("/x")).andExpect(status().isUnauthorized()); }
}

Test the negative cases: anonymous, wrong role, wrong tenant. Every tenant endpoint deserves a test that user A cannot read tenant B's id. @WithSecurityContext builds custom principals. Use SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors for jwt() and csrf().

22.12 Interview questions and answers

Q1. How does a request flow through Spring Security?

The container calls DelegatingFilterProxy, which delegates to the FilterChainProxy bean, which picks the first matching SecurityFilterChain and runs its filters: context load, headers, CORS, CSRF, authentication, anonymous, exception translation, authorization. Then the request reaches DispatcherServlet, interceptors and the controller.

Q2. Why is DelegatingFilterProxy needed?

The servlet container creates filters itself and knows nothing about Spring. The proxy is the container-managed filter; it looks up a Spring bean by name, so the real filter can use dependency injection and the application context lifecycle.

Q3. Can you have multiple SecurityFilterChains?

Yes, and FilterChainProxy uses only the first match, so order them with @Order, specific matchers first. A chain without a securityMatcher matches everything and must be last. RefinePoint has three: public paths (permit all), /internal/** (internal token), and the default (authenticated).

Q4. What is the difference between 401 and 403?

401: not authenticated, or authentication failed; client should authenticate. 403: authenticated but not permitted. ExceptionTranslationFilter picks: AuthenticationEntryPoint gives 401, AccessDeniedHandler gives 403. An access denial for an anonymous user is treated as 401.

Q5. My @PreAuthorize failure returns 500. Why?

A @ControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) caught AccessDeniedException before it reached ExceptionTranslationFilter. Rethrow it or add a specific handler returning 403.

Q6. How is SecurityContextHolder thread-safe?

By default each thread has its own context through a ThreadLocal, and FilterChainProxy clears it at the end of the request, so a pooled thread does not leak it to the next one.

Q7. How do you propagate the security context to @Async methods?

Wrap the executor with DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor, or use a TaskDecorator that captures, sets and clears the context. Avoid MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL with pools: a thread inherits once at creation and keeps stale identity afterwards. New virtual threads also start without it.

Q8. Explain AuthenticationManager, ProviderManager and AuthenticationProvider.

AuthenticationManager is the interface. ProviderManager implements it by delegating to a list of AuthenticationProviders, choosing by supports(), with an optional parent. Each provider handles one mechanism: password, JWT, and so on.

Q9. How do you add a custom authentication mechanism?

Write a filter (OncePerRequestFilter) that extracts the credential and either calls AuthenticationManager with a custom token and provider, or validates directly and sets the context. Insert with addFilterBefore(filter, BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter.class). Do not also register it as a plain @Component without disabling servlet registration, or it runs twice. ApiKeyAuthenticationFilter is ours.

Q10. What is OncePerRequestFilter?

A base class that guarantees a filter runs once per request, even when the request goes through forwards or error dispatches, by marking it with a request attribute. Use it for authentication filters.

Q11. Why bcrypt and not SHA-256 for passwords?

SHA-256 is fast by design, so a GPU tries billions per second. Bcrypt is deliberately slow with a tunable cost and a built-in salt. Salting stops rainbow tables and makes equal passwords hash differently. Argon2id adds memory hardness.

Q12. How do you migrate from MD5 to bcrypt without forcing resets?

Wrap: store bcrypt(md5(password)) for all rows now, marked as legacy. On next login verify the wrapped form, then re-hash the plain password with bcrypt. DelegatingPasswordEncoder with {id} prefixes makes the mix explicit.

Q13. hasRole vs hasAuthority?

hasRole('X') checks for authority ROLE_X; hasAuthority('X') checks the exact string. Mixing them up is the commonest cause of mysterious 403s. Use authorities for fine permissions (SCOPE_read), roles for coarse groups.

Q14. URL security vs method security?

URL rules are coarse, sit at the edge and also cover non-controller paths. Method rules are close to the business action and can inspect arguments. Use both: authenticated by default at the URL level, specifics on methods. Method security alone leaves gaps; URL rules alone miss object-level rules.

Q15. Why does @PreAuthorize not work on an internal call?

It is proxy-based. this.method() bypasses the proxy, so the check never runs and no error appears. Also it needs @EnableMethodSecurity, and the class must be a Spring bean.

Q16. What changed from Spring Security 5 to 6?

WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter removed; SecurityFilterChain beans. requestMatchers replaced antMatchers. authorizeHttpRequests with AuthorizationManager. @EnableMethodSecurity. Security context save is explicit. jakarta.* namespace. CSRF token handling is deferred and BREACH-protected by default. All dispatches are authorized, including FORWARD and ERROR.

Q17. When is it safe to disable CSRF?
