When authentication comes from a credential the browser does not send automatically, such as a bearer header or API key. If a token lives in a cookie, or you use sessions, keep CSRF on. Non-browser-only APIs do not need it.

Q18. CORS vs CSRF?

CORS loosens the same-origin policy so that approved origins can read responses; it is enforced by the browser. CSRF is an attack in which another site triggers an authenticated request. CORS does not stop CSRF: simple cross-site form POSTs are sent without any preflight.

Q19. Why is CORS configured in Spring Security rather than only in MVC?

Preflight OPTIONS requests carry no credentials. If security filters run first they respond 401 and the browser reports a CORS error. .cors(...) installs CorsFilter ahead of authentication.

Q20. Explain OAuth2 roles.

Resource owner: the user who owns the data. Client: the application acting for them. Authorization server: authenticates and issues tokens. Resource server: API that accepts tokens. In RefinePoint: finance user, React app, Keycloak, our services.

Q21. OAuth2 vs OIDC vs SAML?

OAuth2 is delegated authorization, with no standard way to say who the user is. OIDC adds authentication on top with an ID token (JSON/JWT, modern apps). SAML is an older XML-based SSO standard, still common with enterprise identity providers. Keycloak can broker SAML into OIDC for our apps.

Q22. Walk through authorization code + PKCE.

The client makes a random verifier and sends its SHA-256 as a challenge in the authorize redirect. The user logs in; the authorization server returns a one-time code. The client posts the code and the verifier to the token endpoint. The server hashes the verifier, compares it, and issues tokens. Stealing the code alone gets nothing.

Q23. Why are implicit and password grants deprecated?

Implicit returns tokens in the URL, exposing them to history, logs and referrers, with no client authentication and no refresh. Password gives the client the user's password and rules out MFA and federation. Both are removed in OAuth 2.1; code + PKCE replaces both.

Q24. How should a SPA store tokens?

No storage is perfect. localStorage is readable by any XSS. Memory is safer but lost on reload (use silent renew). The strongest option is a Backend-for-Frontend: the server does OAuth and holds tokens, and the browser only has an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite session cookie, which brings CSRF protection back into play.

Q25. Access token vs refresh token vs ID token?

Access: short-lived, for the API. Refresh: long-lived, sent only to the authorization server to get new tokens, stored securely, rotated. ID: for the client, describes the login, never sent to APIs.

Q26. What is refresh token rotation?

Each refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. If an old one is presented again, it means theft, so the server revokes the entire family. This limits the damage of a stolen refresh token.

Q27. What is inside a JWT and is it encrypted?

Header (alg, kid), payload (claims) and signature, base64url-encoded and dot-separated. It is signed, not encrypted: anyone can decode it, but nobody can change it without breaking the signature.

Q28. RS256 vs HS256?

HS256 uses one shared secret, so every verifier can also forge. RS256 signs with a private key and verifies with a public key, so services can verify but never mint. Across microservices use asymmetric keys; ES256 gives smaller signatures.

Q29. How does a resource server verify a token without calling Keycloak on every request?

It fetches public keys once from JWKS and caches them. Verification is a local signature check plus claim checks (exp, iss, aud). It refetches when it sees an unknown kid, which is how key rotation works. If Keycloak is down, valid tokens still work as long as keys are cached.

Q30. How do you revoke a JWT?

You can't directly; design around it. Use short expiry with refresh rotation, a jti deny-list in Redis for urgent cases, a per-user valid-after timestamp, or introspection/opaque tokens where instant revocation matters more than latency. State the trade-off: revocation means bringing state back.

Q31. What claims must you validate?

Signature with a pinned algorithm, exp, nbf, iss, and aud. Spring validates iss and timestamps; aud needs spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.audiences or a custom validator. Skipping aud allows a token issued for another API in the same realm to be used against yours.

Q32. What is the alg: none attack and the key confusion attack?

none: attacker removes the signature and sets alg to none; bad libraries accept it. Confusion: the server expects RS256, but the attacker signs with HS256 using the public key as the secret, and a naive library verifies with it. Fix both by fixing the accepted algorithm on the verifier side and never trusting the header's choice.

Q33. RefinePoint's API key token sets alg: none. Isn't that a vulnerability?

No, because that Jwt object is built in memory by ApiKeyAuthenticationFilter after the key is verified, and is never parsed from a request. The alg: none attack applies to a decoder that accepts tokens from outside; ours accepts only signed tokens through NimbusJwtDecoder. The synthetic token lets downstream code treat keys and users identically. It is a good example of understanding where a rule applies.

Q34. How does Keycloak map to Spring authorities?

Spring's default converter reads only scope/scp into SCOPE_*. Keycloak puts roles in realm_access.roles, so we supply a Converter<Jwt, AbstractAuthenticationToken>. Ours maps each realm role to ROLE_<name> and returns a JwtAuthenticationToken.

Q35. Realm roles or client roles?

Realm roles are global: one per platform concept. Client roles are per application, useful when several apps have separate permission sets. For a SaaS tenant model, neither is enough: tenant roles live in the application's own database, because one user can be OWNER in one workspace and VIEWER in another.

Q36. Why not put tenant roles in the JWT?

The token grows with memberships, role changes lag until the token expires, and the mapping couples Keycloak to business data. Looking up membership per request (cached briefly) gives near-immediate effect. We do that through WorkspaceAccess. The trade-off is a short staleness window from the cache.

Q37. How do you prevent IDOR in a multi-tenant system?

Check membership centrally, then scope every query with the tenant id from the verified context, never with an id from the client alone. Add safety nets (@TenantId, Row-Level Security), tests that try cross-tenant access, and 404 responses. UUIDs help against enumeration but are not authorization.

Q38. Why use an interceptor rather than a filter or @PreAuthorize for org access?

An interceptor runs after authentication, knows the mapped route, and applies automatically to every org-scoped path. A filter is earlier and coarser. Per-method annotations can be forgotten. A central default check plus stricter annotations is "secure by default"; forgetting an annotation then fails closed.

Q39. Can the client just change X-Org-Code to access another tenant?

Changing it is harmless if the server treats it as a claim to verify: OrgAuth and WorkspaceAccess check the caller's role in the named workspace. A header is input, not proof. The vulnerability appears only if code trusts it without checking membership.

Q40. How do you store API keys?

Generate with SecureRandom, show once, store a SHA-256 hash plus a short prefix for display, with expires_at, revoked_at and last_used_at. Scope them narrowly. Compare by hash lookup. Because keys are high-entropy, a fast hash is correct, and bcrypt would add latency per request for no security gain.

Q41. API key vs OAuth client credentials?

API keys are simple and long-lived, with no expiry by default and no standard scopes; they suit customers scripting against you. Client credentials give short-lived tokens, central revocation and scopes, but require the caller to implement a token flow. Many SaaS products offer keys first for adoption.

Q42. Compare options for service-to-service authentication.

Shared token: simplest; a leak compromises everyone. Client credentials: per-service identity with audit, needs an authorization server. Forwarded user token: preserves the user, but with confused-deputy risk if audiences are broad. mTLS: strong transport identity, usually with a mesh such as Istio. Mature setups combine mTLS for "which service" with a JWT for "which user".

Q43. Why compare secrets in constant time?

String.equals exits at the first different character, so response timing leaks how many leading characters were right; attackers can recover a secret byte by byte. MessageDigest.isEqual looks at all bytes.

Q44. How do you verify a webhook, and what are the common bugs?

Compute HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body with the shared secret and compare in constant time; check a signed timestamp for replays; dedupe by event id. Common bugs: hashing re-serialized JSON rather than raw bytes, == comparison, no replay window, no secret rotation support.

Q45. What is SSRF and how do you prevent it?

The attacker makes your server send requests to internal targets (http://169.254.169.254/..., localhost admin ports). Prevent by allowing only HTTPS, resolving and rejecting internal ranges, disabling redirects, and filtering egress at the network level. Resolve-then-connect leaves a DNS-rebinding window, so pin the resolved IP or rely on egress rules.

Q46. How does Java deserialization become RCE?

readObject runs code in classes on the classpath during reconstruction. Chains of existing "gadget" classes end up invoking something dangerous, before your cast ever happens. Avoid native serialization, set ObjectInputFilter, and avoid Jackson polymorphic default typing. Log4Shell was a related lesson: JNDI lookup from a log message loaded remote code.

Q47. How do you prevent SQL injection when the sort column comes from the client?

Bind parameters cannot stand for identifiers. Map the requested name through a whitelist (Map.of("date", "created_at")) and reject others. Spring Data's Sort needs the same care for native queries; JpaSort.unsafe is called unsafe for a reason.

Q48. Where do you keep secrets in a Spring Boot deployment?

Environment variables or mounted files from a secret manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Kubernetes Secrets). In code, reference ${KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_CLIENT_SECRET:} with no real default. Do not log the environment; restrict actuator env. Plan rotation: for example Paddle signature checks accept several h1s during a change.

Q49. How do you protect login from brute force and credential stuffing?

Per-account and per-IP rate limits, progressive delay rather than permanent lockout (a lockout lets an attacker lock victims out), MFA, breached-password checks, identical errors for unknown user and wrong password, CAPTCHA after failures. With Keycloak, enable brute-force detection. At the gateway, per-IP limits cover the rest.

Q50. Which client IP do you use for rate limiting?

One your own infrastructure establishes, never one the client can set. X-Forwarded-For is client-controlled unless every hop rewrites it, and trusting it gives an attacker a fresh rate-limit bucket per request. Our gateway buckets on the connection's remote address, and the audit trail reads X-Real-IP set by nginx. The catch: behind a proxy the raw remote address is the proxy's, so forwarded-header handling must trust only that proxy.

Q51. Why are in-memory rate limits acceptable, and when are they not?

Each instance counts alone, so with N instances the effective limit is up to N times higher. As abuse protection that is a fine floor and needs no extra infrastructure. For contractual quotas or billing use a shared store, such as Redis with an atomic Lua script. Our gateway's buckets are documented as per gateway, and plan limits are enforced separately (PlanLimits).

Q52. Which security headers matter and what do they do?

HSTS forces HTTPS. CSP restricts script sources, the main XSS mitigation. X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff stops MIME sniffing. X-Frame-Options/frame-ancestors stop clickjacking. Referrer-Policy limits URL leakage. Cache-Control: no-store keeps sensitive responses out of shared caches. An embedded app such as a marketplace iframe needs frame-ancestors opened for that host only.

Q53. How do you test security rules?

@WebMvcTest with the security config imported, @WithMockUser, and .with(jwt())/.with(csrf()) post-processors. Prove the negatives: anonymous gets 401, wrong role 403, wrong tenant 404. Add a route inventory test asserting that every mapped endpoint requires authentication unless listed public, so a new endpoint cannot be accidentally open.

Q54. @WithMockUser passes but production returns 403. Why?

@WithMockUser bypasses token conversion, so a bad Converter or claim shape is never tested. Authorities may be ROLE_admin in the test but SCOPE_x in production. Use jwt().jwt(j -> j.claim("realm_access", ...)) with the real converter, or a Testcontainers Keycloak integration test.

Q55. Design authentication and authorization for a new multi-tenant SaaS.

OIDC provider, authorization code + PKCE for the UI, stateless resource servers validating RS256 tokens with JWKS. Tenant in URL path; central interceptor for membership; role and permission table per tenant; org_id on every table and in every query; API keys hashed, scoped and excluded from admin paths; services authenticated on internal routes; webhook HMAC; gateway rate limits; outbox-backed audit trail. This is RefinePoint's shape, and each choice has a trade-off you can explain.

Q56. A JWT was leaked in logs. What do you do?

Treat it as compromised until expiry. If short-lived, wait or add its jti to a deny-list; if a refresh token leaked, revoke its session in Keycloak. Fix log masking, purge logs, check access by that token through the audit trail, and consider rotating signing keys only if a key itself leaked. Rotating the key logs everyone out.
